e: LDA is a strong, bulky, non-nucleophilic base that removes alpha protons quickly and cleanly without attacking the carbonyl carbon itself, driving deprotonation essentially to completion at low temperature.

q: An enol is best described as which of the following?
e: Keto-enol tautomers differ only in the position of a proton and a double bond: the keto form has C=O and a C-H at the alpha carbon, while the enol form has C=C-OH. They are neutral isomers, not charged species.

q: An enolate anion is the resonance-stabilized species formed by removing a proton from the carbonyl oxygen itself, not from the alpha carbon.
e: An enolate is formed by removing an alpha C-H, not an O-H; a simple ketone or ester typically has no O-H to remove in the first place. The resulting negative charge is then delocalized onto oxygen by resonance.

q: Benzaldehyde (PhCHO) cannot form a simple enolate at the position where its carbonyl is attached to the ring because:
e: The 'alpha carbon' on the aryl side of PhCHO is part of the aromatic ring; removing a ring C-H there would destroy aromaticity and is not the kind of alpha-deprotonation relevant to enolate chemistry, so PhCHO's only true alpha hydrogens would have to come from an alkyl substituent, which it lacks.

q: A much stronger base is required to deprotonate an alpha carbon than to deprotonate the O-H of an alcohol because:
e: Even though both deprotonations are stabilized somewhat by electronegative oxygen, the alcohol O-H is still considerably more acidic, so only a weak-to-moderate base is needed there, while alpha C-H deprotonation needs a much stronger base such as an amide base.

q: Between the two major resonance structures of an enolate, which one is generally considered the larger contributor to the true structure?
e: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it stabilizes negative charge better, making the oxygen-centered resonance form the greater contributor even though many enolate reactions proceed through the carbon end as the nucleophile.

q: Rank these from most acidic to least acidic: (A) an alpha C-H of acetone (pKa about 20), (B) an alpha C-H of ethyl acetoacetate (pKa about 11), (C) a vinylic C-
e: Ethyl acetoacetate's central CH2 sits between a ketone and an ester carbonyl, giving it two stabilizing resonance pathways and a much lower pKa than acetone's single-carbonyl-stabilized alpha H, while a vinylic C-H has essentially no special stabilization and is among the least acidic C-H bonds listed.

q: Diethyl malonate's alpha CH2 (flanked by two ester carbonyls) has a pKa of about 13, which is noticeably higher (less acidic) than a 1,3-diketone's central CH2
e: In an ester, resonance donation from the alkoxy oxygen competes with the carbonyl's ability to stabilize an adjacent negative charge, making ester groups somewhat less effective than ketone carbonyls at lowering alpha C-H pKa, which is why malonates (two esters) are less acidic than 1,3-diketones (two ketones).

q: A nitrile group (C≡N) adjacent to a CH2, as in a beta-ketonitrile, can also help stabilize an alpha carbanion by resonance delocalization into the nitrile, simi
e: Nitriles, like carbonyls, have a pi system into which a negative charge on the adjacent carbon can be delocalized, so alpha hydrogens next to a nitrile are likewise more acidic than ordinary alkane C-H bonds, though typically less so than those next to a ketone.

q: Why does an ester's alpha C-H (pKa about 25) tend to be less acidic than a ketone's alpha C-H (pKa about 20), even though both groups contain a carbonyl?
e: The same resonance donation from the ester's -OR oxygen that makes ester carbonyls less electrophilic toward nucleophiles also makes them somewhat less effective at stabilizing an adjacent carbanion than a ketone carbonyl is.

q: A carboxylic acid's own O-H proton is far more acidic (pKa about 4-5) than its alpha C-H (pKa about 25-30), so under mild base, deprotonation occurs at the O-H,
e: Carboxylic acids have two acidic sites, but the O-H is dramatically more acidic because its conjugate base (carboxylate) is stabilized by two equivalent resonance structures with the negative charge shared between both oxygens; a much stronger base is needed to reach the alpha carbon, and the carboxylate must usually be protected or already formed first.

q: In 2-methylcyclohexanone, how many distinct alpha carbons bear alpha hydrogens available for enolate formation?
e: The carbonyl of cyclohexanone is flanked by two different alpha carbons, C2 and C6. Putting a methyl on C2 still leaves one alpha hydrogen there, and C6 still has two, so enolization can happen on either side. Watch what that does to C2: it is a stereocenter in the ketone, and forming the enolate on that side flattens the carbon and destroys the stereocenter, which is why alpha stereocenters racemize under base.

q: Why is a nitro group (-NO2) an especially strong activator of an adjacent alpha C-H's acidity, often outperforming even two ketone carbonyls?
e: Like a carbonyl, the nitro group has resonance forms that can accept and stabilize a developing negative charge on the adjacent carbon, making nitroalkane alpha hydrogens strongly acidic despite nitro not being a classic carbonyl-type carbon.

q: A compound with alpha hydrogens flanked by a ketone on one side and a nitrile on the other would be expected to have alpha C-H acidity roughly comparable to a s
e: A nitrile does provide meaningful resonance stabilization of an adjacent carbanion (just generally less than a carbonyl), so a beta-ketonitrile's alpha C-H is typically considerably more acidic than a simple ketone's (often in the pKa 9-13 range), not merely equal to it.

q: Why can triethylamine (a weak, non-bulky amine base, pKa of conjugate acid about 10-11) only partially and reversibly deprotonate a simple ketone's alpha carbon
e: Acid-base equilibria favor the side with the weaker acid and weaker base; since a 1,3-diketone is more acidic than triethylammonium, its deprotonation is favorable, but a simple ketone is less acidic than triethylammonium, so that deprotonation is unfavorable and only a small equilibrium concentration of enolate forms.

q: Sodium hydroxide (pKa of water, conjugate acid, about 15.7) is commonly used to generate useful concentrations of a 1,3-diketone's enolate, but would be a poor
e: Because a 1,3-diketone's pKa (~9-11) is well below water's pKa (~15.7), hydroxide readily and nearly completely deprotonates it; a monoketone's pKa (~20) is well above water's pKa, so hydroxide deprotonates it to only a tiny, unfavorable extent, illustrating why base strength must be matched to the acidity of the specific alpha hydrogens involved.

q: An alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone (an enone) can, under basic conditions, form an extended dienolate by losing a hydrogen from the gamma carbon rather than from
e: Number the enone out from the carbonyl: C1 is the carbonyl carbon, C2 is alpha, C3 is beta and C4 is gamma. Taking the gamma hydrogen gives the extended dienolate, an anion delocalized along O-C1-C2-C3-C4 with its charge density on the oxygen, on C2 and on C4 - including the carbon that was just deprotonated. Deprotonating the alpha-prime carbon on the other side of the carbonyl gives the cross-conjugated dienolate instead, and the two names are not interchangeable.

q: Why is it generally true that an alpha carbon bonded to a quaternary (fully substituted) adjacent carbon can still have acidic alpha hydrogens, but a carbon wit
e: Enolate formation requires removing an actual hydrogen from the alpha carbon; if that specific carbon has been substituted until it bears no hydrogens (as in a ketone with a fully branched alpha carbon), there is no alpha C-H to remove at that position, regardless of what is going on elsewhere in the molecule.

q: Between the alpha hydrogens of acetophenone (PhCOCH3, on the methyl side) and the alpha-like aromatic hydrogens of the phenyl ring, only the methyl hydrogens ar
e: Only the sp3 CH3 carbon attached to the carbonyl is the true alpha carbon capable of forming a resonance-stabilized enolate; the ring carbon on the other side of the carbonyl is aromatic and its hydrogens are not involved in this kind of carbonyl-stabilized deprotonation.

q: Consider 1,3-cyclohexanedione. Explain why its pKa (around 5-6) is even lower than that of an acyclic 1,3-diketone like 2,4-pentanedione (pKa around 9).
e: Cyclic 1,3-diketones such as 1,3-cyclohexanedione are known to be notably more acidic than their open-chain counterparts, partly because the enol tautomer is particularly stable and well-conjugated in the ring, pulling the equilibrium and making the corresponding proton unusually easy to remove.

q: If you compare the alpha hydrogens of a ketone to a secondary amide's alpha hydrogens, which is generally more acidic?
e: Nitrogen is a better pi-donor than oxygen, so amide resonance (donation of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl) is even stronger than the ester case, making amide carbonyls notably less effective at stabilizing an adjacent alpha carbanion, which is why amide alpha C-H bonds are less acidic (pKa often above 30) than ketone alpha C-H bonds.

q: Which compound has no alpha hydrogens at all, and so can never form an enolate?
e: The one alpha carbon of 2,2-dimethylpropanal is the quaternary carbon, and it carries no hydrogen. The CHO hydrogen sits on the carbonyl carbon itself rather than next to it, so it is not an alpha hydrogen and it is not acidic. Each of the other three has a CH3 or a CH2 bonded straight to the carbonyl carbon.

q: How many hydrogens of 3-methylbutan-2-one, CH3COCH(CH3)2, are exchanged for deuterium when it is stirred in D2O with a trace of NaOD?
e: Exchange happens through the enolate, so only alpha hydrogens exchange. The two alpha carbons are the CH3 on one side, with three hydrogens, and the CH on the other, with one: four in total. The two methyls of the isopropyl group are beta, one bond too far from the carbonyl, and they stay as they are.

q: (R)-3-Phenylbutan-2-one, PhCH(CH3)COCH3, is stirred with a catalytic amount of NaOH and then recovered. What is observed?
e: The stereocenter is the alpha carbon. Forming the enolate makes that carbon sp2 and flat, and reprotonation happens on either face with equal probability, so the product is a 50:50 mixture. Note what does not happen: a clean inversion. A planar intermediate gives racemization, not inversion.

q: Ethyl acetoacetate, CH3COCH2CO2Et, is treated with one equivalent of sodium ethoxide. Which proton comes off?
e: The central CH2 is alpha to both carbonyls, so its anion delocalizes into two of them at once: pKa about 11, against about 20 for the terminal methyl. The OCH2 hydrogens are on a carbon bonded to oxygen rather than to a carbonyl carbon, so they are not alpha and not acidic. Ethoxide, whose conjugate acid is pKa 16, takes the pKa 11 proton essentially completely and leaves everything else alone.

q: An aldol reaction forms a bond between:
e: The aldol reaction is an enolate (nucleophile, from one carbonyl’s alpha carbon) attacking the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of a second molecule, forming a new C–C bond and a beta-hydroxy carbonyl.

q: An aldol condensation gives (E)-2-methylpent-2-enal as the only product. Which single aldehyde, warmed with dilute NaOH, produces it?
e: Work the condensation backwards. Put water back across the C2=C3 double bond, OH onto C3 and H onto C2, which gives 3-hydroxy-2-methylpentanal. Now cut the C2-C3 bond, the only bond an aldol makes: the alpha fragment keeps the CHO and its methyl and takes a hydrogen back, giving CH3CH2CHO, and on the beta fragment the OH becomes a C=O, giving CH3CH2CHO again. Two propanals, three carbons each, account for the five-carbon chain and its methyl branch.

q: In a crossed (mixed) aldol reaction between two different carbonyl compounds, what is the main practical challenge?
e: With two different carbonyls that can each form enolates and each act as electrophiles, an uncontrolled mixed aldol gives up to four possible products — selectivity requires strategies like using one component in excess or pre-forming one enolate completely before adding the other carbonyl.

q: In a base-catalyzed aldol reaction, the nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl carbon of the second molecule is:
e: Base removes an alpha hydrogen to generate a resonance-stabilized enolate, and it is the nucleophilic alpha carbon of that enolate that attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of a second molecule of aldehyde or ketone.

q: The direct product of an aldol addition (before any dehydration) is classified structurally as a:
e: The new C-C bond forms between the alpha carbon of one molecule and the carbonyl carbon of the other; after protonation, that carbonyl carbon now bears an -OH group that is beta (two carbons away) to the remaining carbonyl group, giving a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound.

q: An aldol addition reaction is reversible under the basic or acidic conditions typically used to carry it out.
e: Both the enolate (or enol) formation step and the C-C bond-forming addition step are equilibria; the aldol product can revert to starting materials (a retro-aldol), which is part of why the overall process is often driven toward completion by subsequent dehydration.

q: Heating an aldol addition product (a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound) under acidic or basic conditions typically leads to:
e: The beta hydroxyl sits one carbon away from an acidic alpha C-H, so water is lost across the alpha-beta bond. Under base that is an E1cb: the alpha proton comes off first and the enolate left behind expels hydroxide. Under acid it runs through the enol instead, whose C=C pushes the protonated hydroxyl out as water. Either route ends at a conjugated alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl, and that conjugation is the payoff that makes an otherwise unpromising elimination worth doing.

q: The overall dehydration step following an aldol addition is favorable largely because the resulting C=C double bond becomes conjugated with the carbonyl group.
e: Conjugation between the new alkene and the carbonyl group extends pi overlap and lowers the overall energy of the product, providing a thermodynamic driving force for elimination of water even though the beta-hydroxy ketone itself is a stable, isolable compound.

q: Under strongly acidic conditions, the first step of an acid-catalyzed aldol reaction (before enol formation) is:
e: In acid-catalyzed mechanisms, the carbonyl oxygen is protonated first, which both activates the carbonyl carbon toward nucleophilic attack and increases the acidity of the adjacent alpha hydrogens, facilitating enol formation in the next step.

q: Heptanedial, OHC-(CH2)5-CHO, is warmed with dilute NaOH. What is the intramolecular aldol condensation product?
e: Number the chain C1 to C7 with the two CHO carbons as C1 and C7. The alpha carbons are C2 and C6, equivalent by symmetry, so take the C2 enolate. C2 attacks C7 and the ring that closes is C2-C3-C4-C5-C6-C7, six atoms, which is one of the two sizes that close readily. Protonation gives 2-hydroxycyclohexane-1-carbaldehyde, and warming eliminates water across the alpha-beta bond, putting the new C=C inside the ring and in conjugation with the CHO.

q: Using an aldehyde that lacks any alpha hydrogens (such as benzaldehyde or formaldehyde) together with a ketone that does have alpha hydrogens is a common strate
e: Because the alpha-hydrogen-free partner cannot form its own enolate, it can only act as the electrophile, while the other carbonyl compound's enolate is the only nucleophile available, greatly simplifying the reaction to essentially one major crossed product.

q: An intramolecular aldol reaction, used to build rings, is most favorable when it forms a ring of what typical size range?
e: As with most ring-forming reactions, five- and six-membered rings form fastest and most favorably due to good orbital alignment and minimal strain, so intramolecular aldol (and aldol condensation) reactions are typically designed to close five- or six-membered rings.

q: A chemist treats excess acetone with a catalytic amount of base. What is the immediate aldol addition product before any dehydration?
e: Acetone's enolate attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second acetone molecule; after protonation, the product is a beta-hydroxy ketone known as diacetone alcohol, which can later be dehydrated (with acid and heat) to the conjugated enone mesityl oxide.

q: Which best describes why an aldehyde is generally a better electrophile in an aldol reaction than a ketone, all else being equal?
e: The same steric and electronic factors that make aldehydes more reactive toward nucleophiles in general (less crowding, less alkyl-group electron donation stabilizing the carbonyl) also make them better electrophilic partners in aldol addition.

q: In a directed (controlled) crossed aldol strategy, a chemist often first converts one carbonyl compound completely into its enolate using a strong base like LDA
e: By using excess strong base to exclusively deprotonate the first compound before the second carbonyl compound is even present, the chemist avoids having two competing enolates form simultaneously, which otherwise leads to an uncontrolled mixture of self- and cross-aldol products.

q: An intramolecular aldol condensation of hexanedial (a six-carbon dialdehyde) under basic conditions is a key step used to build which type of product?
e: A dicarbonyl compound can undergo intramolecular aldol addition when one end's enolate attacks the other end's carbonyl, closing a ring; subsequent dehydration under the reaction conditions gives a cyclic, conjugated unsaturated carbonyl compound, a classic ring-annulation strategy.

q: The retro-aldol reaction (the reverse of aldol addition) is favored by which set of conditions?
e: Because aldol addition is an equilibrium, heating a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound with base (especially when the forward dehydration pathway is blocked, such as when there is no alpha-H available for elimination) can drive the reverse C-C bond cleavage, regenerating the two original carbonyl compounds.

q: A beta-hydroxy ketone that has no hydrogen on the alpha carbon - the one lying between the carbonyl and the hydroxyl-bearing beta carbon - generally cannot unde
e: The standard base-mediated elimination removes an alpha hydrogen (beta to the leaving hydroxyl, which is activated by the adjacent carbonyl) while the hydroxyl group departs; if that specific alpha hydrogen is absent, the usual E1cb route to the enone is blocked.

q: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of an aldol product does not pass through a free carbocation. What pushes the protonated beta hydroxyl out as water?
e: Under acid there is no strong base in the flask, so the molecule tautomerizes to its enol first. Protonating the beta hydroxyl turns it into water, a real leaving group, and the enol C=C pushes in as the water departs, so the departure is assisted and no cation is ever free. Losing the enol OH proton at the end restores the C=O and leaves the conjugated enone. A cation on the beta carbon would in fact be destabilized, not stabilized: it sits two atoms from a strongly electron-withdrawing carbonyl that has no pi density to lend it.

q: When comparing an aldol addition performed under acidic versus basic conditions, the key mechanistic difference is that the acid-catalyzed pathway proceeds thro
e: Under acid catalysis, only a small, neutral equilibrium concentration of the enol tautomer (not a charged enolate) acts as the nucleophile toward a protonated, activated carbonyl electrophile; under base catalysis, a genuine enolate anion is generated and attacks a neutral carbonyl electrophile.

q: Cyclohexanone and 4-methylbenzaldehyde are stirred together with NaOH and heated. What is the major product?
e: 4-Methylbenzaldehyde has no alpha hydrogens, so it can only be the electrophile, and cyclohexanone supplies the enolate. The new bond forms at cyclohexanone's alpha carbon, and heat then dehydrates the addition product to put the new C=C in conjugation with both the ketone and the ring, which is why a condensation like this one is hard to stop at the addition stage.

q: A student proposes that the aldol reaction and the Claisen condensation are mechanistically identical in every step, including the final fate of the tetrahedral
e: Both reactions begin the same way, with an enolate attacking a carbonyl to give a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, but what happens next differs: an aldehyde or ketone electrophile has no good leaving group so the intermediate is simply protonated (giving a hydroxyl), while an ester electrophile has an alkoxide leaving group that is expelled to regenerate a carbonyl, which is the defining difference between aldol addition and Claisen condensation.

q: Explain why treating an unsymmetrical ketone like 2-butanone with base in a self-aldol reaction can, in principle, generate a complex mixture of products even w
e: Because 2-butanone is unsymmetrical, it has two distinct alpha carbons (the methyl and the ethyl side), each capable of forming its own enolate; each of those enolates can then add to the single type of carbonyl carbon present, generating several regiochemically distinct beta-hydroxy ketone products rather than one clean outcome.

q: In an intramolecular aldol condensation used for ring synthesis, forming a five- or six-membered ring is strongly favored, but if a substrate's connectivity wou
e: When a dicarbonyl substrate offers more than one combination of enolizable alpha carbon and electrophilic carbonyl, the pathway that leads to the favorable five- or six-membered ring is strongly preferred over one that would form a strained or entropically unfavorable ring, so the reaction effectively self-selects the better regiochemical outcome.

q: An aldol product that still has the alpha hydrogen E1cb needs will not dehydrate, even on prolonged heating with base: its carbonyl and beta-hydroxyl sit on a b
e: Dehydrating an aldol always puts the new C=C between the alpha and the beta carbon, so it is conjugated with the carbonyl by construction - that is never what goes wrong. What can stop it is geometry: at the bridgehead of a small bicycle the two p orbitals are held perpendicular and no pi bond can form. When an aldol condensation fails, look for a geometric obstruction rather than an electronic one.

q: A crossed aldol reaction between an aromatic aldehyde (no alpha hydrogens, such as benzaldehyde) and acetone under basic conditions, followed by dehydration, ty
e: Acetone is the only partner able to form an enolate (benzaldehyde has none), so its enolate selectively attacks the aldehyde carbonyl; subsequent base- or heat-promoted dehydration gives a conjugated aryl enone, a classic and reliable crossed aldol condensation outcome.

q: A chemist wants to isolate the aldol addition product (beta-hydroxy ketone) without any dehydration occurring. Which set of conditions is most appropriate?
e: Dehydration of the aldol product generally requires more vigorous conditions (heat, stronger acid or base, or longer times) than the initial addition step, so keeping conditions mild and the reaction time short allows the kinetically formed beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound to be isolated before the thermodynamically favored elimination occurs.

q: Why is it generally true that an aldol condensation product (the dehydrated enone) cannot undergo a simple retro-aldol reaction to regenerate the original two c
e: The retro-aldol mechanism specifically relies on the beta-hydroxy group and the adjacent carbonyl to drive C-C bond cleavage back to two carbonyl fragments; once dehydration has occurred and that hydroxyl is gone, replaced by a C=C double bond, the structural feature required for straightforward retro-aldol cleavage is no longer present.

q: Two equivalents of acetaldehyde undergo a base-catalyzed aldol reaction followed by dehydration. What is the final condensation product?
e: Acetaldehyde's enolate attacks the carbonyl of a second acetaldehyde molecule to give 3-hydroxybutanal, which readily dehydrates under the reaction conditions (conjugation with the aldehyde provides the driving force) to give the alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehyde crotonaldehyde.

q: (E)-2-Methylpent-2-enal, CH3CH2CH=C(CH3)CHO, is an aldol condensation product. Which single aldehyde, condensed with itself, gives it?
e: Put the water back across the C=C - OH on the beta carbon, H on the alpha - and then cut the alpha-beta bond, which is the only bond the aldol made. Both halves come out as CH3CH2CHO, so propanal acted once as the nucleophile and once as the electrophile. Counting carbons is the quick check: two three-carbon molecules give the six carbons of the product, because a condensation loses only water.

q: A Claisen condensation is essentially an aldol-type reaction between two:
e: Claisen condensation is the ester analog of the aldol: an ester enolate attacks a second ester’s carbonyl carbon, and the tetrahedral intermediate expels an alkoxide (acyl substitution) rather than just forming an alcohol.

q: Unlike the aldol reaction, the Claisen condensation product loses a leaving group because:
e: Because the electrophile is an ester (with an OR leaving group attached), the tetrahedral intermediate collapses by expelling alkoxide, giving a β-ketoester rather than a β-hydroxy product.

q: What is the key thermodynamic driving force that pulls a Claisen condensation to completion, even though the starting ester enolate equilibrium is unfavorable?
e: The β-ketoester product has a doubly-stabilized, very acidic alpha proton; its deprotonation by excess alkoxide base is essentially complete, continuously removing product and driving the overall equilibrium toward completion.

q: The classic Claisen condensation of ethyl acetate with sodium ethoxide produces which well-known beta-ketoester product?
e: Two molecules of ethyl acetate combine: one is deprotonated at its alpha carbon by ethoxide to form an enolate, which attacks the carbonyl of a second ethyl acetate molecule; loss of ethoxide from the tetrahedral intermediate gives ethyl acetoacetate, a classic beta-ketoester.

q: The base typically used in a classic Claisen condensation, such as sodium ethoxide, must match the ester's alkoxy group (for example, NaOEt with an ethyl ester)
e: If the alkoxide base differs from the ester's own alkoxy group, it can also act as a nucleophile toward the ester carbonyl (transesterification) or get incorporated into the leaving group step, complicating the product mixture; matching the base to the ester's OR group avoids this issue.

q: A Claisen condensation between two molecules of ethyl acetate, when performed with only a catalytic (substoichiometric) amount of sodium ethoxide, can still pro
e: False. The final deprotonation - the step that drives the whole reaction - takes a full equivalent of alkoxide and does not give it back until the acidic workup, because the product is held as its enolate until then. A catalytic amount of base would therefore drive only a catalytic amount of product. This is the most common misconception about the reaction, and it is why calling a Claisen base-catalyzed is imprecise.

q: To isolate the neutral beta-ketoester product at the end of a Claisen condensation, which final step is necessary?
e: The reaction mixture at the end of a Claisen condensation contains the sodium salt of the acidic beta-ketoester (since it was deprotonated in the final, driving step); an acidic aqueous workup is required to protonate this enolate and recover the neutral beta-ketoester product.

q: An ester that has no alpha hydrogens at all, such as ethyl benzoate, can still act as the nucleophile in a Claisen-type condensation by forming its own enolate.
e: An ester with no alpha hydrogens cannot be deprotonated to form an enolate, so it cannot serve as the nucleophile in a Claisen condensation; it can, however, still act as the electrophile if combined with a different ester or ketone that does have alpha hydrogens, a strategy used in crossed Claisen condensations.

q: Which intermediate is common to both the aldol reaction and the Claisen condensation mechanism?
e: Both reactions begin identically: an enolate nucleophile attacks an electrophilic carbonyl carbon, generating a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. What happens to that intermediate next (simple protonation versus expulsion of a leaving group) is what differentiates the aldol reaction from the Claisen condensation.

q: In a crossed (mixed) Claisen condensation designed to give a single clean product, one common strategy uses an ester that lacks alpha hydrogens (such as ethyl b
e: Just as in a crossed aldol reaction, removing the possibility that one partner forms its own competing enolate (because it has no alpha hydrogens to deprotonate) simplifies the reaction to one dominant enolate attacking one dominant electrophile, favoring a single crossed product.

q: Why is diethyl carbonate, (EtO)2C=O, a useful electrophilic partner in a crossed Claisen-type reaction used to install a -CO2Et (carboethoxy) group onto a keton
e: Because diethyl carbonate has no alpha hydrogens, it cannot compete as a nucleophile; its carbonyl carbon, flanked by two good ethoxide leaving groups, is an excellent electrophile for a ketone enolate, and after loss of one ethoxide the product is a beta-ketoester with a new -CO2Et group on the original ketone's alpha carbon.

q: Ethyl acetoacetate (the Claisen condensation product of ethyl acetate) has a pKa for its central CH2 of about 11, much lower than the starting ester's own alpha
e: The dramatic pKa drop from starting ester to beta-ketoester product means the ethoxide base can essentially completely deprotonate the product (but only poorly deprotonates the starting ester), and it is exactly this favorable, essentially complete final deprotonation that pulls the whole multistep equilibrium toward product formation.

q: An intramolecular Claisen condensation, known as a Dieckmann condensation, is used to form which type of product?
e: The Dieckmann condensation is the intramolecular version of the Claisen condensation: a diester's enolate at one end attacks the ester carbonyl at the other end of the same molecule, expelling an alkoxide and closing a ring to give a cyclic beta-ketoester, typically favoring five- or six-membered rings.

q: If a Claisen condensation is attempted using only enough base to deprotonate a small equilibrium amount of the starting ester's alpha hydrogen, and the beta-ket
e: By Le Chatelier's principle, continuously removing product from an equilibrium (whether by the final deprotonation step under normal conditions or by any other means of product removal) pulls the preceding unfavorable equilibrium (enolate formation and addition) toward producing more product, even if the concentration of the key intermediate at any instant is small.

q: A mixed Claisen condensation between an ester and a ketone (both bearing alpha hydrogens) is often designed so the ketone's enolate is the nucleophile attacking
e: In a mixed Claisen-type reaction between an ester and a ketone, it is advantageous to use conditions where the more easily and more completely formed ketone enolate serves as nucleophile and attacks the ester (which offers an alkoxide leaving group for a clean addition-elimination), giving a good route to a beta-ketoester while avoiding excessive self-condensation of the ketone.

q: Why does a Dieckmann condensation typically fail (or give poor yields) when the diester substrate's chain length would force formation of a three- or four-membe
e: As with other intramolecular ring-closing reactions, the Dieckmann condensation is strongly biased toward forming the kinetically and thermodynamically favorable five- and six-membered rings; substrates geometrically constrained to form much smaller (strained) or much larger (entropically costly) rings react far less efficiently or not at all under standard conditions.

q: In a Claisen condensation mechanism, after the ester enolate attacks the second ester's carbonyl carbon to form the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, what dete
e: The tetrahedral intermediate can revert to starting esters or go forward to expel the ethoxide leaving group; because this addition-elimination sequence (like the earlier enolate formation) is reversible, it is ultimately the final, thermodynamically favorable deprotonation of the acidic beta-ketoester that locks in the product and drives the overall multistep process forward.

q: A student claims that the Claisen condensation can proceed to useful conversion even without any final deprotonation step, as long as enough strong base is used
e: Simply having a fully formed starting enolate does not prevent the subsequent addition and elimination equilibria from running in reverse; what actually commits the reaction to product is that the beta-ketoester, once formed, is acidic enough to be essentially completely deprotonated by the alkoxide present, continuously siphoning material out of the reversible steps and toward the stable enolate salt of the product.

q: Explain why attempting a Claisen condensation on an ester whose alpha carbon is fully substituted (bearing no alpha hydrogens, such as ethyl trimethylacetate, (
e: A Claisen condensation fundamentally requires an enolate nucleophile generated by removing an alpha hydrogen; an ester like ethyl trimethylacetate, whose alpha carbon is fully substituted with three methyl groups and has no hydrogen to remove, simply cannot form that nucleophile and so cannot undergo self-condensation (though it could still act only as an electrophile if paired with a different ester that does have alpha hydrogens).

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a Dieckmann condensation from an ordinary (intermolecular) Claisen condensation?
e: The Dieckmann condensation uses the same fundamental mechanism as the Claisen condensation (ester enolate attacking an ester carbonyl, expelling alkoxide), but because both ester groups are part of one molecule (a diester), the reaction closes a ring instead of joining two separate molecules.

q: Treating diethyl adipate (a six-carbon diester, diethyl hexanedioate) with sodium ethoxide under Dieckmann conditions is expected to give a cyclic beta-ketoeste
e: Diethyl adipate is EtO2C-(CH2)4-CO2Et. Number the chain C1 to C6 taking the two ester carbonyl carbons as C1 and C6, so there are four methylenes between the ester groups. Ethoxide makes the enolate at C2, C2 attacks C6, and the ring that closes contains C2, C3, C4, C5 and C6: five atoms. Five- and six-membered rings are the ones a Dieckmann closure reaches, so this one goes; a diester one carbon shorter would have to close a four-membered ring and does not react this way.

q: A chemist performs a Claisen condensation and, after the reaction, adds aqueous acid to the mixture but observes that essentially no change in the product occur
e: Because the final, product-determining step of a Claisen condensation is deprotonation of the acidic beta-ketoester to its stable, resonance-delocalized enolate salt, the reaction mixture right before workup consists mainly of that salt; a mild acidic workup simply reprotonates it to recover the neutral beta-ketoester, rather than undoing the earlier carbon-carbon bond formation.

q: Which of the following best explains why methyl or ethyl esters are the typical substrates for a Claisen condensation rather than, say, tert-butyl esters?
e: Although in principle many esters can undergo Claisen-type chemistry, using a small, matched alkoxide (methoxide with methyl esters, ethoxide with ethyl esters) keeps the mechanism clean, since the base and the leaving group are then identical and steric hindrance in the addition-elimination step is minimized.

q: A Claisen condensation performed using potassium tert-butoxide as the base with an ethyl ester substrate risks a side reaction because:
e: Using a base whose alkoxide does not match the ester's own -OR group introduces the possibility of that alkoxide itself attacking the ester carbonyl (a transesterification-like pathway) or becoming incorporated into the leaving group step, which is why chemists typically match the base's alkoxide to the ester being used.

q: In a Dieckmann condensation, after the intramolecular ring-closing addition-elimination step gives the cyclic beta-ketoester, what final step (analogous to the
e: Just like the intermolecular Claisen condensation, the Dieckmann condensation relies on the final deprotonation of its acidic cyclic beta-ketoester product by the alkoxide base to lock the equilibrium in favor of the cyclized product, since the earlier intramolecular addition-elimination step alone is reversible.

q: A chemist notices that attempting a Claisen condensation on a simple ester using only weak, catalytic amounts of a non-alkoxide base (such as a very weak amine
e: Even though the overall sequence is ultimately pulled forward by the favorable final deprotonation of the product, the reaction must first generate enough starting ester enolate to initiate the addition step; a base too weak to meaningfully deprotonate the much less acidic starting ester (pKa about 25) will fail to get the sequence going in practical amounts of time.

q: Ethyl propanoate, CH3CH2CO2Et, is treated with NaOEt and then dilute acid. What is the product?
e: The enolate forms at the CH2 alpha carbon and attacks a second molecule's carbonyl carbon, and EtO- leaves. The new bond joins that alpha carbon to the other molecule's acyl carbon, so the skeleton is CH3CH2-CO-CH(CH3)-CO2Et: a five-carbon chain with the ketone at C3 and a methyl at C2. That leftover methyl on the alpha carbon is the giveaway that the nucleophile was propanoate rather than acetate. Ethyl 3-oxopentanoate is the answer you get if you forget it, and ethyl 3-oxobutanoate is what ethyl acetate would have given.

q: Which pair of reagents installs a -CO2Et group on the alpha carbon of cyclohexanone in one step?
e: Diethyl carbonate has no alpha hydrogens, so it can only be the electrophile, and the ketone at pKa 20 is deprotonated in preference to it. The crossed Claisen gives ethyl 2-oxocyclohexane-1-carboxylate. Ethyl acetate would compete as a nucleophile and give a mixture, while ethers and alcohols have no acyl carbon to attack in the first place.

q: Diethyl pentanedioate (diethyl glutarate) is treated with NaOEt. What happens?
e: Number the chain C1 to C5. The enolate at C2 attacking C5 would close C2-C3-C4-C5, a four-membered ring, which is far too strained to form. The intramolecular route is shut, so the substrate does intermolecular chemistry or nothing. Count the ring before predicting any Dieckmann: five and six work, four does not.

q: A beta-ketoester with the skeleton PhCO-CH2-CO2Et is to be made by a crossed Claisen. Which pair of starting materials, with NaOEt, gives it cleanly?
e: Cut the bond between the central CH2 and the acyl carbon on its left. The acyl half, PhCO-, has to come from the electrophile: ethyl benzoate, which has no alpha hydrogens and so can play no other role. The other half, -CH2CO2Et, is the enolate of ethyl acetate. Acetophenone with ethyl benzoate would give a 1,3-diketone instead, and benzaldehyde has no leaving group, so it would give an aldol.

q: Amines are basic because the nitrogen has:
e: Neutral amine nitrogen has one lone pair not involved in bonding, which it can donate to a proton (Brønsted base) or any electrophile (Lewis base).

q: Why are amides far less basic than amines, even though both contain nitrogen?
e: Amide resonance pulls the nitrogen lone pair into conjugation with the carbonyl, making it far less available to accept a proton than a typical amine’s lone pair.

q: Ranking by basicity in water, where does aniline (an aromatic amine) typically fall relative to a simple alkylamine like methylamine?
e: Aniline’s nitrogen lone pair partially conjugates into the benzene ring (similar to amide resonance), making it far less available to accept a proton than an alkylamine’s localized lone pair.

q: Amines are classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary based on:
e: Classification counts how many carbon substituents are bonded directly to nitrogen, regardless of how many N-H bonds remain.

q: What is the approximate geometry around the nitrogen in a typical sp3 amine?
e: With three bonds and one lone pair, nitrogen adopts a pyramidal shape, similar to ammonia.

q: The nitrogen lone pair in an amine is responsible for both its basicity and its nucleophilicity.
e: The same nonbonding electron pair can be donated to a proton (acting as a base) or to an electrophilic carbon (acting as a nucleophile).

q: Compared to alcohols of similar size, amines generally have:
e: Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so N-H bonds are less polarized and hydrogen bonds between amines are weaker than those between alcohols.

q: Which best describes a quaternary ammonium salt?
e: With four bonds to carbon, nitrogen has used its lone pair, so it carries a permanent positive charge and cannot act as a base or donate electrons further.

q: A flask contains cyclohexanone and cyclohexylamine dissolved in diethyl ether. You shake it with 1 M aqueous HCl and separate the layers. Where is each compound
e: The amine (pKaH about 10.6) is fully protonated by 1 M HCl, and the ammonium chloride that results is an ionic salt, so it dissolves in the water layer. A ketone is nowhere near basic enough to be protonated by dilute HCl and stays in the ether. Adding NaOH to the aqueous layer regenerates the free amine, which is extracted back into fresh ether - this is how amines are separated and purified in practice.

q: Which functional group definition correctly describes an amine?
e: Amines feature sp3 (or aryl-attached) nitrogen connected via single bonds to carbon and/or hydrogen, retaining a lone pair.

q: When chemists compare amine basicity using pKa values, the pKa listed usually refers to:
e: Amine basicity is conventionally tabulated as the pKa of the protonated ammonium ion; a higher pKa for the conjugate acid means a more basic amine.

q: Why is methylamine more basic than ammonia in the gas phase and in most basicity comparisons?
e: Alkyl groups are weak electron donors through induction, which helps stabilize the resulting ammonium cation and raises basicity relative to ammonia.

q: Which nitrogen of the amino acid lysine, H2N-CH2CH2CH2CH2-CH(NH2)-COOH, is the more basic?
e: The side-chain nitrogen is an ordinary alkylamine with nothing nearby, pKaH about 10.5. The alpha nitrogen sits one carbon from an electron-withdrawing carboxyl group, whose inductive pull destabilizes the ammonium ion formed on protonation and drops its pKaH to about 9. Induction falls off steeply with distance, which is why four CH2 groups are enough to remove the effect entirely.

q: Among methylamine, dimethylamine, and trimethylamine in aqueous solution, dimethylamine is often the most basic overall. What explains this?
e: More alkyl groups raise inductive electron density, favoring basicity, but also hinder solvation of the resulting ammonium cation in water, which disfavors basicity; these effects roughly balance out to favor the disubstituted amine.

q: In water, trimethylamine is the most basic of the methylamines because it has the most electron-donating methyl groups.
e: Despite having three electron-donating groups, trimethylamine's bulky, poorly solvated ammonium ion makes it comparable to or less basic than dimethylamine in aqueous solution.

q: Among pyrrole nitrogen, pyridine nitrogen, and a simple alkylamine nitrogen, which lone pair is least available to accept a proton?
e: Pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair is required for the ring's aromaticity, so using it to bond a proton would disrupt aromatic stabilization, making it far less basic than pyridine or an alkylamine.

q: An amide nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into the adjacent carbonyl pi system through resonance. What effect does this have on basicity compared to a simple
e: Because the nitrogen lone pair is tied up stabilizing the carbonyl, it is far less available to bond an incoming proton, making amides only weakly basic.

q: Under strongly acidic conditions, why does protonation of an amide occur preferentially at the carbonyl oxygen rather than at nitrogen?
e: O-protonation produces a resonance-stabilized cation where positive charge is shared between O and N, which is more stable than the localized charge from N-protonation.

q: Which order correctly ranks ammonia, methylamine, and aniline from most basic to least basic?
e: An alkyl group raises basicity relative to ammonia through induction, while conjugation with an aromatic ring in aniline drastically lowers it by delocalizing the lone pair.

q: Which substituent, placed para to the amino group on an aniline ring, would make that aromatic amine MORE basic than aniline itself?
e: Electron-donating substituents reduce how much the ring pulls on the nitrogen lone pair, leaving more electron density available on nitrogen for protonation; electron-withdrawing groups do the opposite and lower basicity.

q: Adding a nitro group para to the amino group on aniline increases the resulting amine's basicity.
e: A nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing by both induction and resonance, further depleting the nitrogen lone pair and decreasing basicity rather than increasing it.

q: Imidazole (found in histidine) is considerably more basic than pyrrole even though both contain a pyrrole-type nitrogen. What explains this?
e: One nitrogen in imidazole donates its lone pair to the aromatic system (like pyrrole, non-basic), while the other nitrogen's lone pair is not part of the aromatic system and is readily available to accept a proton, similar to pyridine.

q: Guanidine, (H2N)2C=NH, has a conjugate acid pKa of about 13.6, making it far MORE basic than an ordinary alkylamine - even though its lone pairs are delocalized
e: What matters is which side of the acid-base equilibrium the resonance stabilizes. In an amide, resonance stabilizes the neutral form, so protonation costs that stabilization and basicity collapses. In guanidine, protonating the imine nitrogen gives a cation whose positive charge is shared equally over three nitrogens, so the resonance pays for the protonation instead of opposing it. Same phenomenon, opposite direction.

q: Which correctly ranks these from MOST to LEAST basic: cyclohexylamine nitrogen, pyridine nitrogen, pyrrole nitrogen, amide nitrogen?
e: A localized sp3 lone pair (alkylamine, pKaH about 10.7) is most basic; pyridine's localized sp2 lone pair is next at 5.2; an amide comes next at about -1, its lone pair delocalized into the carbonyl; pyrrole is last at about -4, because its lone pair IS the aromatic sextet and protonating nitrogen would destroy the aromaticity outright.

q: Why is the nitrogen lone pair in a nitrile (R-C triple bond N) much less basic than the lone pair in a typical sp3 amine?
e: Greater s-character lowers the orbital's energy and pulls the lone pair closer to the nucleus, making it less willing to be donated to a proton compared to the higher-energy sp3 lone pair of an amine.

q: Increasing the s-character of the hybrid orbital that holds a nitrogen lone pair tends to decrease that nitrogen's basicity.
e: Higher s-character means electrons are held closer to and more tightly by the nucleus, making them less available to bond an incoming proton, so basicity decreases.

q: An amine nitrogen is constrained in a small, strained ring (such as aziridine) compared to an open-chain secondary amine with the same substitution pattern. How
e: Distorted bond angles in strained rings change the hybridization of the nitrogen lone pair orbital, typically increasing its s-character and somewhat reducing basicity relative to an unstrained analog.

q: Ranking triethylamine, pyridine, aniline, and acetamide from strongest to weakest base, which order is correct?
e: A simple trialkylamine is most basic; pyridine's localized sp2 lone pair is less basic than an alkylamine but more basic than a ring-conjugated arylamine; aniline's delocalized lone pair is weak; the amide is essentially non-basic since its lone pair feeds the carbonyl.

q: Because nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, amines are generally more basic than comparably substituted alcohols or ethers.
e: Lower electronegativity on nitrogen means its lone pair is held less tightly than an oxygen lone pair, making it more willing to accept a proton.

q: Diisopropylamine is a bulky secondary amine that is a poor nucleophile yet still a reasonably strong base in solution. What best explains this apparent contradi
e: A small, unhindered proton can still approach the lone pair easily (supporting basicity), while bulky alkyl groups block approach of larger electrophiles in a substitution reaction, lowering nucleophilicity without lowering basicity.

q: Amines commonly act as nucleophiles toward carbonyls, forming which product after loss of water (with aldehydes/ketones)?
e: A primary amine adds to a carbonyl, and after proton transfers and loss of water, the resulting C=N double bond is an imine.

q: When a primary amine reacts with an acyl chloride or ester, the product (after loss of the leaving group) is a(n):
e: This is nucleophilic acyl substitution — the amine nitrogen ends up bonded to the carbonyl carbon, and the leaving group departs, giving an amide.

q: A secondary amine reacting with an aldehyde/ketone (instead of a primary amine) typically forms what kind of product, since it cannot lose a second proton from
e: With no second N–H to lose, the iminium-like intermediate instead loses a proton from the adjacent alpha carbon, shifting the double bond there and giving an enamine (C=C–N) instead of an imine (C=N).

q: When a primary amine reacts with excess methyl iodide, the ultimate product after repeated alkylation is:
e: Exhaustive SN2 alkylation keeps adding methyl groups to nitrogen until all four positions are filled, giving a permanently charged quaternary ammonium salt.

q: Amines react with strong acids such as HCl to form:
e: The nitrogen lone pair is protonated by the strong acid, giving a positively charged ammonium salt with the chloride as counterion.

q: Cyclohexylamine is treated with (1) excess CH3I, then (2) acetic anhydride. What is the outcome?
e: Excess CH3I exhaustively methylates the nitrogen to cyclohexyltrimethylammonium iodide. That nitrogen has four bonds, a full positive charge and no lone pair, so it cannot attack the anhydride - and it has no N-H to lose even if it could. Order matters: run the acylation first and the amide forms cleanly.

q: Treating a primary or secondary amine with an acyl chloride (R-COCl) gives which product?
e: The amine nitrogen attacks the acyl chloride carbonyl carbon, chloride leaves, and loss of a proton from nitrogen gives a neutral amide.

q: Reacting a primary amine with nitrous acid (HNO2) at low temperature generates a reactive intermediate known as a:
e: Nitrosation of the primary amine followed by loss of water forms the diazonium ion, R-N2+.

q: Aryl diazonium salts (made from aromatic primary amines plus HNO2) are stable enough to be isolated and stored at room temperature for long periods.
e: Aryl diazonium salts are typically only stable at low temperature (around 0 to 5 degrees C) and must be used immediately in further reactions rather than stored.

q: Direct SN2 alkylation of ammonia or a primary amine with an unactivated alkyl halide is often a poor way to make a single clean product because:
e: Each alkylation product still bears a nucleophilic nitrogen that can react further with remaining alkyl halide, so a statistical mixture of alkylation levels usually results.

q: When converting an amine to an amide using an acyl chloride, chemists commonly add a base like pyridine or triethylamine mainly to:
e: Each amide-forming step releases HCl, which would otherwise protonate and deactivate remaining amine; an added base consumes the HCl, keeping the reaction moving.

q: A primary amine condenses with an aldehyde, losing water to form R2C=N-R'. What is this type of product commonly called?
e: The C=N product formed from a primary amine and a carbonyl compound after loss of water is classically known as an imine or Schiff base.

q: A secondary amine reacting with a ketone forms an enamine instead of an imine. Why?
e: After the secondary amine adds to the carbonyl and loses the OH as water, nitrogen still bears one substituent and no remaining N-H to lose, so the molecule instead loses an alpha C-H to form the carbon-carbon double bond of an enamine.

q: Before any water is lost, an amine first adds to an aldehyde or ketone carbonyl to give a tetrahedral intermediate commonly called a:
e: The initial addition product, bearing both an OH and an NR2 group on the same carbon, is the hemiaminal, which can then dehydrate to the imine or enamine - though it is rarely isolable, since it usually dehydrates about as fast as it forms.

q: Tertiary amines can form stable, isolable imines or enamines when reacted with ketones, because nitrogen still has a lone pair available.
e: Although tertiary amines can add to a carbonyl using their lone pair, they have no N-H to lose in the dehydration step, so a stable neutral imine or enamine cannot form at that nitrogen.

q: You need to convert butan-2-one plus methylamine into N-methylbutan-2-amine, CH3CH2CH(NHCH3)CH3. Which reagent completes the job?
e: This is a reductive amination. The ketone and the amine condense to the iminium ion and NaBH3CN reduces it. The mildly acidic pH is what makes it work: acidic enough to dehydrate the hemiaminal, not so acidic that the amine is all protonated, and NaBH3CN is attenuated enough to survive those conditions and to ignore the ketone. LiAlH4 added first would simply reduce the ketone to the alcohol.

q: Put the steps of imine formation in order: (i) loss of water, (ii) protonation of the OH, (iii) attack by nitrogen on the carbonyl carbon, (iv) loss of a proton
e: Attack comes first (iii), because the amine is the nucleophile and the carbonyl carbon the electrophile. A proton transfer then converts the zwitterion into the neutral hemiaminal (v). The OH is a terrible leaving group, so it is protonated to water (ii), which leaves with a push from the nitrogen lone pair to give the iminium ion (i). Finally the iminium loses its N-H proton to give the neutral imine (iv).

q: Primary aliphatic diazonium salts (from alkylamine plus HNO2) are extremely unstable and rapidly decompose with loss of what gas?
e: Alkyl diazonium ions lose N2 almost immediately because there is no resonance stabilization of the cation, generating a carbocation that goes on to form substitution or elimination products.

q: Aryl diazonium salts are synthetically valuable mainly because the N2+ group on the ring can be replaced to give:
e: Diazonium salts undergo a range of substitution reactions (with water, copper halides, or cyanide, for example) that install many different functional groups onto the aromatic ring.

q: Reductive amination of a ketone with a primary amine and a reducing agent such as sodium cyanoborohydride is useful because it:
e: The amine and ketone first condense to an iminium/imine intermediate, which the mild reducing agent then reduces in the same reaction vessel, avoiding isolation of the reactive intermediate.

q: The Gabriel synthesis produces pure primary amines without contamination by secondary or tertiary amines, unlike a direct SN2 alkylation of ammonia.
e: Phthalimide blocks two of nitrogen's bonding positions during alkylation, and subsequent hydrolysis or hydrazine treatment releases only the desired primary amine, avoiding over-alkylation.

q: Which reagent reduces an amide all the way to the corresponding primary amine, removing the carbonyl oxygen entirely?
e: LiAlH4 is a strong enough hydride reducing agent to convert the amide carbonyl carbon into a CH2 group, converting the amide directly into an amine.

q: A chemist treats a tertiary amine with excess acetic anhydride, expecting amide formation. What actually happens at that nitrogen?
e: Amide formation requires the nitrogen to lose a proton after acyl transfer to become neutral; a tertiary amine has no N-H to lose, so it cannot form a stable neutral amide at that nitrogen, even though it may transiently act as a nucleophile or catalyst.

q: In the Gabriel synthesis, after an alkyl halide reacts with potassium phthalimide, what is the purpose of the subsequent hydrazine (or strong hydrolysis) step?
e: Hydrazine (or acidic/basic hydrolysis) breaks both amide linkages of the phthalimide ring, liberating the primary amine cleanly from the alkylated nitrogen.

q: Aromatic primary amines react with HNO2 to give diazonium salts that can be briefly used cold, while aliphatic primary amines give diazonium salts that decompos
e: Conjugation between the diazonium nitrogen and the aromatic ring delocalizes positive charge in the aryl case, slowing decomposition, whereas the alkyl diazonium ion has no such stabilization and loses N2 almost instantly, generating a reactive carbocation.

q: Secondary amines reacting with nitrous acid form stable N-nitrosamines (R2N-NO) rather than diazonium salts, because they lack a second N-H to lose after the in
e: After nitrosation, a secondary amine's nitrogen has no remaining N-H to lose on the way to a diazonium-type species, so the reaction stops at the stable N-nitrosamine.

q: During reductive amination of a ketone with a primary amine at mildly acidic pH, why is sodium cyanoborohydride (NaBH3CN) preferred over sodium borohydride (NaB
e: At the mildly acidic pH typically used, NaBH3CN reduces the more reactive, protonated iminium ion much faster than it reduces the neutral carbonyl starting material, improving yield of the desired amine over simple alcohol byproducts.

q: An amine is treated with excess alkyl halide in a classic direct SN2 alkylation. Even with careful stoichiometry, why doesn't the reaction stop cleanly at the s
e: Because the secondary (and even tertiary) amine products are still nucleophilic, and proton transfer equilibria can regenerate free amine from its ammonium salt, the reaction tends to give a mixture of alkylation levels rather than one clean product.

q: Which sequence correctly describes converting an aryl diazonium salt into an aryl fluoride without relying on nucleophilic aromatic substitution?
e: The Balz-Schiemann reaction converts an aryl diazonium salt (commonly as its tetrafluoroborate) into the corresponding aryl fluoride upon heating, with loss of nitrogen gas.

q: A primary amine is treated with one equivalent of an acid chloride in the presence of excess pyridine as a base. What roles does pyridine play, and why is it ch
e: Pyridine's job is to take the HCl each acylation releases, so the amine is not consumed as a base — and it can do that job without getting in the way, because it carries no N–H and so cannot be acylated into the product. It is not that pyridine fails to attack the acid chloride: it does, giving an N-acylpyridinium ion, and that ion is a better acylating agent than the acid chloride was, so the acyl group simply passes on to the amine. That relay is why pyridine and DMAP catalyze acylations rather than obstructing them. NaOH is the wrong choice for a different reason: hydroxide would attack the acid chloride and hydrolyze it to the carboxylate before the amine got its turn.

q: For a ring system to be aromatic, it must be cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, and have how many pi electrons (by Hückel’s rule)?
e: Hückel’s rule requires 4n+2 pi electrons (n = 0, 1, 2...) in a cyclic, planar, fully conjugated system — benzene’s 6 pi electrons fits n=1.

q: Cyclobutadiene (4 pi electrons) is anti-aromatic rather than aromatic because:
e: 4 pi electrons fits the 4n pattern (n=1), which Hückel’s rule predicts is destabilizing (anti-aromatic) rather than stabilizing.

q: Is the cyclopentadienyl cation (4 pi electrons, planar, cyclic) aromatic, anti-aromatic, or non-aromatic?
e: With 4 pi electrons in a planar, fully conjugated ring, it fits the 4n pattern (n=1) that Hückel’s rule predicts is destabilizing — anti-aromatic, and indeed very unstable/reactive.

q: Cyclooctatetraene dianion is planar, cyclic and fully conjugated with 10 pi electrons. 1,3,5-Cyclooctatriene is cyclic and planar but has two sp³ CH₂ carbons an
e: Work the requirements in order rather than counting first. The dianion is cyclic, planar and fully conjugated, so the count is allowed to decide: 10 fits 4n+2 with n = 2, so it is aromatic. The triene fails the conjugation requirement before the count is ever reached — two sp³ carbons break the loop of p orbitals — so it is non-aromatic, and its 6 pi electrons are beside the point. The trap is answering antiaromatic for the triene: antiaromatic means passing all three structural tests and then landing on 4n, which a ring with an sp³ carbon in it never does.

q: Benzene satisfies Hückel's rule with 6 pi electrons corresponding to n = 2 in the 4n+2 formula.
e: 4n+2 with n = 2 gives 10, not 6. Benzene's six pi electrons correspond to n = 1: 4(1) + 2 = 6. The n = 2 count of 10 belongs to species such as the cyclooctatetraene dianion and the naphthalene ring system.

q: How many pi electrons are delocalized in the aromatic ring system of naphthalene (two fused benzene rings)?
e: Naphthalene has five formal double bonds worth of pi electrons delocalized over the fused bicyclic system, totaling 10 pi electrons, which fits 4n+2 with n = 2.

q: Every atom in an aromatic ring must have which type of hybridization so that a continuous ring of p orbitals can form?
e: sp2 hybridization leaves one unhybridized p orbital per atom perpendicular to the ring plane, allowing continuous pi overlap all the way around.

q: Aromatic compounds like benzene typically undergo substitution reactions rather than addition reactions because addition would destroy the aromatic stabilizatio
e: Addition across a ring double bond would convert an sp2 carbon to sp3, breaking conjugation and losing the large resonance stabilization energy, so substitution (which preserves the ring) is favored instead.

q: 1,3,5,7-Cyclooctatetraene, if forced to be planar, would have 8 pi electrons. Why is the actual molecule not considered aromatic?
e: Real cyclooctatetraene twists out of planarity into a tub shape, which avoids the destabilization of antiaromaticity (8 pi electrons would be 4n) by sacrificing full conjugation rather than staying planar.

q: In Huckel's rule (4n+2), the variable n must be a non-negative integer (0, 1, 2, 3, ...).
e: n = 0 gives 2 pi electrons, n = 1 gives 6, n = 2 gives 10, and so on; n cannot be negative or fractional.

q: Is the cyclopropenyl cation (a three-membered ring with 2 pi electrons, planar and fully conjugated) aromatic?
e: Even very small rings can be aromatic if they meet all the criteria; 2 pi electrons satisfies 4n+2 when n = 0, making the cyclopropenyl cation aromatic and unusually stable for a carbocation.

q: Pyridine's nitrogen lone pair occupies an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring, so it does not participate in the aromatic pi system.
e: Because the lone pair is in-plane rather than in a p orbital perpendicular to the ring, it is not part of the 6 pi electron aromatic system, which is why pyridine's nitrogen remains basic.

q: In furan, how does oxygen contribute to the aromatic pi system?
e: Furan has two ring double bonds (4 pi electrons) plus one oxygen lone pair donated into a p orbital, giving 6 total pi electrons and satisfying Huckel's rule; the other lone pair stays in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane.

q: Rank cyclopentadiene, the cyclopentadienyl cation, and the cyclopentadienyl anion from most to least stable relative to a typical non-aromatic comparison.
e: The cyclopentadienyl anion has 6 pi electrons and is aromatic (very stabilized), the neutral diene is simply conjugated, and the cation has 4 pi electrons and is antiaromatic (highly destabilized), making the anion by far the most stable of the three.

q: Because pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic pi system, pyrrole is far less basic than a typical secondary amine.
e: Protonating pyrrole's nitrogen would remove that lone pair from the aromatic system and destroy aromaticity, so the lone pair is much less available to accept a proton than in ordinary amines.

q: Which species below is classified as antiaromatic?
e: Cyclobutadiene is cyclic, planar, and fully conjugated with 4 pi electrons, which fits 4n (n = 1) rather than 4n+2, making it antiaromatic and highly unstable/reactive.

q: The cycloheptatrienyl cation (tropylium) is aromatic even though it is a seven-membered ring, because it has 6 delocalized pi electrons over a planar, fully con
e: Tropylium's positive charge sits in an empty p orbital identical in symmetry to the other six carbons' p orbitals, giving a fully conjugated 6 pi electron aromatic system despite being a seven-membered ring.

q: A compound is planar, cyclic, and fully conjugated with 8 pi electrons. What is its classification?
e: 8 pi electrons fits the 4n pattern (n = 2), so a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring with this electron count is antiaromatic, typically destabilized relative to an open-chain analog.

q: A molecule is cyclic and has 6 pi electrons, but one ring atom is sp3 hybridized, breaking the conjugation. Is the molecule aromatic?
e: Having the right pi electron count is necessary but not sufficient; an sp3 atom interrupts the continuous ring of p orbitals needed for full conjugation, so the molecule is non-aromatic regardless of electron count.

q: Cyclobutadiene's high reactivity is explained by calling it non-aromatic: it is simply an ordinary, unstabilized diene.
e: Non-aromatic means neither stabilized nor destabilized — an ordinary diene, which cyclobutadiene plainly is not. It is cyclic, planar and fully conjugated with 4 pi electrons, so it is antiaromatic: actively destabilized relative to an open-chain diene, which is why it dimerizes on sight and can be observed at all in a frozen matrix at 4 K.

q: Why does the aromatic stabilization of benzene show up experimentally as a lower-than-expected heat of hydrogenation?
e: If benzene were just three isolated double bonds, hydrogenation would release about three times the heat of one alkene's hydrogenation; the actual value is substantially lower, revealing the extra stability (resonance energy) from aromatic delocalization.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes non-aromatic from antiaromatic compounds?
e: Non-aromatic means the compound fails at least one structural requirement and behaves like an ordinary conjugated or non-conjugated system; antiaromatic means all structural requirements are met but the electron count is 4n, producing a system that is destabilized relative to the open-chain analog.

q: Cyclooctatetraene dianion (with 2 extra electrons added, giving 10 pi electrons total, planar) would be predicted to be aromatic.
e: Adding two electrons to the 8 pi electron tub-shaped neutral molecule gives 10 pi electrons (4n+2 with n=2); when the ring flattens to allow full conjugation, this dianion is indeed aromatic.

q: What structural feature allows benzene's six carbon-carbon bonds to all have the same intermediate length (between single and double bond length) rather than al
e: Because the pi electrons are delocalized over all six p orbitals rather than localized into three discrete double bonds, every C-C bond has equal, intermediate bond order and length (about 1.39 Angstroms).

q: Thiophene's sulfur contributes both of its lone pairs to the aromatic pi system, giving 8 pi electrons in total.
e: One lone pair can occupy the ring p orbital; the other stays in an sp² orbital lying in the ring plane, where it is perpendicular to the pi system and contributes nothing to it. Two ring C=C (4 electrons) plus that one donated pair gives 6, which is why thiophene is aromatic — and the spare in-plane pair is what sulfur still has available for ordinary chemistry.

q: A large annulene has 4n+2 pi electrons but is too strained to stay planar. What happens to its aromaticity?
e: Huckel's rule assumes a continuous ring of overlapping p orbitals, which needs a planar ring. A large annulene can satisfy the electron count and still twist out of plane to relieve strain, and the overlap goes with it.

q: Which best explains why the cyclopentadienyl anion is far easier to form than a typical alkyl carbanion?
e: Removing a proton from cyclopentadiene creates a planar, fully conjugated five-membered ring anion with 6 pi electrons, satisfying Huckel's rule, so the resulting aromatic stabilization makes cyclopentadiene unusually acidic for a hydrocarbon.

q: Benzene's resonance (delocalization) energy is typically estimated to be around 36 kcal/mol compared to a hypothetical non-aromatic 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene.
e: This value, derived from comparing the actual heat of hydrogenation of benzene to that expected for three isolated double bonds, quantifies the extra stability aromaticity provides.

q: Imidazole has a five-membered ring containing two nitrogens: N1 carries an H and has no ring double bond, N3 has no H and is part of a ring C=N. How many pi ele
e: Count each nitrogen separately by asking whether it already has a ring double bond. N3 does (the C=N), so its lone pair sits in an sp² orbital in the ring plane and contributes 0 — which is exactly why that nitrogen is the basic one. N1 does not, so its lone pair has to occupy the p orbital and contributes 2. Add the C=C (2), the C=N (2) and N1's pair (2): 6 pi electrons, aromatic. This is the histidine side chain, and the same split explains why histidine has one basic nitrogen and one weakly acidic N–H.

q: Which of these molecules is best described as non-aromatic rather than aromatic or antiaromatic?
e: 1,3-Cyclohexadiene is cyclic but not fully conjugated around the entire ring (it has sp3 carbons interrupting conjugation), so it is simply non-aromatic, unlike fully conjugated cyclobutadiene (antiaromatic) or benzene and pyridine (aromatic).

q: Electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) begins with the aromatic ring acting as a:
e: The electron-rich aromatic pi system attacks an electrophile, forming a resonance-stabilized cationic intermediate (arenium ion/Wheland intermediate), then loses a proton to restore aromaticity.

q: Why does EAS restore aromaticity at the end rather than simply adding across one double bond (like a normal alkene addition)?
e: The strong stabilization of the aromatic system makes substitution (proton loss, keeping the ring intact) thermodynamically favored over addition, which would destroy aromaticity.

q: Which step of the EAS mechanism is typically rate-determining (slowest)?
e: Forming the arenium ion intermediate requires temporarily breaking aromaticity, which costs significant energy — this is the slow, rate-determining step; the final proton loss (restoring aromaticity) is fast.

q: In the first mechanistic step of electrophilic aromatic substitution, the aromatic ring's pi electrons attack the electrophile, temporarily forming which type o
e: Attack of the ring pi system on the electrophile generates a cyclohexadienyl cation (arenium ion) in which one ring carbon becomes sp3, temporarily destroying aromaticity; this cation is stabilized by resonance across three positions.

q: Benzene is treated with (CH₃)₃CCl and AlCl₃, then with CH₃COCl and AlCl₃. What is the major product of the second step?
e: Two decisions, in order. First step: tert-butyl chloride ionizes to a tertiary cation, which is already the most stable arrangement of those carbons, so nothing rearranges and tert-butylbenzene forms cleanly. Second step: an alkyl group is a weak activator and an ortho/para director, so the acylium ion goes ortho or para. tert-Butyl is very bulky, so ortho attack is almost entirely suppressed and the product is essentially all para. The trap is answering meta by reflex because the incoming group is an acyl group — the incoming group never directs; the group already on the ring does.

q: Which reagent sequence converts benzene into butylbenzene, with an unbranched four-carbon chain on the ring?
e: Direct alkylation with 1-chlorobutane fails for a predictable reason: the primary cation undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to the secondary cation before benzene ever attacks, so the product is sec-butylbenzene. Acylation with butanoyl chloride cannot rearrange, because the acylium ion is resonance-stabilized by its oxygen, and it also cannot over-react, because the ketone it installs deactivates the ring. Clemmensen reduction, Zn(Hg) in HCl, then turns the C=O into CH₂ and leaves the straight chain intact. Wolff-Kishner (H₂NNH₂, KOH, heat) does the same job when the molecule cannot survive strong acid.

q: Friedel-Crafts alkylation requires a Lewis acid catalyst such as AlCl3 in order to generate a reactive carbocation electrophile from an alkyl halide.
e: AlCl3 coordinates to the halide and helps ionize the C-X bond, generating (or activating toward) a carbocation electrophile that the aromatic ring can then attack.

q: In Friedel-Crafts acylation, what intermediate is typically generated as the electrophile?
e: A Lewis acid such as AlCl3 helps an acyl chloride lose chloride, forming a resonance-stabilized acylium cation that acts as the electrophile attacked by the aromatic ring.

q: The electrophile in aromatic nitration is the nitronium ion, NO2+, generated from nitric acid and sulfuric acid.
e: Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which then loses water to generate the nitronium ion (NO2+), the actual electrophile attacked by the benzene ring.

q: What is the electrophile in aromatic sulfonation using fuming sulfuric acid?
e: Sulfur trioxide (present in fuming sulfuric acid) is a strong electrophile at sulfur; the aromatic ring attacks sulfur to form a sulfonated arenium intermediate.

q: Halogenation of benzene with Br₂ proceeds readily without any catalyst, because benzene's pi system is a stronger nucleophile than an alkene's.
e: Both halves are wrong. Benzene is a far weaker nucleophile than an alkene precisely because its pi electrons are tied up in the aromatic sextet, and attacking costs about 36 kcal/mol of that stabilization. Br₂ alone adds to an alkene on contact and does nothing at all to benzene; FeBr₃ is needed to polarize the Br–Br bond into an electrophile strong enough to be worth attacking.

q: After an aromatic ring attacks an electrophile to form the arenium ion, which species typically removes the proton in the final deprotonation step?
e: The byproduct generated when the electrophile formed (e.g., FeBr4-, AlCl4-, or HSO4-) is basic enough to pluck off the proton from the sp3 ring carbon, regenerating the aromatic ring and the original catalyst.

q: Why is a Friedel-Crafts alkylation prone to carbocation rearrangement side products when a secondary or primary alkyl halide is used?
e: Since a free (or nearly free) carbocation is generated, it can rearrange via hydride or alkyl shifts to a more stable cation before the aromatic ring traps it, often giving unexpected substitution patterns.

q: Why can Friedel-Crafts acylation avoid the rearrangement problem that plagues Friedel-Crafts alkylation?
e: The acylium ion's positive charge is delocalized onto oxygen through resonance, making it stable enough that it does not need to rearrange to a more stable carbocation, unlike many alkyl cations.

q: A major practical advantage of Friedel-Crafts acylation over alkylation is that the product ketone, once formed, deactivates the ring, preventing a second acyla
e: The carbonyl group is electron-withdrawing and deactivates the ring toward further EAS, so acylation self-limits to mono-substitution, unlike alkylation where the alkyl product activates the ring toward further alkylation.

q: Why does Friedel-Crafts alkylation often give polysubstituted (over-alkylated) products even when only one equivalent of alkyl halide is used?
e: Alkyl groups are weak activators (electron-donating by induction/hyperconjugation), so the mono-alkylated product is actually more reactive than the starting benzene, making it prone to react again and give polyalkylation.

q: Which statement correctly describes why EAS reactions are favorable overall despite requiring a high-energy intermediate?
e: The overall reaction is driven forward because regenerating the aromatic ring in the final step releases substantial stabilization energy, even though the first step requires climbing over a substantial barrier to form the arenium ion.

q: In iodination of benzene, an oxidizing agent is typically needed because I2 alone is too weak an electrophile and the reaction is otherwise reversible.
e: Unlike bromination and chlorination, direct iodination is thermodynamically unfavorable without help; an oxidant (such as nitric acid or hydrogen peroxide) is used to drive the reaction forward, often by removing HI as it forms.

q: Which reagent or condition removes an –SO₃H group from a benzene ring, and why is that worth having?
e: Sulfonation is the one reaction of the five that runs in both directions. Concentrated or fuming acid drives it on; hot dilute aqueous acid drives it back off. That makes –SO₃H a placeholder: install it so that it occupies the para position, run the substitution you actually want at ortho, then boil the sulfonic acid away. Nothing else in the EAS toolkit can be put on and taken off on demand, which is what makes an otherwise unreachable ortho product reachable.

q: Which of the following is the correct overall electrophile sequence in generating the nitronium ion from nitric acid and sulfuric acid?
e: Sulfuric acid, a stronger acid than nitric acid, protonates nitric acid's hydroxyl oxygen; the resulting species readily loses water, leaving behind the linear, highly electrophilic nitronium ion.

q: Why can EAS reactions be run on benzene derivatives but the aromatic ring never acts as a nucleophile toward a simple alkyl halide without a Lewis acid catalyst
e: Benzene's aromatic pi system is a relatively weak nucleophile compared to, say, a free carbanion, so it generally needs help activating the electrophile; a Lewis acid catalyst polarizes or ionizes the C-X bond to create a sufficiently reactive electrophilic species.

q: During the arenium ion (sigma complex) stage of EAS, the positive charge is delocalized evenly over all six ring carbons, which is why the intermediate is so st
e: One carbon is sp³ and out of the pi system entirely, so five carbons are left holding a pentadienyl cation — and resonance puts the charge on just three of those five, the two ortho and the one para to the sp³ center. That partial delocalization is real stabilization and is why the reaction runs at all, but it is nowhere near the six-carbon aromatic delocalization that was given up, which is why the arenium ion sits at an energy maximum for the whole route.

q: The resonance-stabilized arenium ion intermediate in EAS has the positive charge delocalized over how many ring carbons (for substitution on an unsubstituted be
e: One ring carbon is sp³ and out of the pi system. The other five hold a pentadienyl cation, and its three resonance structures place the positive charge on the two carbons ortho to the sp³ center and the one carbon para to it — three carbons.
