The two carbons meta to the sp³ center carry no charge in any structure, and that is exactly why some substituents send an incoming electrophile meta: meta is the attack whose arenium ion never puts charge on the substituent's own carbon.

q: Using excess AlCl3 in Friedel-Crafts acylation is necessary in part because the Lewis acid forms a complex with the ketone product, requiring a full stoichiomet
e: The carbonyl oxygen of the product ketone strongly complexes with AlCl3, sequestering it; an aqueous workup is then needed to free the product and regenerate the catalyst, which is why acylation needs more than catalytic AlCl3 while some other EAS reactions need only a trace.

q: Which best describes the overall role of a Lewis acid catalyst (such as FeBr3) in aromatic halogenation?
e: The Lewis acid coordinates to one halogen atom of X2, pulling electron density away and making the other halogen atom electrophilic enough to be attacked by the relatively weak nucleophile that is the aromatic ring.

q: Which of these statements about the EAS mechanism is FALSE?
e: The final deprotonation is actually fast because it restores aromaticity and is thermodynamically favorable; the slow, rate-determining step is instead the initial attack that forms the high-energy, non-aromatic arenium ion.

q: A chemist attempts Friedel-Crafts alkylation on nitrobenzene using methyl chloride and AlCl3, but no reaction occurs. What is the most likely explanation?
e: Strong deactivators like -NO2 pull electron density out of the ring so much that the ring is not nucleophilic enough to attack even a reactive alkyl cation electrophile, a key limitation of Friedel-Crafts chemistry.

q: In aromatic sulfonation, the reaction is reversible, and heating a sulfonated ring in dilute aqueous acid can remove the sulfonic acid group, regenerating the o
e: Unlike most EAS reactions, sulfonation's equilibrium can be shifted either direction depending on conditions; excess SO3 favors sulfonation, while dilute hot aqueous acid favors desulfonation, a useful synthetic trick for temporarily blocking a ring position.

q: Why can aromatic sulfonation be strategically used as a temporary "blocking group" in multistep aromatic synthesis?
e: Because sulfonation is reversible, chemists can install a sulfonic acid group to occupy and direct substitution at a particular ring position, then later remove it, effectively using it as a temporary placeholder.

q: Chlorination (Cl₂/FeCl₃), nitration (HNO₃/H₂SO₄) and Friedel–Crafts alkylation (RCl/AlCl₃) all need help generating their electrophile. Which statement about th
e: Nitronium ion forms directly from nitric and sulfuric acid without a separate Lewis acid catalyst on the ring, whereas molecular halogens and alkyl halides are generally not electrophilic enough on their own and need a Lewis acid (FeX3 or AlCl3) to generate a reactive electrophile.

q: An electron-donating group like –OCH₃ on benzene directs further EAS substitution to the:
e: Strong electron donors (via resonance) stabilize the arenium intermediate best when the positive charge lands ortho or para to the substituent, directing new substitution there.

q: A nitro group (–NO₂) is an EAS deactivator and directs incoming electrophiles to the:
e: Strong electron-withdrawing groups destabilize the arenium intermediate least when the positive charge is meta (avoiding direct resonance overlap with the withdrawing group), so meta substitution dominates.

q: Aniline nitrated directly with HNO₃/H₂SO₄ gives about 47 % 3-nitroaniline — a meta fraction dozens of times larger than an –NH₂ group should ever allow. Why, an
e: Ask what is actually on the ring under the reaction conditions. Nitrating acid is overwhelmingly acidic and aniline is a base, so most of it exists as the anilinium ion. –NH₃⁺ has no lone pair left to donate and carries a full positive charge next to the ring, which makes it a deactivating meta director — the opposite of what –NH₂ does. Both species react, giving roughly 2 % ortho, 47 % meta and 51 % para: the para still comes from the trace of free amine, and the huge meta fraction is the anilinium's. Aniline also oxidizes badly in nitric acid. The fix is a nitrogen that cannot be protonated: acetic anhydride gives acetanilide, still an ortho/para director but a milder one, so nitration goes cleanly para; aqueous acid or base then hydrolyzes the amide back to the free amine.

q: Anisole (methoxybenzene) undergoes EAS predominantly at which ring positions relative to the -OCH3 group?
e: The -OCH3 group is an electron donor through resonance, placing extra electron density (and stabilizing the resulting arenium cation) most effectively at the ortho and para positions.

q: Which sequence makes 3-nitroacetophenone — an acetyl group and a nitro group meta to each other — starting from benzene?
e: Acylate first. Acetophenone's acetyl group is a deactivating meta director, so the nitro group lands meta to it and the product is 3-nitroacetophenone. The other order fails outright: nitrobenzene's ring is far too electron-poor for Friedel–Crafts, which does not run on strongly deactivated rings at all, so the second step would simply not happen. Two independent reasons to acylate first, and either one settles it. Note also what this route cannot reach — the para isomer is not available from these two reactions in either order.

q: Halogens such as chlorine on a benzene ring are overall rate-decreasing (deactivating) for EAS, yet they still direct new substituents to the ortho and para pos
e: The strong electronegativity of halogens withdraws electron density through the sigma bond (slowing the reaction overall), but a lone pair on the halogen can still donate into the ring by resonance, which best stabilizes the arenium cation when the positive charge lands ortho or para to the halogen.

q: Which classification applies to an alkyl group such as -CH3 attached to benzene, in terms of both reactivity and directing effect?
e: Alkyl groups donate electron density into the ring through hyperconjugation/induction, which both speeds up EAS (activating) and best stabilizes the cationic intermediate at the ortho and para positions.

q: A carbonyl-containing group such as -CHO (an aldehyde) attached to benzene is an EAS deactivator and a meta director.
e: The carbonyl carbon is electron-poor and, through resonance, withdraws electron density most strongly from the ortho and para positions, destabilizing cationic intermediates there, so substitution is directed to meta and the ring reacts more slowly overall.

q: Which group below is the one common EAS deactivator that directs ortho/para rather than meta?
e: Halogens are unique among common deactivators: their lone pair resonance donation directs ortho/para even though their strong inductive electron withdrawal makes the ring less reactive overall (deactivating).

q: Why do most meta-directing groups also happen to be deactivating groups, rather than activating?
e: Groups like -NO2, -C(=O)R, and -CN pull electron density out of the ring (lowering reactivity everywhere) and, through resonance, destabilize positive charge most severely at ortho/para, leaving meta as the relatively least-bad (least destabilized) option.

q: Aniline (aminobenzene, with -NH2) is a very strong activator for EAS because the nitrogen lone pair can be donated into the ring by resonance.
e: The nitrogen lone pair is readily donated into the aromatic pi system, placing significant negative character at the ortho and para positions and strongly activating the ring, making aniline react in EAS even without a catalyst in some cases.

q: When toluene (methylbenzene) undergoes nitration, which product distribution is expected?
e: The methyl group is a weak activator and an ortho/para director, so nitration gives mostly ortho- and para-nitrotoluene with only a few percent meta — about 58% ortho, 37% para and 4% meta in practice. Ortho actually leads, because there are two ortho positions to one para and a methyl group is small enough not to get in the way. Bulk changes that: nitrating tert-butylbenzene gives almost entirely para, because ortho attack now runs into the substituent.

q: If benzoic acid (C6H5COOH) undergoes bromination, where would the new bromine substituent be expected to go predominantly?
e: The carboxylic acid group is electron-withdrawing by resonance and induction, deactivating the ring and directing incoming electrophiles to the meta position, where the destabilizing resonance effect is least severe.

q: Why does an -NH2 or -OH substituent direct EAS to ortho and para rather than meta, even though nitrogen and oxygen are electronegative atoms that might be expec
e: Resonance donation of the lone pair into the ring pi system outcompetes the modest inductive electron withdrawal from these electronegative atoms, so the net effect is strong activation and ortho/para direction.

q: m-Xylene (1,3-dimethylbenzene) is nitrated. Both methyl groups direct ortho/para relative to themselves, so positions 2, 4 and 6 are all electronically favored.
e: Electronics first, then sterics. Positions 2, 4 and 6 are each ortho or para to at least one methyl, and position 2 is ortho to both — on electronics alone it should win. But position 2 sits directly between the two substituents, and the incoming electrophile has to fit between them while that carbon goes sp³; in practice the position is almost entirely shut down. Positions 4 and 6 are equivalent by symmetry and take essentially all the product. The general rule this illustrates: a position with a substituent on each side is rarely substituted, however good it looks electronically.

q: The trifluoromethyl group, -CF3, attached to benzene is a deactivator and a meta director, similar in directing behavior to -NO2 even though it contains no pi b
e: Even without resonance capability, the three highly electronegative fluorines withdraw electron density strongly through induction alone, destabilizing positive charge most at ortho/para and making meta the relatively favored position, while also slowing the reaction overall.

q: Among -NH2, -CH3, and -Cl, which is the strongest activator of EAS on a benzene ring?
e: -NH2 is a powerful resonance electron donor (strong activator), -CH3 is only a weak inductive/hyperconjugative donor (mild activator), and -Cl is actually a net deactivator despite directing ortho/para, so -NH2 is by far the strongest activator of the three.

q: A sulfonic acid group, -SO3H, on a benzene ring acts as an EAS activator and directs ortho/para.
e: The statement is false: -SO3H is electron-withdrawing by induction and resonance, making it a deactivator and a meta director, similar in behavior to -COOH and -NO2.

q: Which resonance structure best explains why an electrophile attacking para to an -NH2 group on aniline is especially stabilized?
e: When the electrophile attacks para to -NH2, one of the resonance structures of the arenium cation places the positive charge on the ring carbon directly attached to nitrogen, allowing the nitrogen lone pair to form a new pi bond and place the positive charge formally on nitrogen (stabilized by its lone pair), which is an especially low-energy resonance contributor.

q: Why is meta attack on anisole (methoxybenzene) less favorable than ortho or para attack, even though meta attack is not directly destabilized by the methoxy gro
e: Resonance donation from the oxygen lone pair can only stabilize the arenium cation when one resonance structure places positive charge on the ring carbon attached to the methoxy group; this happens for ortho and para attack but not meta attack, leaving meta relatively less stabilized and thus disfavored.

q: If bromobenzene undergoes further bromination, the second bromine enters mainly at the meta position, since bromine deactivates the ring.
e: Deactivating and meta-directing are two separate claims, and the halogens are the one common case where they come apart. Bromine withdraws inductively, which slows the reaction — that half is right. But its lone pair still donates by resonance, and that donation is available in just the arenium ions that put positive charge on the carbon bearing the bromine, which is what ortho and para attack do. So the major products are o- and p-dibromobenzene, formed more slowly than benzene's own bromination.

q: A nitrile group, -C triple bond N, attached to benzene behaves most similarly to which other substituent in terms of its effect on EAS?
e: The nitrile's carbon is electron-poor and can accept electron density by resonance from the ring, withdrawing density most strongly from ortho/para positions, so it behaves like other deactivating, meta-directing groups such as -NO2 and -CHO.

q: An ester group, -COOCH3, attached to benzene is expected to be an EAS activator because it contains an oxygen atom with lone pairs that could donate into the ri
e: The statement is false; the carbonyl carbon directly attached to the ring is electron-poor and withdraws electron density by resonance, making -COOCH3 an overall deactivator and meta director, similar to other carbonyl-containing groups, despite having oxygen atoms present.

q: In EAS on para-xylene (1,4-dimethylbenzene), where would a new electrophile most likely attack, given that both methyl groups are ortho/para directors relative
e: Since both methyl groups favor ortho/para positions relative to themselves, and the remaining open ring positions are ortho to one methyl and meta to the other, those positions receive reinforcing activation from one group and are not disfavored strongly by the other, making them the preferred sites.

q: Fluorobenzene reacts in EAS more slowly than benzene itself, even though fluorine is the most electronegative halogen and might be expected to donate its lone p
e: True, though not for the reason the question hints at. Fluorine's resonance donation is genuinely the best of the halogens, because its 2p lone pairs match carbon's 2p in size, not because it is electronegative. Electronegativity works the other way: it drives strong inductive withdrawal through the sigma bond. The two effects nearly cancel, so fluorobenzene is only a little slower than benzene — much less deactivated than chlorobenzene or bromobenzene — while the strong resonance donation makes it the most para-selective of the halobenzenes.

q: Which best describes the inductive versus resonance effects of an -NH2 group on a benzene ring?
e: Nitrogen is modestly electronegative, causing a small inductive electron-withdrawing effect, but its lone pair's resonance donation into the aromatic pi system is much more significant, so the overall and net effect is strong activation directed to ortho/para.

q: A student claims that because -Cl deactivates the ring, it must also be a meta director, by analogy with -NO2. What is wrong with this reasoning?
e: While it is a useful generalization that most deactivators are meta directors, halogens are the key exception: their resonance donation (available due to a lone pair adjacent to the ring) still directs ortho/para even as their strong induction deactivates the ring, so deactivating and meta-directing are not always linked.

q: If a ketone group, -C(=O)CH3, is present on a benzene ring, subsequent nitration would be expected to occur predominantly at which position?
e: The carbonyl carbon is electron-poor and, by resonance, withdraws electron density most strongly from the ortho and para positions, destabilizing cationic intermediates there, so the meta position is favored for the incoming nitronium ion.

q: Ortho and para positions are favored by activating groups because, in at least one resonance structure of the arenium ion intermediate, the positive charge ends
e: This is the core reasoning behind ortho/para direction: only attack at ortho or para positions generates a resonance structure with positive charge adjacent to the donor substituent, where it can be most effectively stabilized by an adjacent lone pair or electron-rich group.

q: An amide group, -NHC(=O)CH3 (as in acetanilide), is a weaker activator and ortho/para director than a free -NH2 group, even though both have a nitrogen lone pai
e: In an amide, the nitrogen lone pair is partially pulled away into conjugation with the carbonyl group, leaving less electron density available to donate into the aromatic ring than a free amine has, so acetanilide activates the ring less strongly than aniline while still directing ortho/para.

q: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy primarily tells you about a molecule’s:
e: Different bonds (O–H, C=O, C≡N, etc.) vibrate at characteristic frequencies, so IR is mainly used to identify functional groups.

q: A broad absorption around 3200–3550 cm⁻¹ is most characteristic of:
e: An alcohol O–H is broadened by hydrogen bonding and falls in the 3200–3550 window, well clear of the sharp, strong C=O near 1700. A carboxylic acid O–H is broader still and sits lower, sprawling over 2500–3300, so it is not what a band confined to 3200–3550 is reporting.

q: A strong, sharp absorption around 1700-1750 cm⁻¹ most strongly suggests the presence of a:
e: The C=O stretch is a strong, sharp, and very diagnostic IR absorption typically found around 1700-1750 cm⁻¹ (exact position shifts slightly by functional group: ester, ketone, acid, amide, etc.).

q: Which functional group is most likely responsible for a very broad absorption spanning roughly 2500-3300 cm⁻¹ in an IR spectrum?
e: Carboxylic acids form strong hydrogen-bonded dimers, producing an unusually broad O-H stretch that spans and overlaps the C-H stretching region.

q: A typical dialkyl ketone C=O stretch appears in IR around:
e: Simple ketones show a strong, sharp carbonyl stretch near 1715 cm⁻¹; other carbonyl types shift higher or lower depending on the neighboring atoms.

q: A secondary amine (R2NH) typically shows two separate N-H stretching bands in its IR spectrum.
e: A primary amine has two N-H bonds and shows two bands; a secondary amine has only one N-H bond and shows a single N-H stretch.

q: A C-H stretching absorption appearing above 3000 cm⁻¹ most strongly suggests the carbon involved is:
e: C-H bonds on sp2 or sp carbons are stronger and stretch above 3000 cm⁻¹, while ordinary sp3 alkane C-H stretches fall just below 3000 cm⁻¹.

q: A weak-to-medium absorption around 2100–2260 cm⁻¹, accompanied by a sharp, narrow band at 3300 cm⁻¹, most likely indicates:
e: The 2100–2260 window holds both C≡C and C≡N, and intensity alone will not separate them: the alkyne band is weak, and vanishes entirely when the alkyne is symmetric, while a nitrile is sharp and medium. The discriminator is the second band — a sharp, narrow 3300 is the ≡C–H of a terminal alkyne, where an O–H at the same wavenumber would be broad and a nitrile has nothing there at all. An aromatic ring or a ketone absorbs nowhere near this region.

q: IR spectroscopy alone can usually determine the complete three-dimensional structure of an unknown molecule.
e: IR reveals which functional groups are present from characteristic bond vibrations, but not the full connectivity or 3D arrangement of atoms; other tools like NMR and mass spec are needed for that.

q: A sharp absorption near 2250 cm⁻¹ that is NOT accompanied by a sharp C-H stretch near 3300 cm⁻¹ most likely belongs to a:
e: Both nitriles and alkynes absorb near 2100-2260 cm⁻¹, but only a terminal alkyne also shows the sharp sp C-H stretch near 3300 cm⁻¹; a nitrile has no such C-H to produce that band.

q: The 'fingerprint region' of an IR spectrum, used to distinguish very similar molecules from each other, spans roughly:
e: Below about 1500 cm⁻¹, absorptions arise from complex combinations of bending and skeletal vibrations unique to each molecule, making this region a usable fingerprint even when individual bands are hard to assign.

q: A bond between two lighter atoms, such as C-H, generally stretches at a higher wavenumber than a bond between a carbon and a heavier atom, such as C-Cl, all els
e: Vibrational frequency increases as reduced mass decreases, so light-atom bonds like C-H vibrate much faster, and thus at higher wavenumber, than heavier-atom bonds like C-Cl.

q: An ester C=O stretch typically appears at a slightly higher wavenumber (about 1735-1750 cm⁻¹) than a ketone C=O (about 1715 cm⁻¹) mainly because:
e: The alkoxy oxygen withdraws electron density inductively and its resonance donation into the carbonyl is weaker than an amide nitrogen's, leaving the ester C=O stiffer and higher in frequency than a simple ketone.

q: Aldehydes can often be distinguished from ketones in IR by the presence of:
e: The C-H bond directly on the carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde gives a characteristic weak doublet near 2720 and 2820 cm⁻¹ that ketones, lacking that C-H, do not show.

q: An amide carbonyl typically absorbs at a lower wavenumber (about 1630-1695 cm⁻¹) than a ketone (about 1715 cm⁻¹) because:
e: Nitrogen's lone pair delocalizes strongly into the carbonyl pi system, increasing single-bond character in C=O and lowering its stretching frequency relative to a ketone.

q: Conjugating a ketone's carbonyl with an adjacent C=C double bond, forming an enone, typically lowers the C=O stretching frequency compared to the unconjugated k
e: Conjugation delocalizes pi electron density between the alkene and the carbonyl, giving the C=O bond more single-bond character and a lower force constant, shifting the stretch lower.

q: Compared to a simple alcohol's O-H stretch, a carboxylic acid's O-H stretch in IR is typically:
e: Carboxylic acids hydrogen-bond strongly to form dimers even in dilute solution, producing a very broad O-H absorption from roughly 2500-3300 cm⁻¹, broader than a typical alcohol O-H band.

q: An unknown compound's IR spectrum shows a single, moderately broad N-H stretch near 3300 cm⁻¹ with no second N-H band nearby. This is most consistent with:
e: A primary amine's two N-H bonds give two stretching bands, and a tertiary amine has no N-H at all, so a single N-H band points to a secondary amine.

q: A sharp, strong absorption near 3300 cm⁻¹ together with a weak triple-bond stretch near 2120 cm⁻¹ is most diagnostic of:
e: The sharp high-frequency band near 3300 cm⁻¹ comes from a C-H bonded directly to an sp carbon, which only a terminal alkyne has; an internal alkyne lacks that C-H band.

q: A higher carbonyl stretching wavenumber generally corresponds to a carbonyl bond with a higher force constant, meaning a stiffer, more double-bond-like C=O.
e: Stretching frequency scales with the square root of the force constant divided by reduced mass, so for similar atoms a stiffer, more double-bond-like bond vibrates at a higher wavenumber.

q: Cyclopentanone's carbonyl stretch appears at a noticeably higher wavenumber than cyclohexanone's. This ring-size effect is best explained by:
e: As ring size decreases and angle strain increases, the carbonyl carbon's bonding shifts in a way that stiffens the C=O bond, shifting the stretch to higher wavenumber; this trend continues for even smaller rings.

q: Why does conjugating a carbonyl with an aromatic ring, as in acetophenone, lower the C=O stretching frequency relative to a simple aliphatic ketone?
e: The ring donates electron density through conjugation, reducing the double-bond character of C=O, which softens the bond and lowers its stretching frequency compared to an unconjugated ketone.

q: A dilute solution of an alcohol in an inert solvent shows a sharp O-H stretch near 3600 cm⁻¹, but a concentrated solution of the same alcohol shows a broader ba
e: At low concentration, alcohol molecules are mostly isolated with a free O-H; at higher concentration, extensive hydrogen bonding weakens the O-H bond and broadens and lowers its absorption.

q: A carboxylic acid anhydride typically shows two distinct C=O stretching bands rather than one, due to vibrational coupling between the two carbonyl groups.
e: The two nearby carbonyls in an anhydride couple vibrationally, splitting the absorption into two bands, often one near 1820 and one near 1760 cm⁻¹, both higher than a typical ester.

q: Even though the aldehyde C-H doublet near 2720 and 2820 cm⁻¹ sits close to other C-H absorptions, it remains diagnostically useful mainly because:
e: Although weak, the aldehydic C-H doublet falls below most alkane and alkene C-H stretches, so even a small, distinct pair of bands there is a reliable clue when paired with a carbonyl absorption.

q: Rank the following from LOWEST to HIGHEST typical carbonyl stretching wavenumber: amide, ketone, ester, acid chloride.
e: Stronger resonance donation and weaker inductive withdrawal (as in an amide) lowers the frequency, while poor resonance donation with strong inductive withdrawal (as in an acid chloride) raises it the most, placing amide lowest and acid chloride highest.

q: An unknown shows a strong absorption near 1715 cm⁻¹ and a very broad absorption spanning roughly 2500-3300 cm⁻¹ that overlaps the C-H stretches, with no separat
e: A carbonyl stretch combined with a very broad, hydrogen-bonded O-H absorption smeared across the C-H region, rather than a sharp free O-H, is the classic signature of a carboxylic acid dimer.

q: IR spectroscopy using standard, non-polarized techniques can readily distinguish between two enantiomers of a chiral molecule.
e: Enantiomers have identical bond types and strengths, so their standard IR spectra are essentially indistinguishable; other techniques are needed to tell them apart.

q: An acid chloride's C=O stretch, around 1790-1815 cm⁻¹, is higher than both an ester's and an amide's mainly because:
e: Good pi donors, like an amide nitrogen, soften the C=O bond by adding single-bond character; chlorine's lone pairs overlap poorly with carbon, so its strong inductive pull dominates and stiffens the bond.

q: An unknown of formula C₄H₈O₂ shows IR bands at 2960 (medium), 1735 (very strong, sharp) and 1240 (strong), with a completely flat baseline from 2400 to 3600 cm⁻
e: The flat baseline from 2400 to 3600 is the decisive observation: it rules out every structure containing an O-H, which kills the acid and both alcohols. The survivor has to put both oxygens elsewhere, and 1735 is the ester carbonyl - a ketone would be 1715, an acid 1710, an aldehyde 1725 with a weak C-H doublet near 2720 and 2820 that is absent here. The strong 1240 band is the ester C-O.

q: ¹H NMR chemical shift (in ppm) tells you mainly about a hydrogen’s:
e: Electron-withdrawing groups nearby deshield a proton, shifting its signal downfield (higher ppm); shielded protons appear upfield.

q: The n+1 rule in ¹H NMR predicts that a proton with n chemically equivalent neighboring protons will show how many peaks (splitting)?
e: Spin-spin coupling with n equivalent neighbors splits a signal into n+1 peaks (e.g., 3 neighboring H’s give a quartet).

q: Why do aromatic (benzene-ring) protons typically appear far downfield (~7-8 ppm) in ¹H NMR compared to typical alkyl protons (~1-2 ppm)?
e: The delocalized aromatic pi electrons circulate in the applied magnetic field, generating a local magnetic field that reinforces the external field right at the ring’s edge, deshielding those protons and pushing their signal downfield.

q: In ¹H NMR, the integrated area under a peak tells you mainly about:
e: Integration is proportional to the number of protons contributing to a signal, so comparing integrated areas gives the ratio of protons in each chemically distinct environment.

q: Tetramethylsilane (TMS) is used as the standard reference in ¹H NMR mainly because its protons are:
e: TMS's methyl protons are more shielded than almost any organic proton, so they appear as a single peak at the upfield end of the spectrum (defined as 0 ppm), and TMS is unreactive and easily evaporated from the sample afterward.

q: A proton's chemical shift in ppm is essentially independent of the specific magnetic field strength of the NMR spectrometer used to record it.
e: Reporting shift as a ratio (ppm) relative to the operating frequency cancels out the field-strength dependence, which is exactly why ppm, rather than raw Hz, is used for comparing spectra from different instruments.

q: Deuterated chloroform (CDCl3) is a commonly used NMR solvent mainly because:
e: Replacing ordinary hydrogens with deuterium removes the solvent's own strong ¹H signal, leaving a largely clean baseline so the sample's proton signals can be seen clearly.

q: An aldehyde's C-H proton typically appears much further downfield (around 9-10 ppm) than a typical vinyl proton (around 5-6 ppm) mainly because:
e: The carbonyl's electron-withdrawing oxygen and its magnetic anisotropy both pull electron density away from the adjacent aldehyde proton, pushing its signal further downfield than an ordinary vinyl proton.

q: Hydroxyl (O-H) and amine (N-H) proton signals in ¹H NMR are often broader and appear at less predictable chemical shifts than typical C-H signals mainly because
e: Fast proton exchange (often catalyzed by trace acid, base, or water) averages the local environment and can broaden or shift the O-H/N-H signal, making it variable from sample to sample and solvent to solvent.

q: Spin-spin coupling between protons in ¹H NMR occurs primarily through space rather than through the chemical bonds connecting them.
e: Coupling is transmitted through the bonding electrons connecting the nuclei, which is why it typically falls off sharply beyond three bonds, not through direct spatial proximity.

q: Vicinal coupling, the most common type discussed in an introductory course, refers to coupling between protons that are separated by how many bonds?
e: Vicinal coupling is coupling between protons on adjacent (neighboring) carbons, which are three bonds apart (H-C-C-H), and is the basis of the simple n+1 splitting rule.

q: A compound of formula C₉H₁₀O₂ gives a ¹H NMR with four signals: 8.0 ppm (2H, d, J = 8 Hz), 7.3 ppm (2H, d, J = 8 Hz), 3.9 ppm (3H, s), 2.4 ppm (3H, s). Its IR h
e: All four options are C₉H₁₀O₂, so the formula eliminates none of them and the spectrum has to. Two 2H doublets sharing one J is the para-disubstituted pattern, so the ring carries two different groups at the 1 and 4 positions — which rules out ethyl benzoate, whose monosubstituted ring gives a 5H multiplet and whose ethyl group would give a quartet and a triplet, not two 3H singlets. The flat baseline above 3100 rules out the acid O–H. The 3H singlets separate the two esters: 3.9 ppm is a methyl on oxygen (the 3.3–4.5 window), 2.4 ppm a methyl on the ring. In 4-methylphenyl acetate nothing would appear near 3.9.

q: Comparing CH3Cl, CH2Cl2, and CHCl3, the chemical shift of the carbon-bound proton(s) moves progressively further downfield as the number of chlorine atoms incre
e: Each electronegative chlorine pulls electron density away inductively; stacking more of them on the same carbon compounds this effect, progressively deshielding the remaining protons and pushing the shift downfield.

q: Geminal coupling and vicinal coupling differ in that:
e: Geminal protons share one carbon (two bonds apart), while vicinal protons sit on neighboring carbons (three bonds apart); both can show coupling, but the structural relationship and typical coupling constants differ.

q: For an ethyl bromide fragment, CH3-CH2-Br, the n+1 rule predicts what splitting pattern for the two proton environments?
e: The CH3 protons have two neighboring CH2 protons, giving n+1 = 3 peaks (a triplet); the CH2 protons have three neighboring CH3 protons, giving n+1 = 4 peaks (a quartet).

q: Two protons on the same carbon can be diastereotopic and show different chemical shifts if replacing each one individually (in turn) with a test group would cre
e: When a molecule contains another stereocenter or similar feature, the two protons on a CH2 are no longer related by a simple symmetry operation, so they occupy genuinely different environments and can show different shifts and even couple to each other.

q: A terminal alkyne's C-H proton typically appears around 1.8-3.0 ppm, noticeably more upfield than a typical vinyl proton (around 4.5-6.5 ppm), even though the a
e: Unlike the carbonyl or aromatic pi systems, the circulating electrons around a linear triple bond generate an induced field that shields, rather than deshields, a proton sitting along the bond's axis, pulling its shift upfield despite the carbon's high s-character.

q: Vinyl (alkene) protons typically appear downfield, around 4.5-6.5 ppm, compared to ordinary alkyl protons. This is mainly due to:
e: The pi electrons of the C=C double bond circulate under the applied field and generate a local induced field that adds to the external field in the plane of the alkene, deshielding the attached protons and shifting them downfield.

q: A highly symmetric molecule like tert-butanol, (CH3)3C-OH, shows how many distinct ¹H NMR signals?
e: The nine equivalent methyl protons give one signal, and the single O-H proton gives a separate signal, for two total distinct environments despite there being ten hydrogens overall.

q: A typical vicinal coupling constant (3J) between protons on adjacent sp3 carbons usually falls in roughly what range?
e: Vicinal (three-bond) proton-proton coupling constants in freely rotating alkyl chains commonly fall around 6-8 Hz, a useful benchmark when analyzing splitting patterns.

q: Protons that are chemically equivalent to each other by molecular symmetry do not produce visible splitting from coupling to one another.
e: Although equivalent protons can technically couple, the splitting is not observed because identical nuclei in identical environments produce overlapping, indistinguishable transitions, so equivalent protons appear to ignore each other.

q: Why does adding a drop of D2O to an NMR sample often cause an O-H or N-H peak to shrink or disappear from the ¹H NMR spectrum?
e: O-H and N-H protons exchange rapidly with any other exchangeable protons present, including the large excess of deuterium in added D2O, converting O-H/N-H into O-D/N-D, which is invisible in a standard ¹H NMR spectrum.

q: For an isopropyl group, -CH(CH3)2, attached to a larger chain, the n+1 rule predicts what splitting for the central CH proton and the two equivalent CH3 groups?
e: The central CH proton is flanked by six equivalent methyl protons, giving n+1 = 7 peaks (a septet), while each methyl group's protons see only the one CH neighbor, giving n+1 = 2 peaks (a doublet).

q: A CH2 group flanked by a stereocenter elsewhere in the molecule can show an unusually complicated splitting pattern (such as an ABX-type pattern) rather than a
e: When the two CH2 protons are diastereotopic due to a nearby stereocenter, they are no longer chemically equivalent, so each can have its own shift and couple to the other proton on the same carbon as well as to outside neighbors, producing a more complex multiplet.

q: The simple n+1 rule for predicting splitting patterns assumes that a proton couples equally (with the same coupling constant) to all of its neighboring protons;
e: The n+1 rule is a simplification that works cleanly only when all relevant coupling constants are similar; unequal coupling constants to different sets of neighbors produce more complex patterns that must be analyzed as separate couplings rather than a single n+1 multiplet.

q: Rank the following methyl groups from most upfield to most downfield based on typical ¹H NMR chemical shift: CH3 attached to a plain alkyl carbon, CH3 attached
e: Plain alkyl CH3 is least deshielded (around 0.9 ppm); a carbonyl-adjacent CH3 is pulled somewhat downfield (around 2.1 ppm) by the electron-withdrawing carbonyl; an aromatic-ring CH3 is shifted further by ring anisotropy (around 2.3 ppm); and an O-CH3 is most deshielded (around 3.3-3.8 ppm) by the directly attached electronegative oxygen.

q: Why do long-range couplings across four or more bonds usually fail to produce visible splitting in a routine ¹H NMR spectrum of a simple flexible molecule?
e: Coupling is transmitted through bonding electrons, and its magnitude typically shrinks quickly as the number of intervening bonds grows, so beyond three bonds the coupling constant in a flexible, saturated system is usually too small to resolve as visible splitting.

q: An ethanol sample's O-H proton integrates to 1H in theory, but the measured integration can vary noticeably between samples and conditions. The most likely expl
e: Because O-H protons exchange rapidly with any available exchangeable protons (like trace water), the effective population and position of this signal is sensitive to moisture and sample purity, making its integration and shift less reproducible than for non-exchangeable C-H protons.

q: A proton held directly above the face of a benzene ring in a rigid molecule appears at 0.5 ppm, upfield of an ordinary alkane proton, while the protons on the r
e: One proton is shielded and the other deshielded by the same ring, so the ring's effect cannot be a single number attached to the group: it has a direction. The circulating pi electrons reinforce the applied field outside the ring and oppose it above the face - magnetic anisotropy. Geometry, not just which atoms are nearby, sets the shift.

q: Two protons related by an internal mirror plane of symmetry within an otherwise achiral, conformationally averaged molecule will typically give the same ¹H NMR
e: Protons related by a genuine symmetry operation of the molecule, such as reflection through an internal mirror plane, occupy equivalent environments on a time-averaged basis and therefore resonate at the same chemical shift.

q: ¹³C NMR typically shows each chemically distinct carbon as:
e: ¹³C is only ~1.1% natural abundance, so two ¹³C atoms are rarely adjacent — carbon-carbon coupling is negligible, giving simple, usually unsplit peaks (with standard decoupling).

q: A carbonyl carbon in ¹³C NMR typically appears:
e: Carbonyl carbons are strongly deshielded by the adjacent electronegative, pi-bonded oxygen, pushing their signal far downfield (160–220 ppm).

q: Why is ¹³C NMR generally less sensitive (requiring more sample/scans) than ¹H NMR?
e: Both the rarity of the ¹³C isotope and its inherently weaker NMR signal (lower gyromagnetic ratio) compared to ¹H make ¹³C NMR much less sensitive, requiring longer acquisition times.

q: In a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum, each peak generally corresponds to:
e: Each unique carbon environment gives rise to its own peak, regardless of how many hydrogens are attached to that carbon, which is different from how ¹H NMR integration works.

q: A ketone or aldehyde carbonyl carbon in ¹³C NMR typically appears in roughly what chemical shift range, making it the most downfield common signal?
e: Carbonyl carbons are strongly deshielded by the attached oxygen and the carbon's bonding, placing their signals well downfield of essentially all other common carbon environments.

q: A compound of formula C₅H₁₀O has a ¹³C spectrum with three peaks: 212, 35 and 8 ppm. In DEPT-135 the 212 peak is absent, the 35 peak points down, and the 8 peak
e: A peak at 212 that is absent from DEPT is a ketone carbonyl with no attached hydrogen. That rules out the aldehyde, whose carbonyl carbon carries an H and would appear in DEPT, and the alcohol, which has no carbonyl and would put its C-O carbon near 70. Three peaks for five carbons means the molecule is symmetric, and the down peak at 35 (a CH2) with the up peak at 8 (a CH3) puts an equivalent CH2 and CH3 on each side of the carbonyl. Pentan-2-one is unsymmetrical and gives five peaks.

q: The typical chemical shift range for ¹³C NMR signals (roughly 0-220 ppm) is much wider than for ¹H NMR (roughly 0-12 ppm). This is best explained by:
e: Because carbon sits at the center of bonding with more direct exposure to hybridization and substituent effects, its chemical shift is more sensitive to structural differences, spreading ¹³C signals over a much wider ppm range than ¹H signals.

q: In a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum, peak height or area reliably indicates the number of carbons contributing to that signal, the same way integrat
e: Differences in relaxation times and the nuclear Overhauser effect between different carbons (especially quaternary versus protonated carbons) make simple peak height or area an unreliable guide to the number of carbons in ¹³C NMR, unlike in ¹H NMR.

q: Aromatic ring carbons typically appear in ¹³C NMR in roughly what chemical shift region?
e: The delocalized pi system and partial double-bond character of aromatic carbons deshield them into the roughly 100-150 ppm region, distinct from both simple alkyl carbons and carbonyl carbons.

q: In a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum, why do we typically NOT observe splitting of one carbon's signal due to coupling with a neighboring carbon (car
e: Because ¹³C is rare (about 1.1 percent natural abundance), the odds that two bonded carbons are both the ¹³C isotope in the same molecule are very low, so carbon-carbon coupling is statistically almost never observed in a routine spectrum.

q: In a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum, each carbon peak typically appears as a single, unsplit line even though most carbons have one or more attached
e: A decoupling pulse sequence continuously flips the attached protons' spins during the ¹³C experiment, averaging out C-H coupling so each unique carbon gives one clean singlet instead of a complex multiplet.

q: A ketone's carbonyl carbon (around 205-220 ppm) appears at a higher chemical shift than an ester's carbonyl carbon (around 165-175 ppm). This difference is main
e: The ester oxygen's lone pair donates into the carbonyl pi system by resonance, increasing electron density at the carbonyl carbon and shielding it relative to a ketone, which lacks that extra donating oxygen.

q: Alkyne carbons typically appear around 65-90 ppm in ¹³C NMR, noticeably more upfield than alkene or aromatic carbons (roughly 100-150 ppm), even though all are
e: The linear, cylindrically symmetric pi system of a triple bond interacts with the applied field differently than a planar double bond's pi system, producing an anisotropic effect that shields sp alkyne carbons relative to sp2 alkene or aromatic carbons.

q: Because of its molecular symmetry, how many distinct ¹³C NMR signals would toluene (methylbenzene) show, given that the ring carbons pair up by symmetry?
e: Toluene has a mirror plane that makes the two carbons ortho to the methyl group equivalent to each other, and the two meta carbons equivalent to each other, giving five unique carbons total: the methyl carbon, the ipso carbon, the equivalent ortho pair, the equivalent meta pair, and the para carbon.

q: In a DEPT experiment, quaternary carbons (carbons with no attached hydrogens) are distinguished from CH, CH2, and CH3 carbons because:
e: DEPT transfers polarization from attached protons to the carbon nucleus, so a carbon with no attached hydrogens has nothing to receive that transfer from and simply does not show up in the DEPT spectrum.

q: Quaternary carbons typically show weaker peak intensities in a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum compared to protonated carbons of similar abundance.
e: Quaternary carbons lack the nuclear Overhauser enhancement from directly attached protons and often relax more slowly, both of which tend to make their signals weaker relative to protonated carbons, even at equal molar amounts.

q: Between a simple aldehyde's carbonyl carbon and a simple ketone's carbonyl carbon, which is generally found further downfield in ¹³C NMR?
e: Ketone carbonyl carbons typically fall around 205-220 ppm, while aldehyde carbonyl carbons are usually a bit more shielded, around 190-205 ppm, due to differences in the groups attached to the carbonyl carbon.

q: An sp3 carbon directly attached to a hydroxyl oxygen (as in an alcohol) typically appears around 50-90 ppm in ¹³C NMR, well downfield of a typical alkane carbon
e: Oxygen's electronegativity pulls electron density away from the carbon it is bonded to, deshielding that carbon and shifting its signal downfield relative to an ordinary alkane carbon.

q: Two carbons related by an internal mirror plane of symmetry in an achiral molecule will typically give the same ¹³C NMR chemical shift.
e: Just as with ¹H NMR, carbons related by a genuine symmetry operation of the molecule occupy chemically equivalent environments and therefore resonate at the same shift.

q: A carboxylic acid's carbonyl carbon (roughly 170-185 ppm) and an ester's carbonyl carbon (roughly 165-175 ppm) can sometimes be distinguished mainly by:
e: The shift ranges for these two carbonyl types overlap somewhat, so chemists often combine the ¹³C shift with other evidence, such as the presence of a broad O-H absorption in IR or an O-H proton in ¹H NMR, to tell them apart confidently.

q: A nitrile carbon (C of a C≡N group) typically appears around 115-120 ppm in ¹³C NMR, a range that must be interpreted carefully because:
e: 115-120 ppm sits inside the 110-160 aromatic range and at the bottom of the alkene range, so the shift on its own cannot prove a nitrile. What settles it is a second technique: a sharp, medium IR band near 2250 cm⁻¹ in a region where almost nothing else absorbs.

q: A para-disubstituted benzene ring with two different substituents, which breaks the ring's six-fold symmetry down to a single mirror plane, would be expected to
e: The mirror plane running through the two substituted carbons makes the two carbons next to one substituent equivalent to each other, and the two carbons next to the other substituent equivalent to each other, giving four unique aromatic carbons: the two substituted carbons plus the two equivalent pairs.

q: Why do we not typically observe carbon-carbon (¹³C-¹³C) spin coupling in a routine ¹³C NMR spectrum, even though carbons are directly bonded to each other throu
e: Since roughly 99 percent of carbon atoms are the spin-inactive ¹²C isotope, the probability that a given ¹³C nucleus happens to be bonded to another ¹³C nucleus is small, so carbon-carbon coupling is rarely visible above the noise in a normal spectrum.

q: A molecule can sometimes show a different total number of distinct ¹H NMR signals than distinct ¹³C NMR signals for the same structure. What is one reasonable e
e: Because chemical shift differences and coincidental overlaps differ between ¹H and ¹³C environments, and because symmetry can relate protons without necessarily relating the carbons carrying them (or vice versa), the number of resolved signals does not have to match between the two spectra.

q: In a DEPT-135 experiment, CH and CH3 carbons appear as positive peaks, CH2 carbons appear as negative (inverted) peaks, and quaternary carbons are absent altoge
e: Because DEPT signal phase and intensity depend on the number of attached protons, comparing a DEPT-135 spectrum to the standard ¹³C spectrum lets chemists sort carbons into CH3/CH, CH2, and quaternary categories, something ordinary ¹³C peak height cannot reliably do.

q: ¹³C NMR chemical shifts generally follow the same electronegativity-based deshielding trends seen in ¹H NMR, where attaching a more electronegative atom shifts
e: Both techniques respond to the same underlying electron-withdrawing inductive and resonance effects, so electronegative substituents deshield nearby carbons in ¹³C NMR in a way that parallels ¹H NMR trends, even though the absolute ppm shifts differ in scale.

q: Neopentane, (CH3)4C, has five carbon atoms but shows only two signals in ¹³C NMR. This is best explained by:
e: The four methyl groups are related by the molecule's high symmetry (effectively a tetrahedral arrangement around the central carbon), making them all chemically equivalent and giving just one methyl signal plus one signal for the unique central quaternary carbon.

q: Obtaining a good ¹³C NMR spectrum often requires longer acquisition times or more scans rather than simply increasing sample concentration, partly because:
e: Slow relaxation, particularly for quaternary carbons lacking nearby protons to help them relax, limits how quickly a ¹³C signal can be repeatedly sampled, so extending the number of scans (not just raising concentration) is often needed to achieve a usable spectrum.

q: A ¹³C spectrum of a compound with one oxygen-bearing functional group has its most downfield signal at 171 ppm and nothing at all between 186 and 220 ppm. What
e: Two windows do the work. A ketone or aldehyde carbonyl carbon comes at 190–220; an ester, acid or amide carbonyl is pulled upfield to roughly 165–185, because the attached O or N donates a lone pair into the C=O and puts electron density back on that carbon. A signal at 171 with a clean 190–220 region therefore says acid derivative and rules out ketone and aldehyde. What it does NOT do is say which acid derivative: those three overlap almost completely — acetamide 172.7, ethyl acetate 171.1, acetic acid 178 — so separating them needs the IR carbonyl position or an O–H / N–H signal, not the ¹³C shift.

q: In ¹³C NMR, a carbon's chemical shift is strongly affected by nearby electronegative atoms even two or three bonds away, similar to the pattern seen in ¹H NMR,
e: Inductive electron withdrawal from an electronegative atom propagates through several bonds in both ¹H and ¹³C NMR, deshielding nearby nuclei, with the effect weakening as the number of intervening bonds increases.

q: In mass spectrometry, the molecular ion peak (M+) corresponds to:
e: The molecular ion forms when the neutral molecule loses an electron in the ionization source, giving a radical cation at the molecule’s full mass.

q: A mass spec fragmentation pattern showing loss of 15 mass units from the molecular ion is most consistent with loss of:
e: A mass loss of 15 corresponds to CH₃ (methyl, 12+3=15), a very common fragmentation for molecules with a methyl group attached to a stabilizing center.

q: In mass spectrometry, the "base peak" refers to:
e: The base peak is defined as the most intense peak in the spectrum (100% relative abundance) — it is often, but not always, the same as the molecular ion peak.

q: In mass spectrometry, the term m/z refers to:
e: Mass spectrometers separate and detect ions based on their mass-to-charge ratio, m/z, which for most singly charged ions in an intro course is essentially equal to the ion's mass.

q: In electron ionization (EI) mass spectrometry, the molecular ion is typically formed by:
e: A high-energy electron beam knocks one electron out of the neutral molecule, leaving behind an odd-electron, positively charged species called the molecular ion or radical cation.

q: The molecular ion peak (M+) always corresponds to the most intense peak in the entire mass spectrum.
e: The most intense peak is called the base peak, and it is very often a fragment ion rather than the molecular ion, especially for molecules that fragment easily; M+ itself can be weak or even absent for some compounds.

q: The relative height of the M+1 isotope peak compared to M+ in a mass spectrum is mainly useful for estimating:
e: Since about 1.1 percent of carbon atoms are naturally ¹³C, the M+1 peak's relative intensity grows roughly in proportion to the number of carbons present, giving a rough estimate of carbon count.

q: A compound containing a single chlorine atom typically shows an M+2 peak with what approximate relative intensity compared to M+?
e: Chlorine's two natural isotopes, 35Cl and 37Cl, occur in roughly a 3:1 ratio, so a single-chlorine compound's M+2 peak (containing 37Cl) appears at roughly one-third the height of the M+ peak (containing 35Cl).

q: A compound containing a single bromine atom typically shows M+ and M+2 peaks of roughly what relative intensity to each other?
e: Bromine's two natural isotopes, 79Br and 81Br, occur in nearly equal abundance, so a single-bromine compound shows M+ and M+2 peaks of roughly similar height, a distinctive pattern compared to chlorine.

q: Loss of a methyl radical, corresponding to a mass loss of 15 units, from the molecular ion is a common fragmentation for branched alkyl compounds.
e: Cleaving off a methyl group is a frequent and often favorable fragmentation pathway, especially when it generates a more stable remaining cation, which is common in branched structures.

q: A mass spectral fragment showing a loss of 18 mass units from the molecular ion most commonly indicates loss of:
e: Loss of 18 mass units corresponds to H2O, a very common fragmentation pathway for alcohols (and some other oxygen-containing compounds) under electron ionization conditions.

q: The nitrogen rule states that, for typical organic compounds containing only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, and similar common elements, the molecular weig
e: Because nitrogen has an odd valence (typically three bonds) while carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen follow patterns that keep the overall mass even in their absence, each nitrogen atom added in a stable structure shifts the molecular weight's parity, making an odd number of nitrogens correspond to an odd molecular weight.

q: A loss of 28 mass units from a molecular ion is ambiguous on its own because it could correspond to either:
e: Both CO (common from ketones, aldehydes, and aromatic ethers) and C2H4 (common from retro-type eliminations) have a mass of 28, so this loss alone does not uniquely identify the fragmentation pathway without additional supporting evidence.

q: Alpha cleavage, the preferential breaking of a bond adjacent to a heteroatom such as nitrogen or oxygen, is a favorable fragmentation pathway mainly because:
e: When the bond next to an oxygen or nitrogen breaks, the heteroatom's lone pair can donate into the resulting cation through resonance, stabilizing it and making that fragmentation pathway especially favorable.

q: A McLafferty rearrangement in a carbonyl-containing compound requires the presence of what structural feature, and produces what kind of products?
e: The McLafferty rearrangement requires a gamma-hydrogen relative to the carbonyl so that a six-membered transition state can form, transferring that hydrogen and cleaving a bond to release a neutral alkene while leaving behind a stable, even-electron cation.

q: The characteristic tropylium cation at m/z 91 is commonly observed in the mass spectra of which class of compounds?
e: Benzylic cleavage of an alkylbenzene's side chain generates a benzylic cation that readily rearranges into the highly stable, resonance-delocalized seven-membered tropylium cation, observed at m/z 91.

q: More highly branched alkanes generally show a weaker molecular ion peak than their straight-chain isomers, because branching provides additional, more easily ac
e: Branch points allow formation of more stable secondary or tertiary carbocations upon fragmentation, making it energetically easier for the branched molecular ion to fall apart rather than survive intact, weakening the M+ peak relative to a straight-chain isomer.

q: A loss of 43 mass units from a molecular ion commonly corresponds to loss of which fragment(s)?
e: Both the isopropyl radical (C3H7, mass 43) and the acetyl cation-forming group (CH3CO, also mass 43) are common fragments lost from molecular ions, so a loss of 43 alone is often ambiguous without further context.

q: In the mass spectrum of a simple aldehyde, a loss of 29 mass units from the molecular ion most commonly corresponds to loss of:
e: Alpha cleavage adjacent to the aldehyde carbonyl commonly ejects the formyl radical, CHO, which has a mass of 29, leaving behind a stabilized carbon-centered cation.

q: Aromatic compounds often show a strong, easily recognized molecular ion peak relative to many aliphatic compounds mainly because:
e: The aromatic ring can delocalize the positive charge and radical character of the molecular ion over the ring system, stabilizing it and making the intact M+ more likely to survive and be detected as a prominent peak.

q: An unknown shows a molecular ion at m/z 120 with an M+1 peak about 8.8% as tall, no M+2 of any significance, a base peak at m/z 105, and a further strong fragme
e: M+1 at 8.8% of M means about 8.8/1.1 = 8 carbons. The missing M+2 rules out chlorine, whose M+2 would stand at roughly a third of M, and the flat baseline above 3100 rules out benzoic acid's very broad O-H. The base peak at 105 is M - 15, a methyl lost by alpha cleavage to leave the benzoyl cation, which then loses CO to give the phenyl cation at 77. Benzaldehyde has no methyl to lose and weighs 106.

q: When an alkane's molecular ion fragments by breaking a carbon-carbon bond, the fragmentation pathway that generates the most stable resulting carbocation (terti
e: Fragmentation in the gas phase favors pathways that produce the most stable cation, following the same substitution-based stability trend (tertiary greater than secondary greater than primary) used to rationalize carbocation stability throughout organic chemistry.

q: An unknown compound's mass spectrum shows significant fragment peaks corresponding to loss of 15 (a methyl group) and loss of 29 (an ethyl-related fragment) fro
e: Alpha cleavage on either side of an asymmetric ketone's carbonyl generates two different acylium-type cations, explaining why both a methyl loss (15) and a loss consistent with the other alkyl substituent pattern can appear together in the spectrum of a compound like methyl ethyl ketone.

q: Loss of a single hydrogen atom, a mass loss of just 1 unit, from the molecular ion is relatively uncommon as a dominant fragmentation pathway compared to loss o
e: Because forming larger, more stable radicals (or undergoing favorable rearrangements like McLafferty) is usually more thermodynamically favorable than simply ejecting a lone hydrogen atom, simple H-loss is typically a minor pathway rather than the dominant one.

q: A high-resolution mass spectrometer can distinguish between two different molecular formulas that share the same nominal (whole-number) mass, such as C2H4O and
e: Individual isotopes have exact masses that are not perfectly whole numbers (for example, carbon-12 is defined as exactly 12, but hydrogen and oxygen have slightly different fractional exact masses), so formulas with the same nominal mass usually have distinguishably different exact masses when measured with sufficient precision.

q: The relative intensity of a peak in a mass spectrum reflects the relative abundance of that particular gas-phase ion reaching the detector, which is governed by
e: Mass spectral peak intensities depend on how readily a given ion forms and survives under gas-phase ionization and fragmentation conditions, a distinct context from solution-phase stability, solubility, or reactivity, which are not what mass spectrometry intensities measure.

q: A cyclic secondary alcohol's mass spectrum can show both a loss of 18 (water) and a loss of 28 (often consistent with ethylene or CO) from the molecular ion. A
e: Molecular ions are not limited to a single fragmentation route; different bonds can break under the conditions of electron ionization, so a cyclic alcohol can plausibly show both a straightforward water loss and a separate ring-related elimination pathway in the same spectrum.

q: For a simple carboxylic acid, a loss of 45 mass units from the molecular ion typically corresponds to loss of:
e: Alpha cleavage adjacent to the carbonyl-bearing carbon of a carboxylic acid commonly ejects the COOH group, which has a combined mass of 45, leaving behind the remaining alkyl cation.

q: Why does electron ionization (EI) typically produce a radical cation (an odd-electron species) as the molecular ion, rather than an even-electron cation?
e: Since a neutral organic molecule normally has all its electrons paired, knocking out just one electron during EI necessarily leaves an odd, unpaired electron along with the resulting positive charge, producing a radical cation.

q: Combining the nitrogen rule with an observed odd molecular ion mass for a compound containing only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen, what can be concluded
e: According to the nitrogen rule, an odd molecular weight for a typical CHNO compound implies an odd number of nitrogen atoms, since each nitrogen (with its odd valence pattern) shifts the overall parity of the molecular mass.

q: What does the open double-lined arrow mean in retrosynthesis?
e: It points the other way in time from an ordinary reaction arrow, which is why it is drawn differently.

q: What is a disconnection?
e: Nothing physically breaks. You are asking which two pieces, joined by a reaction you know, would give that bond.

q: What makes a disconnection legitimate?
e: If you cannot say what reagents would rejoin the pieces, you have drawn a picture rather than planned a synthesis.

q: Target: 1-phenylpentan-1-one, PhCO(CH2)3CH3, starting from benzene. Which disconnection leads to the cleanest route?
e: A C-C bond joining a ring to a carbonyl carbon is the acylation retron, and the forward step is benzene plus CH3(CH2)3COCl with AlCl3. Naming that forward reaction is what makes the cut legal. The alkylation cut builds the wrong skeleton - an alkylbenzene with no carbonyl at all - and its cation would rearrange on the way. An aldol needs two carbonyl partners and there is one here, and a Wittig makes an alkene rather than a ketone.

q: You disconnect the C-C bond of PhCH(OH)CH3 at the carbinol carbon. Which polarity assignment can you actually run?
e: Every polar disconnection hands you one nucleophile and one electrophile, because that is what a polar bond-forming reaction is. Ph- has an equivalent you can buy into - PhMgBr - and the carbonyl carbon of acetaldehyde is already the electrophile. The reversed assignment would need an anion at acetaldehyde's carbonyl carbon, which is not a reagent at this level, and two nucleophiles or two electrophiles cannot bond to each other at all.

q: Your analysis ends at bromobenzene, magnesium and propanal. In what order do you run them forwards?
e: A tree is read back from its leaves, so the last disconnection you drew is the first reaction you run. The Grignard has to exist before it has anything to attack, so bromobenzene meets magnesium in dry ether first and the aldehyde goes in second. Putting the aldehyde in early, or everything in at once, leaves magnesium and a carbonyl in one flask with no control over what forms.

q: What is a retron?
e: Learning to see retrons is most of what makes an experienced chemist fast at this.

q: A beta-hydroxy ketone is the retron for which reaction?
e: Disconnect between the alpha carbon and the carbinol carbon: the fragments are an enolate and a carbonyl.

q: A 1,3-dicarbonyl is the retron for which reaction?
e: Disconnect between the alpha carbon and the second carbonyl, giving an ester enolate and an ester.

q: A cyclohexene is the retron for which reaction?
e: One disconnection undoing two bonds, which is why it is the highest-value move in the list.

q: A tertiary alcohol is the retron for which reaction?
e: Any C-C bond to the carbinol carbon can be disconnected into a carbanion and a ketone.

q: Which is generally the best place to disconnect?
e: Functional groups are where reactivity lives, so those bonds are the ones you have reactions for.

q: When do you stop disconnecting?
e: A question usually names the permitted starting materials, and that constraint is the real definition of done.

q: Disconnecting 2-phenylbutan-2-ol at the ethyl group gives which pair?
e: The synthons are the carbanion and the ketone; their equivalents are the Grignard and acetophenone.

q: Target: butanoic acid from propan-1-ol and any one-carbon reagent. What does the carbon count force?
e: Count first: propan-1-ol has three carbons and butanoic acid four, so exactly one C-C bond is formed and the new carbon is the carboxyl carbon itself. That is a one-carbon extension, and two of them land at acid level: PBr3, NaCN, then H3O+ with heat; or PBr3, Mg, then CO2 and workup. Oxidizing propan-1-ol gives propanoic acid, because no oxidation has ever added a carbon.

q: Why write the forward route out at the end?
e: The forward list is a claim: every step has reagents, a product, and a check that it survives the next step.

q: Which disconnection undoes two bonds at once?
e: Cutting across a six-membered ring containing an alkene gives a diene and a dienophile.

q: Target: hexan-3-one, permitted pieces acetylene and bromoethane. Which backward move comes first?
e: The permitted pieces are two carbons each, so the six-carbon skeleton has to be assembled by acetylide alkylations - and those build alkynes, not ketones. Rewriting the ketone as hex-3-yne cuts nothing, but it turns the target into one whose C-C bonds you have a reaction for, which is what an FGI is for. Cutting next to the carbonyl first gives aldol fragments with alpha hydrogens on both sides, so the forward reaction would be a mixture, and a Grignard on CO2 makes carboxylic acids.

q: Why is a shorter route usually preferred?
e: Though the arithmetic is worth doing: a longer route of good steps can beat a shorter one of poor steps.

q: What should you do before disconnecting anything?
e: The difference tells you how many C-C bonds must form and what size pieces you need.

q: Which starting-material pair is the aldol disconnection of PhCH(OH)CH2COCH3?
e: Cut the bond between the carbinol carbon and the alpha carbon: the fragments are the enolate of acetone and benzaldehyde. It is a good disconnection precisely because benzaldehyde has no alpha hydrogen, so only one partner can enolize and no mixture results.

q: You disconnect a beta-hydroxy ketone into two fragments that both have alpha hydrogens. What is wrong?
e: Either partner can enolize and either can be attacked, so a simple base gives all four aldol products. The disconnection is clean only if one partner has no alpha hydrogen, or if one enolate is formed quantitatively first with a strong hindered base.

q: Roughly how many ways are there to make a C-C bond in an introductory course?
e: Which is what makes synthesis learnable: the skeleton can only be built in a few places.

q: 1-bromopropane is treated with NaCN, then with H3O+ and heat. What is the product?
e: Cyanide does an SN2 on the primary halide to give butanenitrile, four carbons, and hot aqueous acid hydrolyzes the nitrile to the acid. LiAlH4 on that same nitrile would have given butan-1-amine instead, which is the pair worth keeping straight.

q: Which reagent is missing? Cyclohexanone + ?, then H3O+ workup, gives 1-ethylcyclohexan-1-ol.
e: A C-C bond to a carbinol carbon means a carbanion attacked the carbonyl carbon, and the carbanion here carries two carbons. Ethanol is not nucleophilic at carbon at all, cyanide would give a cyanohydrin, and bromoethane is an electrophile rather than a nucleophile.

q: Conjugate addition builds a bond at which carbon?
e: Two positions away from the carbonyl, which is the third attachment point a carbonyl offers.

q: Why is counting carbons the fastest diagnostic?
e: And roughly what size pieces you need, which narrows ten reactions to two or three.

q: Which enolate reactions are essentially one idea?
e: An enolate attacking something electrophilic, differing in what the electrophile is.

q: A carbonyl offers how many distinct attachment points for a new carbon?
e: The carbonyl carbon, the alpha carbon via an enolate, and the beta carbon via conjugate addition.

q: A move up or down the oxidation ladder needs what kind of reagent?
e: Sideways moves within one level are substitutions and need no redox reagent at all.

q: Alcohol to alkyl halide is which kind of move?
e: One bond to an electronegative atom traded for another, with the hydrogen count unchanged.

q: Which conditions give a trans alkene from an alkyne?
e: A dissolving-metal reduction through radical anions, which adopt the less hindered arrangement.

q: How do you make an aldehyde from an ester using only standard reagents?
e: Down two rungs and back up one, because the reduction cannot be stopped halfway.

q: You need the anti-Markovnikov chloride from 2-methylpropene. Which route delivers it?
e: The peroxide effect belongs to HBr alone: the radical chain works because H-Br has the right bond strengths, and HCl and HI add Markovnikov whatever is in the flask. So there is no one-step anti-Markovnikov chloride. Hydroboration-oxidation puts the OH on the less substituted carbon, giving 2-methylpropan-1-ol, and SOCl2 then swaps OH for Cl without touching the skeleton. Had the target been the bromide, HBr with peroxides would have done it in one step.

q: Which sequence gives an anti diol from an alkene?
e: The epoxide is opened by backside attack, putting the oxygens on opposite faces.

q: Which sequence converts propan-1-ol into propan-2-ol?
e: Dehydrate to propene, then hydrate under acid: Markovnikov puts the OH on the more substituted carbon, which is C2. Every other route here returns the oxygen to C1, because PBr3 and NaOH both act at the same carbon and each redox pair comes back down to the carbinol carbon it started from.

q: Hex-1-yne is treated with H2O, H2SO4 and HgSO4. What is the product?
e: Markovnikov hydration puts the oxygen on the more substituted alkyne carbon, giving an enol that tautomerizes to the methyl ketone. Hydroboration-oxidation of the same alkyne with a bulky borane is the anti-Markovnikov partner and gives hexanal instead.

q: How do you control where an alkene forms from an alcohol?
e: Acid-catalyzed dehydration gives Zaitsev and can rearrange; E2 on a halide lets you choose.

q: Which groups also destroy a Grignard?
e: Any acidic proton, which is also why the reaction is run in scrupulously dry ether.

q: What protects an alcohol from a Grignard?
e: TBSCl with imidazole replaces the O-H with an O-Si bond, leaving no acidic proton.

q: How is a silyl ether removed?
e: The Si-F bond is exceptionally strong, so fluoride pulls the silicon off under conditions that disturb nothing else. Mild aqueous acid is exactly what a silyl ether is chosen to survive, which is what makes it orthogonal to an acetal.

q: What protects a ketone from a hydride or Grignard?
e: The acetal has no C=O and no electrophilic carbon, so there is nothing to attack.

q: A molecule has an aldehyde and an ester, and you want to reduce only the ester. Protect?
e: The aldehyde is the MORE reactive of the two, so there is no way to reach the ester selectively.

q: Why is adding an extra equivalent of Grignard, rather than protecting, a poor plan when the substrate has a free OH?
e: The acid-base reaction is instant and consumes a full equivalent. What is left is a heterogeneous magnesium alkoxide that ties up reagent and makes the addition unreliable, so it is a bench expedient at best and protection is the answer a synthesis question wants.

q: Why can a silyl ether be removed without disturbing the rest of a molecule?
e: The driving force is the Si-F bond, one of the strongest single bonds in chemistry, so TBAF strips the silicon under conditions that are neither strongly acidic nor basic nor oxidizing - which is exactly what lets it act on a molecule carrying almost anything else.

q: You need a Grignard reagent from 5-bromopentan-2-one. What is step one?
e: Without protection, the first Grignard that forms attacks the ketone of the next molecule and the reagent destroys its own starting material. The acetal removes the electrophile, the Grignard then forms cleanly, and the aqueous acid workup after the addition takes the acetal off again.

q: What happens to a Grignard in wet solvent?
e: Water does exactly what an alcohol O-H does, which is why dry ether is essential.

q: Methyl 4-oxopentanoate is treated with (1) ethylene glycol and H+, (2) LiAlH4, (3) H3O+. What does the sequence accomplish?
e: LiAlH4 cannot tell a ketone from an ester and would reduce both, so the ketone is masked as an acetal first, reduced past, and unmasked in the workup. The acetal is inert to hydride, which is precisely why it is the standard carbonyl mask.

q: What should you do after finishing a retrosynthetic analysis?
e: Errors of order are invisible in a retrosynthetic tree and obvious in a forward list.

q: What is wrong with a route giving a single enantiomer from achiral inputs?
e: Getting one enantiomer needs a chiral reagent, catalyst, starting material, or a resolution.

q: What final check catches an extra carbon in your route?
e: Cyanide, CO2 and formaldehyde routes all add exactly one carbon, so mixing them up is easy.

q: What does the question 'does this product survive the next step' catch?
e: Making an aldehyde and then running a reaction in aqueous base will not leave you with an aldehyde.

q: What should you ask about stereochemistry in a route?
e: If the target has defined stereochemistry, some step has to set it, and you should be able to name it.

q: Benzene is treated with (1) CH3CH2COCl/AlCl3, (2) Zn(Hg)/HCl, (3) HNO3/H2SO4. What is the major product?
e: Acylation puts an unrearranged propanoyl group on, Clemmensen strips it to propyl, and propyl is an ortho/para director, so nitration lands mainly para. Had step 1 been an alkylation with 1-bromopropane, the answer would have been the isopropyl compound instead.

q: Which order makes 3-nitroacetophenone from benzene?
e: The acyl group is a meta director, so nitrating acetophenone puts the NO2 meta and gives the target. The reverse order fails outright, because Friedel-Crafts does not work on a ring already carrying a nitro group.

q: A route ends: ... gives an aldehyde, then NaOH in water, warm, gives the target. What is the objection?
e: An aldehyde with alpha hydrogens enolizes in aqueous base and undergoes an aldol condensation with itself. This is the second of the four questions - does the product of one step survive the next - and an aldehyde followed by base is the commonest way to fail it.

q: Which sequence turns hex-3-yne into (3R,4R)- and (3S,4S)-3,4-dibromohexane and nothing else?
e: Bromine adds anti across a double bond, so the geometry of the alkene decides which diastereomer appears. Lindlar gives the cis alkene, and anti addition to it gives the pair of enantiomers named. Na in ammonia would give the trans alkene and hence the meso (3R,4S) dibromide, and Pd/C would over-reduce to hexane.

q: What is a carbohydrate, in functional-group terms?
e: Every property of a sugar follows from a carbonyl surrounded by alcohols on the same chain.

q: D-glucose is stirred with NaBH4 in water. What is the product?
e: The ring is a hemiacetal in equilibrium with a trace of open-chain aldehyde, and hydride reduces that aldehyde to a primary alcohol. Consuming the open chain pulls the equilibrium across, so the whole sample converts to the alditol.

q: Fructose has its carbonyl at C2. What does that make it?
e: Six carbons and an internal carbonyl: keto- for the position, -hexose for the count.

q: In a Fischer projection, which carbon decides whether a sugar is D or L?
e: One carbon carries the whole label, and it is the one at the bottom of the drawing.

q: Does calling a sugar D tell you which way it rotates polarized light?
e: D fixes one stereocenter's drawn position; the observed rotation is a measured property of the whole molecule.

q: What forms when the C5 OH of glucose adds to its own C1 carbonyl?
e: One alcohol plus one carbonyl gives a hemiacetal; it takes a second alcohol to reach an acetal.

q: Methyl alpha-D-glucopyranoside is warmed in dilute aqueous HCl, then tested with Tollens' reagent. What is seen?
e: A glycoside is a full acetal, so on its own it gives nothing: the ring cannot open. Aqueous acid reverses acetal formation, releasing methanol and free glucose, and the restored hemiacetal then opens to the aldehyde Tollens' oxidizes.

q: Which carbon of the ring form is the anomeric carbon?
e: It was the carbonyl carbon, so after cyclization it holds the ring oxygen and an OH.

q: What are anomers?
e: They differ at the anomeric carbon only, which is the one stereocenter the ring can open and reset.

q: Which reagent converts D-glucose to D-gluconic acid and leaves the secondary alcohols untouched?
e: Bromine water takes the open-chain aldehyde to a carboxylic acid and stops. Chromium(VI) would oxidize the secondary alcohols too, borohydride reduces, and methanol with acid caps the anomeric carbon as a glycoside.

q: Which anomer of D-glucopyranose dominates at equilibrium?
e: Beta puts the anomeric OH equatorial, and glucose is the sugar that can get every substituent equatorial.

q: What makes a sugar a reducing sugar?
e: The test oxidizes the open-chain aldehyde, so the ring has to be able to open to supply it.

q: Capping the anomeric OH with a second alcohol gives what?
e: Two OR groups on the anomeric carbon is a full acetal, and the sugar-specific name for it is glycoside.

q: Which reagent takes D-glucose to D-glucaric acid, the diacid oxidized at both C1 and C6?
e: Bromine water stops at the aldehyde and gives the aldonic acid. Reaching the terminal CH2OH as well needs a stronger oxidant, and warm dilute nitric acid takes both ends at once to give the aldaric acid.

q: Cellulose and amylose are both 1,4 chains of D-glucose. What differs?
e: One stereocenter on one carbon, and the two materials could hardly behave less alike.

q: Why can humans digest starch but not cellulose?
e: The enzyme reads the configuration at the anomeric carbon, and it only fits alpha.

q: Fructose is a ketose, yet it gives a positive Tollens' test. Why?
e: The test medium is basic, and an alpha deprotonation gives an enediol that can collapse to the aldose.

q: Which reagent distinguishes an aldehyde from an acetal at the anomeric carbon?
e: Tollens' oxidizes the free aldehyde a hemiacetal supplies, and an acetal supplies none.

q: Why is beta-D-glucopyranose the most stable common hexose ring?
e: No 1,3-diaxial strain anywhere in the chair, which is a conformational argument, not a new one.

q: In the Fischer projection of a D-aldohexose the C3 OH is drawn on the left. Where does it point in the Haworth ring?
e: Left in Fischer becomes up in Haworth and right becomes down. The rule holds at every carbon but C5, whose OH has become the ring oxygen, and the anomeric configuration is set separately at C1.

q: Which structure is the right way to draw alanine in water at pH 7?
e: The carboxyl (pKa near 2) is a far stronger acid than the ammonium (pKa near 9), so at any pH between them the proton has already moved across. Both ends are charged and the molecule is overall neutral, which is why amino acids behave like salts.

q: Which L-amino acid has the R configuration?
e: Sulfur outranks the carboxyl carbon in CIP priority, so the ranking around the alpha carbon reshuffles.

q: What is the dominant form of an amino acid near neutral pH?
e: A pKa 2 acid and a pKa 9 base in one molecule transfer the proton to each other.

q: Which sequence turns a carboxylic acid into the alpha-amino acid with the same carbon skeleton?
e: Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky puts a bromine on the alpha carbon, and excess ammonia displaces it by SN2. The aldehyde route is Strecker, reaching the same product class from a different start. Both form the stereocenter at a planar intermediate, so both give a racemate.

q: Roughly what is the pKa of an amino acid's alpha-ammonium group?
e: Typical for an alkylammonium ion, pulled down slightly by the adjacent carboxylate.

q: What is the isoelectric point?
e: Plus and minus cancel exactly, which is a property of the pH rather than of the molecule alone.

q: Lysine has pKa values 2.18, 8.95 and 10.53. What is its pI?
