e: Build the charge ladder: +2 below 2.18, +1 from 2.18 to 8.95, zero from 8.95 to 10.53, -1 above. The uncharged form is bracketed by 8.95 and 10.53, so the pI is their average. Averaging the lowest two gives 5.57.

q: Glycine has pKa values 2.34 and 9.60. What is its pI?
e: Half of the sum. Note it is below 7, so an isoelectric solution is mildly acidic.

q: Glutamic acid has pKa values 2.19 (alpha-COOH), 4.25 (side-chain COOH) and 9.67 (alpha-NH3+). Which form is present at pH 7?
e: Take the groups one at a time against pH 7. Both carboxyl pKa values are well below 7, so both are deprotonated. The ammonium pKa is 9.67, so it keeps its proton. Two minuses against one plus is a net -1.

q: Aspartic acid has a pI of 2.77. Why so low?
e: Two acidic groups have to be neutralized before the molecule is uncharged, so the balance point drops.

q: Lysine has a pI near 9.7. What does that tell you?
e: A second amine has to stay protonated, so you must go to high pH before the charge cancels.

q: At pH 7, what is the charge on a lysine side chain?
e: The side-chain ammonium has a pKa near 10.5, so at pH 7 it is overwhelmingly protonated.

q: Which class does phenylalanine's side chain belong to?
e: A benzyl group with no heteroatom, so water pushes it into the protein's interior.

q: Which amino acid can form a covalent cross-link in a protein?
e: Two SH groups oxidize to a disulfide, the only covalent link outside the backbone.

q: Where do nonpolar side chains end up in a folded, water-soluble protein?
e: The hydrophobic effect: burying them frees the water that would otherwise be ordered around them.

q: Histidine is the only side chain with a pKa near 6. Why does that matter?
e: A pKa near the working pH means the residue can act as either an acid or a base in a mechanism.

q: How would you separate two amino acids with pI values of 3.2 and 9.7?
e: A pH between the two pI values forces them to opposite signs, so they migrate in opposite directions.

q: Why is an amino acid least soluble in water at its pI?
e: Without a net charge there is no electrostatic repulsion keeping the molecules apart.

q: How many ionizable groups does aspartic acid have?
e: Two carboxyls and one ammonium, so three pKa values and a pI set by the lowest two.

q: What functional group is a peptide bond?
e: A carboxyl joined to an amine with loss of water gives an amide, and nothing about proteins changes that.

q: Why can a dipeptide not be made simply by heating glycine and alanine together?
e: Nothing tells either molecule which of its two groups to use, so every ordered pairing forms: Gly-Gly, Ala-Ala, Gly-Ala and Ala-Gly. Controlling it means protecting one amine and one carboxyl, activating what is left, coupling, then deprotecting.

q: An amine will not attack a carboxylic acid directly. Which reagent makes the coupling go?
e: An amine meeting a carboxylic acid takes its proton instead of attacking it, and the carboxylate left behind is a poor electrophile. DCC turns the acid's OH into a group that leaves readily, and the amine then does ordinary acyl substitution.

q: Why is rotation about the peptide C-N bond restricted?
e: Rotating would break the overlap that the second resonance structure depends on.

q: Is the peptide nitrogen basic?
e: A lone pair already spent on the neighboring carbonyl cannot also grab a proton.

q: Where is an amide protonated in strong acid?
e: Protonating oxygen keeps the resonance stabilization; protonating nitrogen would destroy it.

q: How does an amide rank among acyl derivatives for reactivity?
e: The strongest lone-pair donation gives the greatest stabilization and the lowest reactivity.

q: What is primary structure?
e: The only level whose structure is its covalent bonds, and the one from which the others follow.

q: Edman degradation is run on the peptide Ala-Gly-Phe-Lys. Which residue is identified, and what is left?
e: Phenyl isothiocyanate is attacked by the free N-terminal amino group, so the reagent reads from the N-terminus and removes one residue per cycle. The shortened peptide survives and goes round again; complete hydrolysis would destroy the order.

q: What contributes most to tertiary structure?
e: Burying nonpolar side chains releases the ordered water around them, which is the large term.

q: Which interaction in a folded protein is covalent?
e: Everything else holding a fold together is noncovalent, which is why folding is reversible.

q: Why does boiling not hydrolyze a protein to amino acids?
e: An amide is the least reactive acyl derivative, and 100 C water is nowhere near enough.

q: Why does proline disrupt an alpha helix?
e: No N-H means no hydrogen bond donor at that position, and the ring restricts the geometry.

q: Which level of structure does a single point mutation change directly?
e: It changes one residue in the sequence, and the other levels change only as a consequence.

q: Trypsin cleaves on the carboxyl side of lysine and arginine. A 300-residue protein holds 12 lysines and 7 arginines, none at the C-terminus. How many fragments?
e: Nineteen cleavage sites cut one chain into twenty pieces, because n cuts give n+1 fragments. A lysine already at the end of the chain would add no cut, which is why the question rules that out.

q: Why can any sequence form a beta sheet in principle?
e: Secondary structure is a backbone property, so the side chains only tip the preference.

q: What makes a protein water soluble?
e: The fold puts the polar residues outside and the nonpolar ones in, which is the hydrophobic effect stated the other way round.

q: How is the lipid class defined?
e: It collects the cell components that dissolve in nonpolar solvents, which is why it holds fats and steroids together.

q: Glyceryl trioleate is stirred with excess H2 over palladium until no alkene remains. What has changed?
e: Catalytic hydrogenation reduces C=C and leaves esters alone, so the product is glyceryl tristearate. Taking the kinks out lets the chains pack, which is why an oil hardens into a fat.

q: Why does a cis double bond lower a fatty acid's melting point?
e: Melting separates molecules, and a bent chain makes much less contact with the next one.

q: Elaidic acid is C18 with one trans double bond and melts near 44 C. What does that show?
e: It is unsaturated and still nearly as high-melting as the saturated acid, because it is still straight.

q: A triglyceride carrying one stearic, one oleic and one palmitic acid is refluxed with excess aqueous NaOH. What is in the flask?
e: Three ester groups means three hydrolyses, and the acyl groups on a natural fat differ, so the products are sodium stearate, oleate and palmitate plus glycerol. Excess hydroxide deprotonates each acid as it forms, so nothing runs back.

q: What does heating a triglyceride with aqueous NaOH give?
e: Base-promoted ester hydrolysis three times over, and the excess base deprotonates each acid.

q: Why do phospholipids form bilayers rather than micelles?
e: A one-tailed molecule tapers into a sphere; a two-tailed one is a cylinder and tiles into a sheet.

q: What is the lipid bilayer?
e: Tails inward and heads facing the water on both sides, which is every cell membrane.

q: What does cholesterol do in a membrane?
e: A rigid ring system inserted among flexible chains changes how easily they move.

q: What is partial hydrogenation used for industrially?
e: Removing double bonds straightens chains, so the material packs better and melts higher.

q: Why does partial hydrogenation create trans fats?
e: An alkene that picks up one hydrogen and loses it again does not remember its original geometry.

q: Hydrolyzing a lipid gives exactly two products in equal amounts: one long-chain acid and one long-chain primary alcohol. What was it?
e: One acid and one alcohol in a one-to-one ratio means a single ester joining two long chains, which is a wax. A triglyceride gives three acids and one glycerol, a phospholipid releases phosphate too, and a steroid has no ester.

q: What is a wax, chemically?
e: One ester joining two long chains, which is why waxes are hard and very water-repellent.

q: Why are lipids a compact energy store compared with carbohydrates?
e: A more reduced carbon has further to fall on oxidation, so more energy is released per gram.

q: What is the difference between a nucleoside and a nucleotide?
e: Sugar plus base is a nucleoside; adding the phosphate ester makes it a nucleotide.

q: A DNA strand reads 5'-GGATC-3'. Written in the conventional direction, what is its complement?
e: Pair each base first: G-C, G-C, A-T, T-A, C-G, reading CCTAG alongside the original. That runs 3' to 5', because the strands are antiparallel, so writing it conventionally reverses it to GATCC. The trap is right bases, wrong direction.

q: What kind of bond joins a base to its sugar?
e: A nitrogen displaces the anomeric OH, which is acetal formation with N in place of O.

q: Which carbon of the sugar bonds to the base?
e: The anomeric carbon is the electrophilic one, exactly as in ordinary glycoside formation.

q: Which OH of the sugar carries the phosphate that a polymerase adds to a growing chain?
e: Polymerases use 5 prime triphosphates, and the 3 prime OH of the chain is the nucleophile that attacks one. A 3 prime monophosphate is a perfectly good nucleotide too, but it is not what gets added.

q: What links one nucleotide to the next?
e: One phosphorus esterified to two different sugars, 3 prime of one and 5 prime of the next.

q: Why are nucleic acids called acids?
e: A row of negative charges on the outside, which is also why they dissolve in water.

q: How many hydrogen bonds join a G-C pair?
e: One more than A-T, and that difference shows up directly in melting temperature.

q: What holds the two strands of DNA together?
e: Weak bonds on purpose, because anything read must first be opened without being destroyed.

q: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 30% adenine. What is its guanine content?
e: Pairing forces A to equal T, so 30% adenine means 30% thymine and the two account for 60%. The other 40% is split evenly between G and C because they pair with each other, giving 20% guanine.

q: What does denaturing DNA do?
e: Only the hydrogen bonds between bases are undone, which is why the strands can re-anneal.

q: Why does RNA hydrolyze much faster than DNA in base?
e: An intramolecular attack through a five-membered ring is enormously faster than one from solution.

q: Why is DNA rather than RNA used for long-term storage?
e: Removing one hydroxyl removes the internal nucleophile, and with it the built-in self-destruct.

q: What conditions cleave the base from the sugar?
e: It is an N,O-acetal, and acetals are cut by aqueous acid and stable to base. The rate is very uneven: purines depurinate far more readily than pyrimidines.

q: Why does an incoming nucleoside triphosphate react at all when a polymerase extends a chain?
e: The 3' OH of the growing chain attacks the 5' phosphorus of the incoming triphosphate, and the leaving group is what makes that productive: the outer phosphates are anhydrides, and the departing diphosphate spreads its charge widely.

q: Which part of a nucleotide carries the genetic information?
e: Sugar and phosphate repeat identically along the chain, so only the bases can vary.

q: Why is the carbon of a Grignard reagent nucleophilic?
e: Carbon at 2.55 against magnesium at 1.31, so the bonding electrons sit on carbon.

q: What is umpolung?
e: An alkyl halide's carbon is an electrophile; the Grignard made from it is a nucleophile at the same carbon.

q: 1.0 equivalent of CH3MgBr is added to 4-hydroxybutan-2-one. What is isolated after aqueous workup?
e: The O-H at pKa 16 is deprotonated long before anything adds, so the reagent leaves as methane and the magnesium alkoxide that remains is inert to its own ketone. Workup just protonates it back. Two equivalents fix it.

q: CH3MgBr is added to a compound carrying both a ketone and a secondary amine. What is isolated after workup?
e: An N-H at pKa 36 is still far more acidic than an alkane at 50, so proton transfer happens first and the reagent leaves as methane. The magnesium amide left behind is not nucleophilic enough to add to its own ketone, and workup simply puts the N-H back.

q: Is the C-Mg bond ionic?
e: A Grignard is not a free carbanion, though it behaves like one and the arrow starts at the C-metal bond.

q: Which organometallic is the most reactive?
e: The widest electronegativity gap gives the most carbanion character and the least selectivity.

q: Which organometallic is the most selective?
e: Copper sits close to carbon, so the bond is barely polar and the reagent can be pointed at one site.

q: What does high reactivity cost an organometallic reagent?
e: The two trade against each other more visibly here than anywhere else in the course.

q: Rank C-K, C-Mg, C-Cu and C-B by how nucleophilic the carbon is, most first.
e: Read it straight off electronegativity: the further the metal sits below carbon, the more the bonding pair belongs to carbon. Potassium is furthest, boron nearly matches carbon, and copper sits between - which is exactly the reactivity ladder the chapter is built on.

q: A Grignard reagent is wanted from 1-bromo-4-hydroxybutane. What happens, and what fixes it?
e: Each molecule of reagent is quenched by the O-H of the next one, so the yield collapses. Silylating or otherwise protecting the alcohol first - or reordering the synthesis so the OH appears later - is the standard answer.

q: Which single flask charge will NOT give a new carbon-carbon bond?
e: Ethanol has an O-H at pKa 16 and the Grignard is the conjugate base of an alkane at 50, so the only thing that happens is proton transfer: methane leaves and magnesium ethoxide stays. The other three all join two carbons.

q: Why is a carbon nucleophile needed to build a skeleton?
e: Whatever attacks is what gets attached, so attaching carbon means attacking with carbon.

q: Which two carbon nucleophiles appeared before this chapter?
e: Both are narrow: cyanide brings one carbon with a nitrile attached, and an acetylide must come from a terminal alkyne.

q: How is a Grignard reagent made?
e: The metal inserts into the carbon-halogen bond; nothing is added and nothing leaves.

q: Bromoethane is stirred with magnesium in dry ether, and D2O is then added. What is the product?
e: The same destructive protonation that ruins a wet Grignard, used on purpose. The carbanion takes a deuteron from D2O, so the label lands exactly on the carbon that bore the halide - a clean way to mark one position.

q: Which reaction gives a magnesium alkoxide WITHOUT forming a new C-C bond?
e: Deprotonating an alcohol gives the same magnesium alkoxide that a Grignard addition does, but the reagent has been spent on a proton and no carbon was joined to anything.

q: Why is an aryl Grignard useful even though aryl halides resist substitution?
e: The metal inserts into the C-X bond rather than displacing the halide from behind.

q: If a substrate has an OH and a ketone, which does a Grignard reach first?
e: Proton transfer is the fastest reaction available, so the reagent is spent before it can add.

q: What is the practical signal that a Grignard preparation has failed?
e: Wet or undried glassware leaves an oxide-coated magnesium surface, so the insertion never initiates, the turnings sit there and the solution never goes cloudy gray. Any reagent that does form is protonated to R-H rather than going on to product.

q: A Grignard reagent plus formaldehyde gives what after workup?
e: Formaldehyde has two hydrogens on its carbonyl carbon, so after one R group is added that carbon still carries two.

q: A Grignard plus an aldehyde other than formaldehyde gives what?
e: One hydrogen and one R group were already there; the Grignard adds the second R.

q: A Grignard plus CO2, then acid, gives what?
e: One carbon longer, and it arrives already at the carboxylic acid oxidation level.

q: A Grignard plus an epoxide gives what?
e: The attack is an SN2 at the less hindered carbon, and the alkoxide is protonated on workup.

q: Where does a Grignard attack an epoxide?
e: There is no acid present, so no carbocation character develops and sterics decide.

q: How many equivalents of Grignard does an ester consume?
e: The ketone formed after the first addition is more electrophilic than the ester was.

q: Why can an ester not be stopped at the ketone with one equivalent?
e: The OR group donates into the carbonyl and makes the ester the sluggish one of the pair.

q: What is a Weinreb amide used for?
e: Its chelated intermediate survives until workup, so no second addition can occur.

q: Which pair of electrophiles extends a chain by exactly one carbon?
e: Formaldehyde adds one carbon and stops at a primary alcohol; CO2 adds one carbon already at the acid level. A nitrile R′CN brings R′ along with its carbon, and an epoxide brings two.

q: How many carbons does ethylene oxide add to a chain?
e: Which is why it is the standard two-carbon extension. A substituted epoxide adds more, and the attack still goes at the less hindered carbon.

q: Which target is 1-bromopropane plus Mg plus propanone plus acid?
e: A ketone plus a Grignard gives a tertiary alcohol, here with methyl, methyl and propyl.

q: Which is the last resort for an acidic proton in a Grignard substrate?
e: Two extra steps means two extra yields lost, so it is worth it only when the alternatives fail.

q: You need butan-1-ol from bromoethane. Which sequence works?
e: Two carbons in and four out, so the electrophile has to bring two and leave the OH on the end carbon: that is ethylene oxide, attacked at the less hindered carbon. Formaldehyde adds only one, and CO2 would give an acid.

q: Why does acetaldehyde sometimes give poor yields with a Grignard?
e: A very strong base and an alpha hydrogen in the same flask is an acid-base reaction waiting to happen.

q: What is the correct order of operations for a Grignard reaction?
e: Having the electrophile present while the reagent forms invites enolization and self-condensation.

q: What class of alcohol comes from a Grignard plus an acyl chloride in excess?
e: Two additions again, but not for the ester's reason: an acyl chloride is the most electrophilic acyl derivative, and the ketone it gives is simply still reactive enough to be attacked as fast as it forms.

q: Which is the correct disconnection for a tertiary alcohol?
e: Each cut gives a carbanion and a ketone, and there are three legitimate choices.

q: Why does RLi plus a carboxylic acid stop at the ketone?
e: The ketone does not exist in the flask, so there is nothing for a second equivalent to attack.

q: What makes LDA useful?
e: That pairing is what allows complete enolate formation without attack on the carbonyl.

q: Why is LDA a weaker base than n-BuLi?
e: An amine pKa near 36 against an alkane near 50, and it is still far more than enough.

q: What distinguishes t-BuLi from n-BuLi in practice?
e: Bulk does slow its approach to a hindered carbonyl, but t-BuLi is still a fine nucleophile and the standard reagent for lithium-halogen exchange. LDA is the reagent for which basic-but-not-nucleophilic actually holds.

q: What is the approximate pKa of a terminal alkyne C-H?
e: An alkene is 44 and an alkane 50, so the alkyne is by far the most acidic of the three.

q: What does Na in liquid NH3 give from an internal alkyne?
e: A dissolving-metal reduction through a vinyl radical anion, which settles trans.

q: Why does Ar-Br plus n-BuLi give Ar-Li rather than leaving the lithium on butyl?
e: Lithium-halogen exchange is an equilibrium, and it settles where the carbanion is better stabilized. An sp2 aryl carbanion has more s character than an sp3 butyl one, so it holds its lone pair closer and is the weaker base.

q: Can an organolithium do everything a Grignard does?
e: The extra reactivity is mostly something to manage rather than something to use.

q: Why can an alkyne not be alkylated twice in the same step?
e: Alkylating a terminal alkyne makes it internal, and an internal alkyne has no acidic C-H.

q: Which sequence converts benzoic acid into acetophenone?
e: The first equivalent is spent on the O-H and the second adds to the carboxylate. The dianion cannot collapse, so it survives until workup and only then loses water to the ketone. A Grignard is not reactive enough to attack a carboxylate, and the acid chloride route adds twice.

q: What is the intermediate in the RLi plus carboxylic acid reaction?
e: Two negative charges on one carbon's oxygens. It cannot collapse, because that would mean expelling O2- and adding a third charge, so it survives until workup.

q: Which reagent would you choose to form a ketone enolate completely?
e: Hydroxide gives an equilibrium, n-BuLi attacks the carbonyl, and pyridine is far too weak.

q: Where does a Grignard add to an enone?
e: Hard nucleophile, charge control, and the carbonyl carbon carries the most positive charge.

q: What is the product of an enone plus a cuprate?
e: 1,4 addition gives an enolate, which protonates and tautomerizes back to the ketone.

q: Why can a cuprate couple with a vinyl halide?
e: A vinyl carbon is sp2 and its backside is shielded, so substitution is unavailable.

q: What does (CH3)2CuLi give with (E)-1-bromo-1-hexene?
e: Cuprates couple with vinyl halides, which do no SN2 at all, and the alkene geometry survives the coupling. That retention is most of the reason the reaction is worth running.

q: Which of these will a Gilman reagent NOT do?
e: A cuprate is too mild to be a general carbonyl nucleophile: it leaves esters, amides and nitriles alone, which is exactly why it tolerates them elsewhere in a molecule. What it does instead is conjugate (1,4) addition, coupling with halides — the Corey-House synthesis — and one clean addition to an acyl chloride.

q: Why does an enone have two electrophilic carbons?
e: Resonance puts positive character on the beta carbon as well as the carbonyl carbon.

q: Why can PCC not fix a tertiary alcohol into a ketone?
e: An oxidation at that carbon needs a C-H to remove, and a tertiary alcohol has none.

q: What would a Grignard do to a substrate containing both an enone and an ester?
e: Low selectivity is the cost of high reactivity; a cuprate would leave the ester alone.

q: What kind of control does a soft nucleophile follow?
e: Which points it at the largest LUMO coefficient rather than the largest partial charge.

q: Which metal catalyzes the standard cross-coupling reactions?
e: Copper appears as a cocatalyst in the Sonogashira, but palladium runs the cycle.

q: What are the three steps of the cross-coupling cycle?
e: The first and last names describe what happens to the palladium's oxidation state.

q: Why is 1-bromobutane a poor partner for a Suzuki coupling?
e: An sp3 group on palladium with a hydrogen on the neighboring carbon loses that hydrogen and leaves as an alkene, faster than the two organic groups can join. Aryl and vinyl groups have no such beta hydrogen, which is why they are the partners that work.

q: Why is palladium a catalyst rather than a reagent?
e: Reductive elimination hands back the Pd(0) the cycle started with, so a few mole percent turns over thousands of times.

q: Which coupling uses no organometallic partner at all?
e: An alkene inserts into the Ar-Pd bond instead, so there is no transmetalation step.

q: Why does a Suzuki coupling need a base?
e: A neutral boronic acid transfers its R group poorly; the four-coordinate borate does it well.

q: Why did the Suzuki coupling displace the Stille industrially?
e: The chemistry of the Stille is at least as good; the toxicity of organotin is what settled it.

q: Why does a convergent route return more material?
e: Ten linear steps at 85% gives about 20%; two five-step branches joined gives about 37%.

q: Which functional groups survive a Suzuki coupling?
e: The reactive carbon is bound to a metal throughout and never exists as a free carbanion.

q: Which bond should signal a cross-coupling disconnection?
e: Neither ring is nucleophilic or electrophilic enough for anything from earlier chapters.

q: Bromobenzene, phenylboronic acid, Pd(PPh3)4 and Na2CO3 are heated together. What forms?
e: Pd(0) inserts into the C-Br bond, the borate hands its phenyl across, and reductive elimination joins the two rings. Two aryl pieces, one new aryl-aryl bond.

q: Can an aryl Grignard be made from an aryl bromide?
e: Bromides and iodides go readily. Aryl chlorides are sluggish and need heat or activation, and aryl fluorides do not go at all. The trouble with the reagent is what it does afterward, not whether it forms.

q: In a Suzuki coupling, which partner does palladium add to, and what is the base for?
e: Oxidative addition breaks the Ar-Br bond, which is why the halide sets the scope. Carbonate then adds to boron to give the four-coordinate borate, and only that anionic boron delivers its aryl group to palladium.

q: What does a Wittig reaction convert a C=O into?
e: The new double bond lands exactly at the old carbonyl carbon, in place of its C=O.

q: Butanal, CH3CH2CH2CHO, is treated with Ph3P=CHCH2CH3. What is the major product?
e: Join the aldehyde carbon to the ylide carbon: CH3CH2CH2-CH=CH-CH2CH3, which is hept-3-ene. The ylide carries alkyl groups alone, so it is unstabilized, and an unstabilized ylide gives mainly the Z isomer.

q: Why will a tertiary halide not give an ylide?
e: No phosphonium salt forms, so the route dies at step one - and even if one did form, a tertiary carbon on phosphorus has no hydrogen to remove, so there would be no ylide either.

q: Which pair would you actually run to make 2-methylhept-2-ene, (CH3)2C=CH-CH2CH2CH2CH3?
e: Both of the first two are chemically real disconnections, so the halide decides between them: 1-bromopentane is primary and the SN2 is clean, while 2-bromopropane is secondary and sluggish.

q: What is the four-membered intermediate called?
e: It falls apart in the one way it can, giving the alkene and the phosphine oxide.

q: How does a Wittig differ from an elimination?
e: An elimination forms the C=C between two carbons already bonded, so Zaitsev chooses where.

q: What does cyclohexanone plus Ph3P=CH2 give?
e: An exocyclic alkene, and the less stable of the two isomers, which is exactly the point.

q: What does an unstabilized ylide give?
e: It adds fast and irreversibly, so the geometry of the transition state is locked in.

q: You need (E)-methyl cinnamate, PhCH=CH-CO2Me, with high E selectivity. What do you use with benzaldehyde?
e: That phosphonate anion is the Horner-Wadsworth-Emmons reagent: strongly E-selective, deprotonated by NaH rather than n-BuLi, and its phosphate by-product washes out in water.

q: A route proposes making Ph3P=C(CH3)2 from 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. What is wrong with it?
e: Ph3P=C(CH3)2 comes from the secondary halide 2-bromopropane. A tertiary halide is not an SN2 substrate, and it would in any case give a phosphonium with no alpha hydrogen to remove.

q: What does a primary amine plus a ketone give?
e: One hydrogen is left on nitrogen after the addition, so the C=N+ cation loses it.

q: What does a tertiary amine plus a ketone give?
e: Losing water would demand a nitrogen with five bonds, so the addition simply reverses - which is why tertiary amines serve as bases here.

q: Cyclohexanone is treated with pyrrolidine and a trace of acid, then benzyl bromide, then aqueous acid. What is the product?
e: A Stork sequence: form the enamine, alkylate the alpha carbon with a reactive benzylic halide, then hydrolyze back to the ketone. One alkylation happens, because the first gives an iminium that cannot be turned back into a nucleophile.

q: Which ketone will not give an enamine with pyrrolidine?
e: An enamine needs its last proton to come from the alpha carbon. Benzophenone has no alpha hydrogen, so the sequence gets as far as the cation and stops.

q: How is the equilibrium pulled forward?
e: A Dean-Stark trap or molecular sieves; every step of the sequence is reversible.

q: What is reductive amination?
e: NaBH3CN reduces the imine as it forms, avoiding the over-alkylation of direct SN2.

q: Which reagent reduces an imine in the presence of the ketone it was formed from?
e: Mild enough to leave the ketone alone while reducing the more electrophilic iminium.

q: Why does an enamine alkylate only once?
e: Not a matter of reactivity. The iminium has no nucleophilic carbon, and no base is present to turn it back into an enamine, so a second alkylation is impossible rather than slow.

q: A Stork alkylation with 1-bromobutane gives almost nothing, while the same sequence with allyl bromide works well. Why?
e: The cost of a neutral, controllable nucleophile is a short list of electrophiles: methyl, allylic, benzylic and alpha-halo carbonyls. Acid chlorides always work; ordinary primary halides often do not.

q: Cyclohexanone is treated with H2NNH2, then with KOH and heat. What is the product?
e: A Wolff-Kishner reduction. The hydrazone loses N2 under strong base and heat, leaving a CH2 where the C=O was.

q: What is the Michael acceptor?
e: An alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl, with the beta carbon as the electrophilic site.

q: What spacing does a Michael addition leave?
e: Joining the donor alpha carbon to the acceptor beta carbon puts them five apart.

q: Cyclohexanone is treated with NaOEt, then with methyl vinyl ketone, then warmed. What is the major product?
e: A Robinson annulation. The cyclohexanone enolate adds 1,4 to MVK to give a 1,5-diketone, an intramolecular aldol closes a second six-membered ring onto the first, and dehydration leaves the conjugated enone.

q: Why must the donor be doubly stabilized?
e: Spreading the charge over two carbonyls is what makes the enolate soft rather than hard.

q: An unstabilized lithium enolate, made with LDA at -78 C, is added to an enone. What does it do?
e: Hard, charge-dense and irreversible, so it takes the carbonyl carbon. Under reversible conditions - catalytic alkoxide, warm - the same enolate ends up adding 1,4 instead, which is why the classic Robinson works with an ordinary ketone.

q: What is methyl vinyl ketone used as?
e: Cheap, and the ring its Robinson product gives is the one steroid chemistry needed.

q: Which step makes a Robinson annulation irreversible?
e: Conjugating the alkene with the carbonyl is the stabilization it cannot climb back out of.

q: How do you undo a Robinson annulation on paper?
e: Reverse order: put the water back, break the aldol bond, then cut beta to a carbonyl.

q: Ethyl acetoacetate is treated with NaOEt and then acrylonitrile, CH2=CH-CN. What forms?
e: An alpha,beta-unsaturated nitrile is a good acceptor: the CN withdraws, the beta carbon is electrophilic, and the donor's alpha carbon lands on it, leaving the ketone and the nitrile carbon 1,5 to each other in ethyl 2-acetyl-4-cyanobutanoate.

q: Why does a soft nucleophile add 1,4?
e: Orbital control rather than charge control, and the beta carbon has the larger coefficient.

q: Which reaction sequence builds a cyclohexenone from two acyclic pieces?
e: A Diels-Alder builds a ring too, but it gives a cyclohexene rather than a cyclohexenone.

q: Which of these is not a Michael acceptor?
e: An isolated alkene has no electron-withdrawing group conjugated to it, so its beta carbon is not electrophilic and a nucleophile has nothing to add to.

q: In the Michael addition of diethyl malonate to methyl vinyl ketone, what exists right after the new C-C bond forms?
e: The electrons pushed out of the C=C end up on the carbonyl oxygen, so the first species formed is an enolate; protonation, or tautomerization from the enol, gives the 1,5-dicarbonyl.

q: What does a malonic ester synthesis give?
e: Malonate has two esters: one carboxyl is lost as CO2 and the other stays as the acid.

q: Which sequence makes cyclobutanecarboxylic acid?
e: Two equivalents of base for two alkylations, both spent on the same dihalide, and the second closes the ring. The malonate alpha carbon plus the three carbons of the dihalide make a four-membered ring. Acetoacetate would give a ketone, and cyclobutyl bromide is secondary.

q: What is the approximate alpha pKa of diethyl malonate?
e: Delocalizing the carbanion onto two ester oxygens is worth twelve orders of magnitude.

q: What is the approximate alpha pKa of an ordinary ester?
e: Too high for a convenient base, and a strong base would attack the ester instead.

q: Which target is beyond the reach of a malonic ester synthesis?
e: Its alpha carbon carries two methyls and an ethyl - three substituents - and malonate's CH2 has two acidic hydrogens to give up. The other three need one primary halide each, or two.

q: Why does the intermediate decarboxylate on heating?
e: A six-membered cyclic transition state reaches from the carboxyl O-H to that second carbonyl. It is a ketone in the acetoacetic route and the other carboxyl in the malonic one, and either works.

q: Would an alpha-keto acid decarboxylate on warming?
e: The geometry needs the second carbonyl exactly beta, whether that carbonyl is a ketone or another carboxyl.

q: What product would ethyl acetoacetate plus benzyl bromide give?
e: A methyl ketone carrying the benzyl group, after hydrolysis and decarboxylation.

q: Which halides would make 2-methylpentanoic acid from malonate?
e: The alpha carbon of the target carries a methyl and a propyl, installed in two rounds.

q: Which target is out of reach for an acetoacetic ester synthesis?
e: All four are methyl ketones, so the product class does not decide it. 3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-one would need three methyls on the alpha carbon, and ethyl acetoacetate's CH2 has two acidic hydrogens to give - no choice of halide reaches it.

q: Why must the free carboxylic acid be present before the decarboxylation can happen?
e: No O-H, no six-membered loop. That is why the ester has to be hydrolyzed first, and why the two operations are always written together.

q: Which reagent performs the hydrolysis and decarboxylation?
e: One step does both, because the beta-keto acid does not survive the temperature.

q: What does the alkoxide base need to match?
e: Using ethoxide with an ethyl ester avoids scrambling the ester by transesterification.

q: Ethyl acetoacetate, NaOEt, then 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, then H3O+ and heat. What is the product?
e: The isobutyl group lands on the alpha carbon, and after hydrolysis and decarboxylation the chain is CH3CO-CH2-CH2-CH(CH3)2. Acetoacetate gives a methyl ketone, never an acid.

q: What does a Baeyer-Villiger oxidation do to a ketone?
e: The product is an ester, and almost nothing else in the course touches that bond.

q: What kind of step is the migration?
e: The same motion that rearranges a carbocation, running on a neutral intermediate.

q: What does the migrating group take with it?
e: Which is why it never exists as a free species and never loses its configuration.

q: What is the migratory aptitude order?
e: Carbocation stability arriving from another direction, with hydrogen at the head of it - which is why an aldehyde gives a carboxylic acid.

q: Butanal, CH3CH2CH2CHO, is treated with mCPBA. What is the product?
e: Hydrogen is the best migrator of all, so in an aldehyde the H moves and the product is the carboxylic acid. Propyl formate would come from the propyl migrating, and it does not.

q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone is treated with mCPBA. Where does the inserted oxygen go?
e: The methyl-bearing carbon is secondary and the other is primary, and secondary migrates better, so the ring oxygen ends up attached to the carbon carrying the methyl. The ring still expands to seven.

q: What leaves in a Baeyer-Villiger?
e: The peroxyacid's other half, which is what makes the O-O bond a good place to break.

q: Why is this reaction usable on a chiral center?
e: One of very few reactions at this level where a stereocenter survives a bond change intact.

q: What class of compound is the product?
e: Which you already know how to hydrolyze, so the reaction slots into longer routes.

q: In which ketone is the migration genuinely ambiguous?
e: Its two groups are identical primary ethyls, so whichever one moves gives the same product, ethyl propanoate. In each of the others the two groups sit at clearly different places in the series.

q: What kind of ring expansion is this?
e: One of the few reliable ring expansions at this level, and the only one adding oxygen.

q: Which retrosynthetic clue suggests a Baeyer-Villiger?
e: Esterifying a tertiary alcohol is hard; migrating a tertiary group is the easiest case.

q: Why does aryl migrate well when a phenyl cation is so unstable?
e: The carbocation shortcut predicts the wrong thing here, and the reason it fails is that no free cation is ever made: the migrating carbon is bonded to both the old carbon and the new oxygen at once.

q: Why will chlorobenzene not undergo SN1?
e: The positive charge would sit in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, with no way to delocalize.

q: Put the SNAr steps in order: (i) the halide leaves, (ii) the nucleophile attacks the ipso carbon, (iii) charge spreads onto the nitro oxygens, (iv) aromaticity
e: Addition first. The delocalization onto the nitro groups is what makes the Meisenheimer intermediate survivable long enough for the halide to leave, so it has to come before the loss of halide, and aromaticity is only restored at the very end.

q: What is the SNAr intermediate called?
e: Negatively charged and not aromatic, which is what the withdrawing groups pay for.

q: Why is fluorine the best leaving group in SNAr?
e: The C-X bond is not breaking in the rate-determining step, so what matters is how electrophilic the halogen makes the carbon under attack - and that is electronegativity, which runs the opposite way from leaving-group ability.

q: 1-fluoro-4-nitrobenzene is warmed with sodium ethoxide. What is the product?
e: One nitro group para to the halide is enough to run SNAr with a good nucleophile and some heat. SNAr never rearranges, so there is one product and it sits exactly where the fluorine was - and fluorine being the halide helps here rather than hurting.

q: What is benzyne's extra bond made from?
e: They point away from each other rather than overlapping properly, which is why it is strained.

q: What proved benzyne exists?
e: No direct displacement could put the nucleophile on a carbon that never bore the leaving group.

q: Which nucleophile is used in the classic benzyne reaction?
e: NaNH2 plays both parts: it removes the ortho hydrogen in the elimination and then adds to the benzyne. That is why the reaction cannot be run with a strong base plus a separate weak nucleophile - anything basic enough to make a benzyne is already nucleophilic.

q: Why is the Meisenheimer complex stable enough to form?
e: Delocalization onto the substituents is what makes losing aromaticity affordable.

q: 2-bromo-1,3-dimethylbenzene is treated with NaNH2 in liquid ammonia. What happens?
e: No withdrawing group rules out SNAr, and both positions ortho to the bromine carry methyl groups, so there is no hydrogen for the base to remove and no benzyne either. Recognizing a substrate that runs NEITHER route is the skill being tested.

q: 3-bromoanisole is treated with NaNH2 in liquid ammonia. Which aniline predominates?
e: The benzyne forms between C2 and C3. Amide attacks the carbon that leaves the carbanion nearer the electron-withdrawing methoxy oxygen, which gives the meta product. Two products are possible from any benzyne, but a substituent decides how the two are weighted.

q: Which halide is worst for SNAr?
e: Iodine is the least electronegative of the four, so it activates the carbon least.

q: Why is a benzylic cation stabilized?
e: The charge spreads over the benzylic carbon plus both ortho and the para positions.

q: Which other position uses the same argument?
e: Same argument, counted the same way. An allyl system carries the charge on two positions, its two ends; a benzylic system carries it on four - the benzylic carbon plus both ortho positions and the para.

q: What does hot KMnO4 do to propylbenzene?
e: Chain length makes no difference; everything past the benzylic carbon is cut away.

q: What should a benzoic acid suggest retrosynthetically?
e: Oxidation converts any alkyl chain to a carboxyl, so the chain identity is free.

q: 1-phenylbut-2-ene, PhCH2-CH=CH-CH3, is treated with NBS and light. Where does bromination occur?
e: Bromination goes wherever the most stabilized radical forms. In this substrate the carbon next to the ring is also next to the double bond, so C1 is benzylic and allylic at the same time and there is no competition to resolve.

q: Which sequence converts benzene into 4-nitrobenzoic acid?
e: Friedel-Crafts fails on a nitrated ring, so the alkyl group has to go on first. The methyl then sends the nitro group para. The oxidation must come last, because a carboxyl is a deactivating meta director that would have sent the nitro group to the wrong place.

q: Hot KMnO4 with an acidic workup is used on 1,4-diethylbenzene. What is the product?
e: Every side chain with a benzylic hydrogen is cut back and oxidized, not just one, so both ethyl groups become carboxyls. That compound is the monomer for PET, which is one industrial use of this reaction.

q: Which product comes from isopropylbenzene and hot KMnO4?
e: One benzylic hydrogen is enough, and both methyls go with the rest of the chain.

q: Friedel-Crafts acylation puts an acyl group on benzene. Is the carbonyl carbon benzylic?
e: Benzylic means attached to the ring, and the definition says nothing about hybridization. But every reaction in this section - SN1, SN2, radical abstraction, permanganate - needs an sp3 carbon carrying a hydrogen. Reduce the ketone to CH2 and all of it switches on.

q: How is a benzyl ether removed from an alcohol?
e: Hydrogenolysis cleaves the benzylic C-O bond and gives toluene plus the free alcohol. It is the one deprotection that needs neither acid nor base, which is exactly why the group is worth using.

q: What is a phenol?
e: An OH on a carbon next to the ring is a benzylic alcohol, which behaves quite differently.

q: Rank these for acidity: phenol, 4-nitrophenol, 4-methoxyphenol, 2,4-dinitrophenol.
e: Count the resonance-capable withdrawing groups: two, then one, then none, then a donor pushing the wrong way. Methoxy from para donates its lone pair into the ring, which destabilizes the phenoxide, so 4-methoxyphenol is the weakest acid of the four.

q: Which base deprotonates a phenol?
e: Bicarbonate is not strong enough, which is what makes it useful as a discriminator.

q: Benzoic acid, phenol and cyclohexanol are dissolved in ether. The solution is shaken with aqueous NaHCO3, then with aqueous NaOH. What is left in the ether?
e: Bicarbonate, from carbonic acid at pKa 6.4, pulls out only the benzoic acid at 4.8. Hydroxide then pulls out the phenol at 10. Cyclohexanol at 16 is untouched by both and stays behind - a three-way separation run on nothing but a pKa table.

q: Phenoxide is heated with CO2 at 125 degrees under pressure, then acidified. What is the product?
e: The Kolbe-Schmitt reaction. The phenoxide attacks CO2 with an ORTHO ring carbon rather than with its oxygen, because that is where the charge actually sits - and acetylating the resulting phenol gives aspirin.

q: Is OH ortho/para or meta directing?
e: Donation reaches the ortho and para positions, which is where the substitution goes.

q: What does phenol plus bromine water give?
e: No Lewis acid catalyst is needed, and all three activated positions react at once.

q: Why are quinones colored?
e: A small HOMO-LUMO gap, from two carbonyls conjugated with the two remaining C=C bonds. Losing aromaticity is what makes that chromophore possible, but plenty of non-aromatic compounds are colorless - the conjugation is the cause.

q: Phenol is treated with bromine water. Why is the monobromide not obtained?
e: OH is one of the strongest activators there is, and one bromine barely dents it, so the second and third substitutions are about as fast as the first. Getting monobromination needs deliberately weaker conditions - Br2 in a nonpolar solvent, cold.

q: Which is more acidic, phenol or acetic acid?
e: 4.8 against 10, because a carboxylate spreads charge over two equivalent oxygens.

q: Why does a carboxylate beat a phenoxide at stabilizing charge?
e: A carboxylate spreads its charge over two electronegative oxygens. A phenoxide spreads most of its charge onto ring carbons, which hold it far less well, and that is most of the five-unit pKa gap between them.

q: Why is the 1,4-diene formed rather than the 1,3?
e: Protonation happens at the central carbon of the delocalized anion, which is not where the more stable product would come from.

q: With a withdrawing group, where does the substituted carbon end up?
e: A withdrawing group holds the charge on its own carbon, so that carbon is protonated.

q: Which reaction uses the same electron-then-proton pattern?
e: Both are dissolving-metal reductions running on solvated electrons, and both give the opposite outcome from catalytic hydrogenation on the same substrate.

q: 1-methoxycyclohexa-1,4-diene is stirred with dilute aqueous acid. What forms?
e: Hydrolyzing the enol ether unmasks the ketone at the carbon that carried the OCH3, and the OTHER double bond stays exactly where it was - two carbons away, not in conjugation. Reaching the Michael-accepting cyclohex-2-en-1-one takes a deliberate isomerization with stronger acid or base.

q: Which starting material gives an enol ether on Birch reduction?
e: The methoxy stays on a double bond, and a C=C with an OR on it is an enol ether.

q: Why can an unconjugated diene be functionalized selectively?
e: A conjugated diene reacts as one system, which makes single-site chemistry harder.

q: Methyl benzoate is subjected to Birch conditions, Li in NH3 with t-BuOH. What is the product?
e: An ester carbonyl is an acceptor, so the carbanion sits on the carbon bearing it, that carbon is the one protonated, and it comes out sp3. Same row of the table as benzoic acid, and the same single question answers both.

q: Which single sequence converts anisole into cyclohex-2-en-1-one?
e: Three operations, and the third is the one people drop. The Birch gives the enol ether, mild hydrolysis gives the beta,gamma ketone cyclohex-3-en-1-one, and only a deliberate isomerization moves the double bond into conjugation. Without that step there is no Michael acceptor.

q: A compound has one benzene ring and one isolated C=C. It is treated with Li/NH3/t-BuOH, and separately with H2 over Pd. What differs?
e: Opposite selectivities, and it is the cleanest chemoselectivity pair in the course. Adding an electron is easy for an aromatic ring and hard for an isolated alkene; adding hydrogens from a metal surface is the other way round.

q: Why does a withdrawing group put its carbon sp3?
e: The carbanion sits where the substituent lets it, and that carbon gets the proton.

q: What is a radical anion?
e: Adding a single electron to a neutral molecule gives both at once: the electron is unpaired, and the molecule is now negatively charged. That is the first intermediate of every dissolving-metal reduction.

q: Which position is protonated second?
e: The pentadienyl anion is protonated at its middle carbon, and that is what puts the two remaining double bonds 1,4 rather than 1,3.

q: Why does the Birch not over-reduce to cyclohexane?
e: Adding an electron to an isolated alkene is far harder than to an aromatic ring.

q: Which reagent converts 4-methylbenzenediazonium chloride into 4-iodotoluene?
e: The iodide row is the odd one out: no copper salt is required and plain KI does the job. That is worth noticing, because iodine is also the one halogen electrophilic substitution cannot install cleanly - direct iodination needs an added oxidant.

q: What does warm water give?
e: The standard way phenols are made, since no substitution works at that C-O bond.

q: What is the point of replacing N2+ with H?
e: A substituent installed to control one step and then deliberately deleted, which is a protecting group in aromatic clothes. The NH2 was never part of the target; it was there to steer the bromination, and H3PO2 removes it once it has.

q: Plan a route from benzene to 3-bromophenol, the meta isomer.
e: The nitro group has to go on first and do the directing, because it is the only meta director available here, and bromine lands meta to it. Only then is the nitro group reduced, diazotized and hydrolyzed to OH. Reducing it first fails, because NH2 directs ortho/para.

q: What intermediate forms when a diazonium salt loses N2?
e: Badly unstable, which is why it grabs whatever nucleophile is present at once. In warm aqueous acid that nucleophile is water and the product is the phenol. The copper-catalyzed Sandmeyer rows are the exception: those run through an aryl radical instead.

q: You need a substitution pattern that the groups already on the ring forbid. What is the move?
e: Install a temporary director - usually an amine made from a nitro group - let it steer the substitution where you want it, then diazotize and delete it with H3PO2. You do not argue with directing effects; you change who is doing the directing.

q: Why must an aniline be coupled with a diazonium salt at pH 4-7 rather than in strong acid?
e: Coupling needs the nitrogen lone pair donating into the ring. Protonate the nitrogen and that lone pair is gone, leaving a ring that is deactivated rather than activated - and a diazonium ion is far too weak an electrophile for a deactivated ring.

q: What is a monomer?
e: The repeating piece inside the chain is the repeat unit, which may differ from the monomer.

q: How do you tell addition from condensation quickly?
e: A lighter repeat unit means something was expelled; matching formulas mean nothing was, so for an alkene monomer, addition.

q: What is a thermoset?
e: Heating destroys it rather than softening it, because melting would mean breaking bonds.

q: Halfway through a polymerization you stop it and analyze the mixture. You find long polymer chains plus a great deal of unreacted monomer and almost nothing in
e: In a chain-growth polymerization a chain is either active or dead, and an active chain swallows thousands of monomers in seconds, so the flask holds long polymer beside untouched monomer with little between them. A step-growth mixture is the opposite picture: at 50% conversion the average piece is a dimer, so you would find a broad soup of oligomers and hardly any monomer left.

q: A step-growth polymerization has to reach a degree of polymerization of 200. What conversion does that take?
e: Rearrange DP = 1/(1-p) to p = 1 - 1/DP. With DP = 200 that is 1 - 0.005 = 0.995, so 99.5% of all the functional groups have to have reacted. Read the other way round, the figure that sounds impressive - 99% - buys you only DP = 100, half of what was asked for.

q: Styrene, CH2=CHPh, and terephthalic acid plus ethylene glycol are each polymerized. Which statement is true of BOTH products?
e: The one thing every chain polymer shares is two sites per monomer. Styrene's come from its C=C, terephthalic acid's from its two CO2H groups and the glycol's from its two OH groups. The other three statements are each true of one product and false of the other: only polystyrene keeps its monomer's formula, only the polyester loses water, and only polystyrene grows by a radical chain.

q: Terephthalic acid is heated with glycerol, HOCH2CH(OH)CH2OH. What comes out?
e: Count the reactive sites on one monomer and the answer is settled before any mechanism. The diacid has two, so on its own it would extend a line; glycerol has three, so every glycerol can tie itself to three different chains, and repeating that in all directions makes the whole sample one covalent molecule. The chemistry of each join is ordinary esterification, which is why it is still called a polyester - it is the count, not the reaction, that makes it a network.

q: A polymer's repeat unit is C6H10O5 and its monomer is C6H12O6. What happened at each join?
e: Subtract the formulas: C6H12O6 minus C6H10O5 is H2O. The repeat unit is lighter than the monomer by exactly one water, so a small molecule was condensed out at every join and this was a step-growth. (These are glucose and cellulose.) Counting atoms answered the question without any knowledge of the compound.

q: Two growing polystyrene radicals meet, and the products are one chain ending in a C=C and one chain ending in a saturated CH. What happened?
e: Two dead chains rather than one is the giveaway. Combination couples the two radicals into a single chain of the combined length; disproportionation has one radical take the hydrogen from the carbon next to the other radical center, which leaves that chain with a double bond and makes the abstracting chain saturated. Chain transfer and backbiting both keep the radical count the same, so neither of them can stop two chains at once.

q: What polymer comes from tetrafluoroethylene?
e: Teflon, and there is no head-to-tail question because both carbons are identical.

q: You need polypropylene stiff enough for a car bumper, and your reactor currently uses a peroxide initiator. What do you change?
e: A peroxide gives a free radical chain end, which is planar and has no facial preference, so the methyls land at random and the product is atactic - a goo, whatever its molecular weight. Only a catalyst that holds the chain at a defined metal site forces every monomer to arrive the same way round, and only the isotactic chains that result can pack into crystalline regions. Pressure and transfer agent change the chain length, which is not what is wrong here, and cross-linking would give a thermoset that cannot be molded at all.

q: What tacticity does radical polymerization give?
e: A planar radical has no strong preference about which face the next monomer arrives on.

q: Why is ordinary polystyrene amorphous?
e: Syndiotactic polystyrene has the same phenyl group and is crystalline, melting near 270 C, so bulk is not the cause. Atacticity is.

q: What does a Ziegler-Natta catalyst control?
e: Holding the growing chain at one defined, crowded metal site fixes how every monomer arrives, so the same feature sets the tacticity and suppresses branching. Rate and molecular weight depend on conditions as well.

q: What is nylon 6,6 made from?
e: First number the diamine's carbons, second the diacid's: hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid.

q: What do the numbers in nylon 6,6 count?
e: Six in the diamine and six in the diacid, in that order, readable straight from the name.

q: What is Kevlar made from?
e: Both aromatic and both para-substituted, which is what makes the chains straight.

q: Which resists hydrolysis better?
e: Amides are the least reactive acyl derivative, which carries over to the material.

q: Nylon 6,10 is made from which pair of monomers?
e: The first number counts the carbons of the diamine, so 6 means hexamethylenediamine; the second counts the diacid's, so 10 means sebacic acid, HO2C(CH2)8CO2H - ten carbons including the two carboxyl carbons. Swapping the two slots gives decanediamine with adipic acid, which is a different polymer built from the same two numbers, and 6,6 would need adipic acid in the second slot.

q: Which of these step-growth polymerizations expels NO small molecule?
e: The alcohol adds across the N=C=O group rather than substituting at it, so every atom of both monomers ends up inside the carbamate link and nothing leaves. The polyester and the polyamide each lose water, and the polycarbonate loses HCl because phosgene is an acid chloride. Polyurethane is the reason the class is properly called step-growth rather than condensation.

q: Why does polyester fabric lose strength in hot alkali faster than nylon?
e: The acyl reactivity ladder applied to a material. It is not a blanket ranking: nylon is the one attacked by acid, chlorine and sunlight.

q: Caprolactam is heated with a trace of water and gives nylon 6. What is expelled at each join?
e: Caprolactam is already an amide, closed into a seven-membered ring. The ring opens onto the growing chain end and adds there, so the atoms are rearranged rather than removed and the repeat unit has exactly the monomer's formula. That makes nylon 6 a polyamide reached by a chain-growth ring-opening, which is why the two axes - addition against condensation, and chain-growth against step-growth - have to be asked separately.

q: Is Kevlar a thermoset?
e: No cross-links, so not a network. It has no melt either, decomposing near 500 C and spun from solution.

q: What are the two monomers of a polyester, read backwards?
e: Cut the acyl C-O bond, leaving the oxygen on the alcohol side, and check each fragment has two reactive sites.

q: What happens to a stretched rubber band when heated?
e: The entropic restoring force scales with temperature, unlike almost every other material.

q: Which of these is above its glass transition, and therefore rubbery, at room temperature?
e: Room temperature is roughly 20 C, so compare each Tg with that number. Rubber alone is above its transition, and with no crystallinity and only light cross-linking it is free to deform and spring back. The other three are all below their Tg, which is why they are rigid - and it is also why cooling rubber in liquid nitrogen turns it into a glass that shatters.

q: Rigid drainpipe and flexible flooring can both be made from PVC. What differs between them?
e: The polymer is the same on both sides, which is what makes the case worth remembering. Unplasticized PVC has a Tg near 80 C, well above room temperature, so it is a glass. Mixing in 30 to 40% of a phthalate diester spaces the chains apart and weakens the forces between them, dropping Tg below room temperature - so the same polymer is now above its transition in ordinary use. Nothing chemical has happened, which is why the plasticizer can leach out again and leave old PVC brittle.

q: What do bulky side groups do?
e: They raise Tg and slow crystallization. In polystyrene the random placement is what actually prevents packing.

q: HDPE sits about 140 degrees above its Tg at room temperature, yet it is rigid rather than rubbery. Why?
e: Passing Tg only frees the amorphous fraction; whether the sample then feels rubbery depends on what else is holding it together. In HDPE the crystallites tie the mobile chains to each other exactly as covalent cross-links would, and they keep doing so all the way to Tm at 135 C. The same is true of PET and nylon, which is the reason a polymer needs two transition temperatures rather than one.

q: Polyisoprene can be vulcanized with sulfur and polyethylene cannot. What is the structural reason?
e: Vulcanization needs somewhere for the sulfur to attack. Polymerizing a diene 1,4 leaves a double bond in every repeat unit of polyisoprene, and the C-H bonds next to it are allylic and therefore weak - the same weakness that made allylic radicals easy to form in earlier chapters. A saturated hydrocarbon chain offers nothing comparable, so the double bond left over from the polymerization is not a leftover at all; it is the handle the whole process depends on.

q: A polymer backbone contains esters. What were the monomers?
e: Cut the acyl C-O bond of each ester: OH to the acid side, H to the alcohol side.

q: A disconnection gives a fragment with one reactive group. What does that mean?
e: Every chain-forming monomer must have two, which is what let it join on both sides.

q: How do you check a polyester disconnection by atom count?
e: One water per ester bond, and a diacid-plus-diol repeat unit has two. PET: 166 + 62 - 192 = 36.

q: Why is polyethylene not chemically recyclable?
e: No bond hydrolysis can pick out from any other. Cracking it back to feedstock works, but that is pyrolysis, not selective cleavage.

q: What does an amorphous rigid polymer get its rigidity from?
e: PMMA through bulky side groups; polycarbonate through rigid bisphenol A units in the backbone.

q: You need a clear, rigid sheet that can be sterilized in an autoclave at 121 C. Which polymer, and why?
e: Two requirements have to be met at once. Clear means amorphous, which rules out HDPE whatever its melting point, because crystalline regions scatter light at every boundary. Rigid at 121 C means a Tg above 121 C, which rules out polystyrene - it would soften and distort at 100 C - and rules out plasticized PVC, whose plasticizer has already dropped its Tg below room temperature. Polycarbonate is amorphous because its bisphenol A backbone is too awkwardly shaped to crystallize, and that same rigid backbone puts its Tg near 150 C.

q: What happens to the carbonyl carbon during hydration?
e: A flat carbon turns tetrahedral, and the substituents that sat 120 degrees apart are squeezed to about 109 — which is why crowding decides where the equilibrium sits.

q: Toward nucleophiles, the reactivity order is:
e: Sterics and electronics point the same way, and the hydration table measures it.

q: Cyanohydrin formation is run with HCN plus a catalytic amount of cyanide. What goes wrong if only NaCN is used, with no HCN present?
e: Two species are doing two jobs. Cyanide attacks the carbonyl carbon and leaves an alkoxide, and something has to hand that alkoxide a proton or it simply expels cyanide again and the equilibrium never closes. HCN is the proton source, and giving it up regenerates cyanide for the next turn, which is what makes the cyanide catalytic. HCN alone fails for the opposite reason: with its carbon holding a hydrogen instead of a lone pair, it is a poor nucleophile.

q: Which is hydrated to a greater extent at equilibrium: acetophenone (PhCOCH3) or 2,2,2-trifluoroacetophenone (PhCOCF3)?
e: Three effects are in play and two of them are identical across the pair: both are ketones and both are conjugated with the same ring, so those cancel. What differs is the second substituent. A methyl donates weakly; a CF3 withdraws strongly through three C-F bonds, leaving the carbonyl carbon markedly more electron-poor and the hydrate correspondingly more favorable. CF3 is also the bulkier group, so this is a case where electronics beats sterics — the same reasoning that makes hexafluoroacetone essentially fully hydrated.

q: Starting from butan-2-one, which sequence gives 2-hydroxy-2-methylbutanoic acid?
e: Count the carbons in the target: one more than the ketone, and the new carbon is a carboxyl group sitting next to the old carbonyl carbon, which now holds an OH. That is a cyanohydrin whose nitrile has been hydrolyzed. Reduction would instead give a CH2NH2 and therefore an amino alcohol; a bisulfite adduct adds no carbon at all and just gives the ketone back; and hydration adds no carbon either.

q: Cyanohydrin formation is run near pH 8-10. Why that range?
e: CN- is the nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl, and HCN is the acid that protonates the alkoxide that results. Too acidic and almost everything is HCN, with too little cyanide to start; too basic and there is no HCN left to finish the job, and the alkoxide simply expels cyanide again.

q: Which reagent would you actually put over the arrow to convert butanal into butanoic acid?
e: The tests in this section are diagnostics rather than preparations, so the practical answers are KMnO4, Jones reagent and Ag2O. Jones is the workhorse: it is aqueous, so the aldehyde hydrates and the oxidation runs on to the acid. PCC is deliberately anhydrous and stops at the aldehyde, borohydride reduces rather than oxidizes, and Tollens’ would technically work but nobody burns stoichiometric silver to make an ordinary acid.

q: A molecule contains an aldehyde and, elsewhere, an alkene and a secondary alcohol. Which reagent oxidizes the aldehyde and leaves the other two alone?
e: Take the constraints one at a time. Hot permanganate cleaves the alkene, and Jones oxidizes the secondary alcohol to a ketone as well as taking the aldehyde up, so both are too indiscriminate. PCC is an alcohol oxidant that would also touch the secondary alcohol, and it is the wrong tool for the aldehyde in any case. Silver(I) is the mild option: it takes the aldehyde to the acid and ignores alkenes and alcohols, which is exactly why the expense is sometimes worth paying.

q: Tollens’ reagent oxidizes aldehydes cleanly. Why is it still the wrong choice for preparing a carboxylic acid?
e: A diagnostic reagent is built to be feeble and selective, so that a positive result means one specific thing — and feeble and selective is the opposite of what a preparation wants, where throughput and cost decide. Silver is consumed stoichiometrically, which settles the matter on its own. The basic conditions do give the carboxylate first, but that is undone by acidifying on workup, so it is not the real objection; and leaving alkenes alone is a virtue, not a fault.

q: Why does fructose give a positive Benedict's test?
e: Through an enediol, which is why a free anomeric carbon rather than an aldehyde is the real test.

q: An unknown gives a silver mirror with Tollens’ reagent and no precipitate with Fehling’s solution. What is the best conclusion?
e: A positive Tollens’ needs a carbon carrying both an oxygen and a hydrogen, so an aldehyde or something in equilibrium with one is present; a ketone and a non-reducing sugar are both ruled out by it. The negative Fehling’s then looks like a contradiction, and it is resolved by remembering that Fehling’s has a known blind spot: it is unreliable with aromatic aldehydes. Treating a negative result from a reagent with a known weakness as evidence of absence is the trap being set.

q: Why is sucrose not a reducing sugar?
e: The glycosidic bond ties up both anomeric carbons, and a free one is what a positive test needs.

q: Air oxidizes an aldehyde by a radical chain. Which hydrogen does the chain abstract, and why that one?
e: Radical chains take whichever hydrogen leaves the most stable radical, and here that is the aldehyde C-H at roughly 88 kcal/mol — the weakest C-H in the molecule, because the acyl radical it leaves behind has its unpaired electron next to the carbonyl and delocalized onto it. Oxygen then adds to that acyl radical, and the resulting peroxy radical takes the same hydrogen from the next molecule, so the chain propagates. Acidity governs enolate chemistry, not radical abstraction, and a ketone has no such C-H at all.

q: Convert butan-1-ol into butanoic acid, stopping at butanal on the way to check it. Which two reagents, in order?
e: The first step has to stop one rung short, which means anhydrous conditions: with no water there is no hydrate, and with no hydrate the second oxidation has nothing with an O-H to attack. PCC does that. The second step wants the opposite — aqueous Cr(VI), so the aldehyde hydrates and is oxidized again — which is Jones. Running them in the other order finishes the job before the aldehyde can be isolated, borohydride reduces rather than oxidizes, and Tollens’ is far too weak to touch an alcohol.

q: Propanoic acid is treated with SOCl2, then with one equivalent of aniline (PhNH2) and no other base. What is the yield problem?
e: Each acylation releases one HCl. The most basic species in the flask is the amine, so it takes that proton and becomes an anilinium ion with no lone pair left to attack. One equivalent of amine therefore supplies only half an equivalent of nucleophile. The fix is a second equivalent of aniline, or one equivalent plus pyridine - basic enough to mop up HCl, too weakly nucleophilic to compete for the carbonyl.

q: Which target CANNOT be reached from a carboxylic acid by SOCl2 followed by one nucleophile?
e: Acyl substitution swaps the leaving group and keeps the carbonyl: an alcohol gives the ester, an amine the amide, a carboxylate the anhydride. A secondary alcohol would need the carbonyl reduced AND one new carbon substituent added, which is not a substitution at all - it needs a hydride and an organometallic, and it is a different kind of step.

q: How many equivalents of amine are needed for amide formation?
e: Trace the protons. The first equivalent of amine attacks the acyl chloride, chloride leaves, and the nitrogen still carries a proton it must lose - so one HCl is released per acylation. The most basic thing in the flask is the amine itself, so that HCl protonates a second molecule of amine and switches it off as a nucleophile. Two equivalents therefore give one equivalent of amide; one equivalent gives you half.

q: Pyridine attacks an acid chloride. Why does that not spoil the acylation?
e: Pyridine is a perfectly competent nucleophile toward an acid chloride: it attacks and gives an N-acylpyridinium ion. That is not a loss, because the acylpyridinium is itself a potent acylating agent — it hands the acyl group on to the amine, often faster than the direct route would. This is the whole basis of DMAP catalysis, where 4-dimethylaminopyridine speeds acylations up thousands of times by exactly this detour. And pyridine has no N–H, so unlike the amine it can never end up in the product. The sp² lone pair does explain pyridine's modest basicity (pKaH 5.2); it does not make pyridine a poor nucleophile.

q: Leaving group expelled from an anhydride:
e: Trace the tetrahedral intermediate: the nucleophile has added, and the oxygen now pushes back down and has to expel one of the two acyl-oxygen groups. What leaves is the other half of the anhydride, as a carboxylate. That anion is resonance-stabilized over two oxygens, so it departs willingly - but its conjugate acid is pKa about 5 against HCl's -7, which is exactly why an anhydride sits one rung below an acid chloride.

q: Standard acetylating agent:
e: Work down the ladder. Acetic acid needs activation before an amine or alcohol will acylate at all; ethyl acetate and acetonitrile are at or below the ester rung and far too sluggish. Acetic anhydride is the compromise: reactive enough to acylate an alcohol or an amine directly at room temperature, yet stable enough to weigh out in air, which an acetyl chloride is not.

q: A cyclic anhydride plus an amine first gives:
e: The amine attacks one of the two carbonyls and the tetrahedral intermediate expels the other as a carboxylate - the ordinary anhydride reaction. The difference is that the carboxylate is tethered to the amide by the carbon chain, so it cannot wander off. What you isolate is an amic acid: an amide at one end, a carboxylic acid at the other, on one molecule. Heat that and it loses water and closes to the imide.

q: SOCl2 converts alcohols into:
e: Same reagent, same idea, different substrate. An alcohol's OH is a terrible leaving group; SOCl2 converts it into a chlorosulfite, which is an excellent one, and chloride then displaces it to give the alkyl chloride. On a carboxylic acid the sulfur does exactly the same thing to the carboxyl OH. In both cases the by-products are SO2 and HCl, both gases, so the reaction is pulled to completion.

q: How does esterification via an acid chloride differ from Fischer?
e: Compare the leaving groups. Fischer esterification has to expel water and can re-form the acid just as easily, so it settles at an equilibrium near 65% and must be driven with excess alcohol or by removing water. Acylation of an alcohol by an acid chloride expels chloride, which is far too weak a base to come back and attack the ester, so the reaction runs to completion and needs no acid catalyst.

q: Which sequence converts benzyl bromide, PhCH2Br, into 1-phenylpropan-2-one, PhCH2COCH3?
e: Count first: seven carbons in, nine out, so two have to be added and the product is a ketone. Cyanide adds one by SN2 on the primary benzylic bromide, giving PhCH2CN. A methyl Grignard then adds once to the nitrile carbon - it cannot add twice, because the intermediate is an imine anion rather than a carbonyl - and aqueous workup hydrolyzes that imine to the ketone, which is where the second carbon came from. Route 1 gives an amine, route 3 an acid, and route 4 adds only one carbon.

q: Converting a nitrile into an amide counts as:
e: Count the bonds to heteroatoms on the carbon in question. A nitrile carbon has three, all to the same nitrogen; an amide carbon has three too - two to the carbonyl oxygen and one to nitrogen. Same count means same oxidation level, so adding water across the triple bond is a sideways move along the rung and needs no oxidant. Carry on under the same conditions and hydrolysis goes one step further to the acid, still on the same rung.

q: An unknown C4H7N shows a sharp medium IR band at 2247 cm-1 and no absorption between 1650 and 1800 cm-1. Which structure fits?
e: Two of these can be thrown out on the formula alone: butanamide is C4H9NO and but-1-yne is C4H6 with no nitrogen at all. That leaves two genuine C4H7N isomers, and only the spectrum separates them. C4H7N has two degrees of unsaturation, and both a C-N triple bond and a C=C plus a C=N account for exactly two, so counting does not settle it. The 2247 band does. The 2500-2000 window is almost empty in an ordinary spectrum, and a sharp medium band there means a triple bond - a nitrile, since the alkyne is already gone. The imine CH2=CHCH2CH=NH has nothing to put at 2247 and would instead show a C=N stretch near 1670, which the stem explicitly rules out by reporting nothing between 1650 and 1800. So the answer is butanenitrile, and notice that the negative evidence - an empty region - did as much work as the peak that is there.

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane + NaCN in DMSO, heated. Major product?
e: Start with what cannot happen: three alkyl groups shield the tertiary carbon, so there is no backside attack and no SN2, which takes the nitrile off the table however good a nucleophile cyanide is. DMSO then removes the other escape route — there is no water to solvolyze the halide, so no tertiary alcohol. That leaves elimination. Cyanide is a weak base (HCN pKa 9.2) and a poor one for E2, but with heat and nothing competing it is enough, and Zaitsev gives the more substituted alkene. Notice how much work the solvent is doing: run the same halide in hot aqueous ethanol and solvolysis takes over and you get mostly the alcohol — and still no nitrile. That is the standing limit on cyanide chain extension: primary substrates work, secondary are poor, tertiary give none of the nitrile at all.

q: Dehydrating a primary amide gives:
e: Dehydration removes H2O from RCONH2, and the carbon ends up with three bonds to nitrogen instead of two to oxygen and one to nitrogen - the same count either way. So it is a move along the rung, not a reduction, which is why SOCl2 or P2O5 does it and no reducing agent is involved. Run it the other way with water and heat and the nitrile hydrates back to the amide.

q: RCN with aqueous H3O+ and heat gives:
e: Through the amide, and no oxidant is needed because it is a move along the rung.

q: Nitrile hydrolysis passes through:
e: Water adds across the C-N triple bond to give first an imidic acid, which tautomerizes to the amide - and the amide is a real, isolable compound: stop at milder conditions and that is what you get. Push with more heat and more acid or base and the amide is hydrolyzed in turn to the carboxylic acid. Two acyl substitutions in series, both sideways moves on the same oxidation rung.

q: Why does DIBAL-H stop after a single hydride?
e: One hydride adds to the nitrile carbon and the product is a metalated imine anion. An anion is not an electrophile, so there is nothing left for a second hydride to attack, however long you wait or how much reagent you add - the aldehyde only appears when water hydrolyzes that anion on workup. Contrast LiAlH4, which is not stopped by anything: rationing it to one equivalent does not give an aldehyde, it gives a mixture. The reagent is crippled, not rationed.

q: RX to RCN to RCOOH accomplishes:
e: Follow the carbon. Cyanide does an SN2 on RX and the CN carbon is new, so RCN has one more carbon than RX. Hydrolysis then converts that same carbon into the COOH carbon without adding or losing any, since a nitrile and an acid sit on the same oxidation rung. Net result: one carbon longer, finishing as an acid. The Grignard-plus-CO2 route achieves the identical extension, and you pick between them on what else the substrate carries.

q: Which conditions give clean monohalogenation?
e: The halogen makes the carbonyl harder to protonate, so the second enol forms more slowly.

q: Why does base halogenation run past one halogen?
e: Halogen stabilizes the next enolate's charge, so each step speeds up the one after.

q: 3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-one, CH3COC(CH3)3, is treated with excess I2 and NaOH, then acidified. What is isolated?
e: The only alpha carbon carrying hydrogens is the methyl attached straight to the carbonyl, so base iodinates it three times and hydroxide then adds to the carbonyl and expels the CI3 group. What is left is the acyl fragment, (CH3)3C-CO2H. Count the carbons: six in, five out, because the haloform reaction always costs one.

q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone is treated with one equivalent of Br2 in acetic acid. Where does the bromine end up?
e: Under acid the reaction runs through the enol, and the two enols are free to equilibrate, so the more stable of them - the more substituted one - is the one that reacts and it decides where the halogen lands. That is C2. It is the same more-substituted-is-more-stable logic used for thermodynamic enolates, arriving one section early.

q: You need to convert butanoic acid into 2-aminobutanoic acid. Which sequence does it?
e: A carboxylic acid has essentially no enol of its own, so direct halogenation fails in acid and in base alike. Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky makes the acyl bromide with PBr3 first; that enolizes, brominates at the alpha carbon, and exchanges back to give 2-bromobutanoic acid. Ammonia then displaces the bromide by SN2, in excess because the amino acid product is itself nucleophilic. The product is racemic.

q: Which of these gives a NEGATIVE iodoform test?
e: The test reports a CH3CO fragment, or a CH3CH(OH) fragment that alkaline hypoiodite oxidizes into one. 3-Pentanol is CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2CH3: its carbinol carbon carries two ethyl groups and no methyl, so oxidation gives 3-pentanone, which has no methyl on the carbonyl and can never form a CI3 to expel. The other three all carry the reported fragment.

q: LDA at room temperature - does its own deprotonation reverse and hand the proton back to the base?
e: LDA's deprotonation does not reverse at any temperature, so warmth alone cannot undo it - that is the point of the question. A separate route is still open at room temperature, though: the diisopropylamine LDA generated can shuttle protons between the two enolates, which erodes the regiochemistry over time. An irreversible base, and a route still open.

q: What lets the two enolates interconvert?
e: Leftover ketone or the amine the base generated will do it; NaH is irreversible and still thermodynamic.

q: Why does an enamine stop after one alkylation?
e: No nucleophilic carbon is left and no base is present to restore one, so a second alkylation is impossible.

q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone is added to one equivalent of LDA in THF at -78 C, and iodomethane is then added. What is the major product?
e: LDA at -78 C with the ketone added to the base gives the kinetic enolate, formed at C6 - the open CH2 with two hydrogens. Nothing in the flask can equilibrate it, so C6 is still the nucleophilic carbon when CH3I arrives and the new methyl lands there. Under NaOEt in ethanol at room temperature the same two reagents give 2,2-dimethylcyclohexanone instead.
