q: 2-Methylcyclohexanone is treated with NaOEt in ethanol at room temperature, then with iodomethane. What is the major product?
e: Ethoxide's deprotonation reverses, so the two enolates interconvert and the population collects in the more stable one, the trisubstituted C1=C2 enolate. Alkylation therefore happens at C2, the carbon that already carries a methyl, giving the quaternary 2,2-dimethyl product. Ethoxide being too weak to deprotonate completely is not a problem here; it is the whole mechanism of thermodynamic control.

q: A chemist forms the kinetic enolate of 2-methylcyclohexanone with LDA at -78 C, then lets the flask warm to room temperature for an hour before adding the elect
e: LDA's deprotonation never reverses, so that route really is shut. But forming the enolate also generated a full equivalent of diisopropylamine, which is a proton donor, and warming lets it carry a proton from one alpha carbon to the other. The cold in the recipe is there to stop the amine, not to stop the base.

q: You want 2-benzyl-6-methylcyclohexanone from 2-methylcyclohexanone and benzyl bromide. Which conditions?
e: The benzyl group has to land on C6, the unsubstituted carbon, which means the kinetic enolate: LDA, one equivalent, -78 C, with the ketone added to the base. NaOEt and NaH are both equilibrating conditions that leave a route open between the two enolates, so they alkylate at C2. Adding LDA dropwise to the ketone instead gets the base right and the technique wrong: dripping LDA into a flask of ketone leaves un-deprotonated ketone in solution, and free ketone shuttles protons between the two enolates until the more substituted one wins. The halide is fine either way, since benzylic halides are excellent SN2 partners for an enolate.

q: Why does ammonia plus RX give mixtures?
e: Each added alkyl group pushes electron density onto nitrogen, so the product outruns the ammonia still in the flask.

q: Direct alkylation of ammonia delivers what?
e: Relative rates decide it, so adding less halide does not help; only a big excess of ammonia biases it.

q: You need pentan-1-amine, CH3(CH2)4NH2, and the only carbon source on the shelf is 1-bromobutane. Which sequence works?
e: Count first. 1-Bromobutane has four carbons and the target has five, so the route must ADD one. Azide and Gabriel both hand back exactly the skeleton you put in, so both would give butylamine, one carbon short, and excess ammonia has the same problem plus a mixture. Cyanide brings the extra carbon: 1-bromobutane plus NaCN gives pentanenitrile, and LiAlH4 turns the nitrile carbon into the CH2 bearing nitrogen.

q: Which of these halides would give the best yield in the alkylation step of a Gabriel synthesis?
e: The step is an SN2, so tertiary halides give only alkene, a secondary one gives poor yields with elimination alongside, and bromobenzene is an aryl halide, which does not do SN2 at all.

q: Which single reagent converts butanamide, CH3CH2CH2CONH2, into butylamine?
e: LiAlH4 reduces the amide C=O all the way to CH2, so four carbons go in and four come out: butanamide gives butylamine. Br2/NaOH is the Hofmann rearrangement, which takes the same starting material to PROPYLamine by expelling the carbonyl carbon as CO2 - one substrate, one carbon's difference, decided entirely by the reagent.

q: (R)-2-bromobutane is treated with NaN3, then with H2 over Pd. What is the product?
e: Azide displacement is an SN2: the nucleophile attacks the backside of the C-Br carbon and the configuration inverts. Reducing the azide to the amine never touches that carbon, so the inversion survives into the product. Note that the R/S letter may or may not flip with it - check the CIP priorities separately from the geometry. This control is a reason to pick azide over reductive amination, which builds the bond on a flat C=N and gives a racemic product.

q: 2-Amino-2-methylbutane, (CH3)2C(NH2)CH2CH3, is exhaustively methylated and then heated with Ag2O and water. What is the major alkene?
e: The nitrogen sits on C2, so the beta carbons are the two methyls on C2 and the CH2 of the ethyl group. Taking a hydrogen from a methyl gives 2-methylbut-1-ene, disubstituted; taking one from the CH2 gives 2-methylbut-2-ene, trisubstituted and more stable. Zaitsev would pick the trisubstituted one; Hofmann conditions do not, because the bulky trimethylammonium group shields the more substituted side.

q: How many equivalents of CH3I does 2-aminobutane take?
e: Each equivalent alkylates the lone pair in an SN2; the ammonium salt that results still has an N-H, which a base removes to hand back a neutral, more substituted amine that goes again. The count is the number of N-H hydrogens plus one, so a primary amine takes three.

q: A trialkylamine is treated with H2O2 to give the amine oxide, then heated to 150 C. Compared with a Hofmann elimination, what is different?
e: This is a Cope elimination. The amine oxide's own oxygen removes the beta hydrogen through a flat five-membered transition state, so the C-H and the C-N that break must be on the SAME side - syn-periplanar, the opposite geometric requirement to E2. No hydroxide or other base is needed. The regiochemistry, though, comes out the same as Hofmann: the less substituted alkene, for the same steric reason.

q: Exhaustive methylation then Ag2O and heat converts PhCH2-CH(NH2)-CH3 mainly into PhCH=CH-CH3, not into PhCH2-CH=CH2. Why?
e: Hofmann regiochemistry usually comes from two effects that agree: the bulky leaving group makes the hindered side hard to reach, and the positive nitrogen acidifies the beta hydrogens so the C-H breaks ahead of the C-N. Here one beta position is benzylic, its hydrogen is much more acidic, and removing it gives a conjugated alkene - so the acidity effect wins and the more substituted product forms. The real rule is the most acidic ACCESSIBLE beta hydrogen.

q: Which of these is NOT a reason exhaustive methylation is required before the elimination can happen?
e: The nitrogen stays sp3 throughout - a quaternary ammonium nitrogen has four sigma bonds and is tetrahedral. The other three are genuine consequences of quaternization: what departs is now a neutral trialkylamine rather than R2N-, the positive charge acidifies the beta hydrogens and gives the transition state E1cb character, and the bulk of the N(CH3)3 group is what shields the more substituted beta carbon.

q: An unknown amine consumes one equivalent of CH3I on exhaustive methylation and releases its nitrogen after a single round of Ag2O and heat. What is it?
e: Two independent readings. One equivalent of CH3I means no N-H hydrogens at all, so the amine is tertiary. One round of elimination freeing the nitrogen means only one C-N bond held it to the fragment being degraded, so the nitrogen was not in a ring - a ring would take two rounds, because the first elimination only opens it.
